1939-05-04.text: WASHINGTON, May 4. —Sen. Byrnes (D-SC) said today London had advised the United States that Great Britain was interested in negotiating a barter agreement for American cotton. Byrnes recently outlined a plan by which this country would barter surplus cotton for rubber and tin held by Great Britain and other countries. Preliminary negotiations have been under way in London. The South Carolina senator told reporters today the barter proposal was “meeting a favorable reception in London.”

LONDON— (U.P) —Trade barter negotiations have been opened between Great Britain and the United States, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain announced today in the House of Commons. The primary exchange would be tin and rubber for United States cotton and wheat.

London, May 4 (A). -- Prime Minister Chamberlain urged the House of Commons today to enact the military training bill, estimating conscription will give the government “something in the neighborhood of 800,000 men altogether” over a three year period. Chamberlain spoke as labor reiterated opposition to conscription and as British attention turned toward Poland and Soviet Russia. The sudden resignation of Maxim Litvinoff as Soviet Russia's Foreign Affairs Commissar cast doubt on the results of British-French efforts to bring Soviet Russia into the new security system. The British labor party and trades union council issued a joint statement announcing the decision to oppose the government's move to conscript 20 year old youths. Chamberlain announced conscription did not apply to Ireland.

Statesmen of Europe’s contending alliances looked anxiously to Moscow today for indications of any shift in Soviet Russia's foreign policy following the sudden resignation of Maxim Litvinoff, foreign affairs commissar. Litvinoff, who had been an important figure in international conferences for nearly 20 years, was “released from his duties at his own request” last night and Vyacheslaff Molotoff, premier and right-hand man of Joseph Stalin, took over his work. Britain sought to determine the effect this would have on the British-French effort to bring Russia into their new security system. Many Frenchmen who have dreaded an understanding between Germany and Russia feared Litvinoff's resignation might mean a change in that direction. Nazis hailed with enthusiasm the retirement of Litvinoff, who has been one of the main targets of Nazi propaganda, partly because he is Jewish. At the same t

LONDON, May 4 (®)—A wave of bombing incidents in four cities today followed the sentencing yesterday of two Irish republican army members for an attempt to blow up the Hammersmith bridge in London. Hundreds of theatergoers rushed from two buildings in Liverpool after tear gas bombs exploded under the seats. A bomb shattered part of a house in Birmingham. Shortly afterward explosions wrecked four shop fronts in Coventry. Two shops in a north London district were shattered by blasts. A policeman at another shop found a bomb in time to prevent its exploding. Fifteen persons were taken to hospitals for treatment at Liverpool, where authorities expressed the view the bombings were reprisals for the sentencing of two members of the outlawed IRA which wants all Ireland's connections with Britain severed.

Berlin, May 3.—(#)—Germany moved swiftly today to forestall inclusion of northern European states in the British-French bloc and at the same time sought to isolate Poland, now anxiously considering German demands. Proposals have been sent to six Scandinavian and Baltic countries for bilateral pacts of nonaggression which foreign office quarters indicated involved pledges, either specific or implied, on the part of those countries not to favor any other group of nations. What Chancellor Hitler has launched is a bold diplomatic offensive to destroy what he considers British and French efforts to encircle his country, and to cripple Poland because she refused what he considers a generous offer to settle the Danzig and Pomorze (Polish corridor) problems for at least 25 years. - WARSAW, Poland (WP) — Great Britain has urged foreign Minister Josef Beck to use moderation in his speech tomorrow answering Germany’s demands, and Beck is expected to proclaim Poland's readiness to continue a policy of friendship toward Germany, it was understood today. At the same time Beck will refuse to surrender Danzig as demanded by Adolf Hitler, it was said, and will propose negotiations.

LONDON—British and French negotiations for a military agreement with Russia were temporarily frozen today when the Soviet government failed to provide an explanation for replacing Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov with Premier Viacheslav M. Molotov. Speculation was rife in every European capital concerning the causes behind Litvinov’s retirement and its probable consequence. One fact was evident—it had a close connection to the prolonged negotiations for a British-French-Russian military alliance. The next move in these negotiations was up to Britain. She still is to reply to Russia’s three-point proposal: (1) That the three powers sign an alliance for mutual aid against aggression in Europe; (2) That they sign a military pact designating the exact form of collaboration applying to specific cases; (3) That they pledge their aid to Rumania, Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia in case of

1939-06-14.text: TIENTSIN, China, June 14.—Japanese officers tonight rejected British mediation attempts and widened their demands on the British while Japanese gendarmes, aided by Chinese police, blockaded the British and French concessions, whose approximately 120,000 population was virtually cut off from all supplies. The Japanese military took the position the dispute leading to the blockade—a British refusal to hand over to Japanese four alleged Chinese slayers of a Tientsin official—could not now be settled merely by relinquishing the accused Chinese. The officers advanced five broad demands which they said were necessary if the dispute were to be settled. Statement Is Issued A Japanese statement said: “The British must: first, discontinue protecting anti-Japanese and communistic elements; second, cease supporting Chinese currency; third, cease hoarding goods in Tientsin, thereby causing price incr

TIENTSIN, China.—(U.P.)—Japan, clamping down a progressively tighter military blockade on the British and French concessions today, forbade the entry of vegetables to the area and arrested an American newsreel photographer who sought to film blockade activities. From a comparatively minor dispute between the Japanese and the British, the Tientsin situation had become the first move in a determined big scale Japanese campaign to force the western nations to cooperate in the fight of Japan against China. Four hundred American civilians and 223 United States Marines under Col. William G. Hawthorne were involved in the blockade, along with 6,000 other foreigners and 100,000 Chinese. Britons, particularly, were sought out for special attention. Some of them were forced to remove their socks as the Japanese searched them.

WASHINGTON, June 13—(AP)—By a strictly party vote, the house foreign affairs committee today approved the new administration neutrality bill, a measure so drawn that if war should come to Europe, America’s vast resources would conceivably be available to Great Britain, France and their allies. The legislation, denounced by its foes as “unneutral” and likely to drag the United States into the first foreign conflict that comes along, goes next to the house proper. Action there is planned for late next week. House Leaders Confident Leaders were confident the house would approve the bill, but readily conceded its chances in the senate were of a different sort. There the old isolationist bloc was waiting to fight the measure to the end, and a filibuster against it was considered much more than a possibility. LONDON, June 14—(U.P)—Japan was reported today to have rejected a British proposal tantamount to United States mediation in the Tientsin dispute, before launching a blockade of British commerce. As the cabinet considered the blockade and cautious statements were made to parliament, it was revealed that Great Britain had suggested to Tokio that United States Consul-general John K. Caldwell should act as third member and chairman of a special conciliation tribunal, to have one British and one Japanese member. This tribunal would have decided whether four Chinese accused of assassinating a customs official should be turned over to the Japanese. The British hoped that in consideration of United States interests in Tientsin and elsewhere in China Caldwell’s nomination would have been accepted by Japan. WASHINGTON—American moths, not British bombshells, have tattered the original Star Spangled Banner. On this, the 162nd anniversary of the adoption of the Stars and Stripes as the American flag, the piece of bunting that inspired Francis Scott Key to write the National Anthem isn't exactly unscathed. True, there are a few penetrations described as bullet holes, but those are nothing compared to the jagged spots which are monuments to the obesity of forgotten moths. The forage on the famous flag by insects is at an end, however, now that it has come under the careful guardianship of the Smithsonian Institution. The institution got the Star Spangled Banner from Eben Appleton of New York, grandson of Col. George Armistead, the heroic commander of Ft. McHenry, Baltimore. London, England, June 14—(?)— Prime Minister Chamberlain told the House of Commons today that he had asked the German government to withdraw its consul from Liverpool as a result of the consul’s alleged connection with a recent espionage case. Chamberlain said that after studying the court records he had to accept the conclusion that the German consulate in Liverpool was implicated in a case in which it was alleged that a man named Joseph Kelley had been assisted in making contact with foreign agents to whom plans of a government factory were sold. “We have therefore requested the German government to withdraw Consul Herr Reinhardt,” he said. “The request was made two days ago.” (Walther Reinhardt, the consul in question, had consular positions in Montevideo, Rio de Janeiro, New York, Chicago and Zurich and in 1928 became consul in Seattle, later having transferred to Liverpool.)

Paris, June 14.—(4)—The Hamburg-American liner St. Louis was ordered today to proceed to Europe under full steam with her cargo of 907 homeless German-Jewish refugees who have been granted temporary havens in France, Britain, Belgium and the Netherlands. The orders were sent to the liner through her owners after Morris C. Troper, European chairman of the American Joint Distribution Committee, had an interview with Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet this morning. Some 700 of the refugees are awaiting entrance into the United States under immigration quotas. The liner had been idling in mid-Atlantic while the American committee sought temporary homes for the refugees who have been aboard her since she departed from Hamburg May 15. 1939-06-29.text: London.—(4?)—Winston Churchill, Britain's World War First Lord of the Admiralty, today seconded the fears of French Premier Daladier, who sent France’s parliament home yesterday with forebodings for Europe's peace. Churchill, in a luncheon address to the City Carlton Club, said he did not regard war as inevitable, but declared: “If one were to consider only the German preparations, the tone of their government-controlled press and the speeches of their party leaders, there could be no conclusion possible but that the worst would happen and happen quite soon. “I must consider—I think we must all of us consider—July, August and September as months in Europe in which tension will become most severe. “I am in entire accord with the French Prime Minister that we are in a period of danger more acute and more laden with ugly facts than any which we have ever known in the hard, disturbed period

Poland joined with Great Britain and France today in warning Adolf Hitler that any military thrust in Danzig would create grave danger to European peace. President Ignacy Mościcki speaking to the nation during a naval and military demonstration at the port of Gdynia declared Poland's desire for peace but emphasized that he never would give up the Polish Corridor pathway to the Baltic Sea. The Polish demonstration followed three days of indirect warnings and direct military precautions in Britain and France all designed to convince the Nazi Fuehrer that the Danzig quarrel must be settled peacefully to avoid danger of a general war. Even more important in the long run was a move by Britain and France to speed up formation of the European security front by making further concessions to Soviet Russia for the adherence of Moscow. London, June 28.—()-—Winston Churchill, one of the first British leaders to sound alarm over Germany's secret rearmament, today predicted a summer of tension and cautioned Adolf Hitler to pause and ‘consider well before you take the plunge into the terrible unknown.' Britain's wartime first lord of the admiralty echoed the grim forecast of crisis made in Paris yesterday by Premier Daladier. “I am in a position to know that a state of extreme vigilance is prescribed in many of our defense forces—particularly our air defense forces,” Churchill declared. Churchill, a conservative who sharply criticized the Chamberlain government while it followed the “appeasement” policy but now a supporter of its effort to build an alliance to face the Rome-Berlin axis, aired his views in a luncheon speech before the City Carlton club. “If one were to consider,” he said, “only the German preparations, the

TOKYO (—Japan has accepted Britain's proposal that they seek a settlement of their Tientsin crisis at a Tokyo conference table but Wednesday night important differences of view cropped out, British spokesmen, including Prime Minister Chamberlain, insisted that only local issues connected with the Japanese army's 15-day old blockade of the British and French concession at Tientsin would be considered. But Japanese, especially military leaders, indicated that demands for Britain's cooperation in Japan's program for a “new order in East Asia,” especially its economic phases, would figure in the negotiations. It was believed the talks would begin this week on the arrival of officials from Tientsin.

Jerusalem, June 29, (7P)—Eleven Arabs were slain and five wounded, authorities said by unidentified Jews, in six incidents today in the neighborhood of the Jewish city Tel Aviv. (A new wave of Arab-Jewish disorders started in the Holy Land after the British government announced a plan May 17 to establish a permanent Arab state in Palestine with a Jewish minority. In May 74 were killed and 110 wounded. On June 19, eighteen Arabs were killed by a bomb explosion in the Haifa market).

BERLIN, June 28—(4)—Britain has sent a note to Germany which officials said tonight expressed willingness to discuss a new British-German naval treaty to replace that of 1935 denounced by Chancellor Hitler April 28. The note, delivered by Sir Nevile Henderson, British ambassador, to Baron Ernest von Weizsäcker, state secretary in the foreign office, “also was said to have denied Britain was trying to ‘encircle’ Germany and asked a number of questions relating to naval matters. It was a reply to the German note of April 28 ending the 1935 treaty. Officials said that Germany’s answer would be made soon. In denouncing the naval treaty Hitler charged that by an “encirclement policy the British government has onesidedly withdrawn the basis for the naval treaty.”
Washington, June 29 (#)--The senate ratified today a treaty with Great Britain providing for the exchange of 600,000 bales of American cotton for British rubber.

1939-07-27.text: LONDON, (AP).—Scotland Yard put Prime Minister Chamberlain and other cabinet members under special guard today, held three men for examination and questioned scores in a search for terrorists following yesterday's series of five bombings. The explosions, in which one life was lost, occurred as the House of Commons adopted drastic measures to combat the outlawed Irish Republican Army. Afternoon newspapers said Scotland Yard was looking for “a man with a slouch” who was believed seen yesterday at Kings Cross Station just before an explosion there with one and perhaps two companions. LONDON, July 27.—(AP)— Astronomers tonight will get the closest look at Mars they have had in 15 years but no one expected to find indications that the planet is peopled by mechanized monsters or little red men. Observers have been viewing Mars for some days already with important results and although tonight will mark Mars’ nearest approach on the 1939 flirtation with the earth—a mere 36,000,000 miles separating them—the observations will continue for some weeks. At Bloemfontein in South Africa, Dr. E. C. Slipher, American astronomer, who discovered indications last week of plant life on Mars, studied the ruddy planet Wednesday night but wind scarcely perceptible to the layman made the telescope sway so that the image danced too much for proper study. Slipher, however, took several photographs which will be added to the collection of the Lowell Observatory, Flagstaff, Arizona. Dr. W. H.

LONDON, July 26.— (4) — An outbreak of bombing attributed to the Irish Republican Army today wrecked a canal bridge near Liverpool, and shattered baggage checkrooms in two of London's largest railway stations. A fourth explosion in a Liverpool mailbox tore the front from a district post office. Spurred by the blasts at King’s Cross and Victoria railway stations, in which one person was fatally injured and nearly a score of others hurt, the House of Commons approved without division a bill to curb the I.R.A. and sent it to the House of Lords. The Liverpool explosions occurred several hours after the London blasts. Destruction of the wooden swing bridge at Liverpool blocked the Leeds Liverpool canal. Throughout England thousands of police were hurried to vital points to protect them against terrorism, following the two railway station explosions. The first London blast, just after noon at

PARIS, July 27. (AP)—General Joseph Edouard Doumenc, newly appointed member of the superior war council, was designated today to represent the French general staff in military conversations at Moscow with Russian and British commanders. General Doumenc will undertake this mission as soon as negotiations for a British-French-Russian mutual assistance treaty have been completed. Advices from Moscow and London indicated that an agreement was near, and might even be reached in a meeting in Moscow late today. French circles expected it before the weekend. When General Doumenc goes to Moscow he will be accompanied by aides from the French general staff.

LONDON, July 27. (4)—Possibility of Britain denouncing her treaty of amity and commerce with Japan and breaking off current negotiations in Tokyo on China policy was discussed in informed circles in London today. Belief was expressed the United States’ denunciation of her

LONDON (/) — Spurred by an angry British public, Scotland Yard directed a vast hunt today for terrorists who shed blood and destroyed property in a series of five bombings at the same time the House of Commons adopted drastic measures to combat the Irish Republican Army. Authorities said the explosions were in line with an I.R.A. “plans” which Home Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare described to the House of Commons Monday as calling for wrecking of key industries, blasting of Parliament buildings and pollution of water supplies. Police guards kept a close watch on railway and subway stations, on post-offices and other vulnerable points. Persons leaving packages in checkrooms were asked to submit them to inspection. Five men were seized for questioning in London and one in Liverpool, but authorities said none was being detained on specific charges. The most serious bombing yesterday was at busy

LONDON, (AP).— Ten persons were missing and 24 were rescued today from the French tanker Sunik which caught fire after a collision with the Swedish steamer Grangesberg in a dense fog in the English Channel about 50 miles south of Plymouth. The Grangesberg was badly damaged in the bows. She was trying to make Falmouth under her own power. Lloyd's reported the British steamer Dartford rescued 24 of the Sunik’s crew.

(United Press Staff Correspondent) London, July 27 —(UP)— Police reserves were mobilized all over England today to operate Scotland Yard's secret scheme DBD after four bombings ascribed to Irish terrorists. Special watch was made at ports on the west coast for Sean Russell, leader of the Irish Republican Army, who recently returned from the United States, in the belief that he might seek to come to England to lead terrorist operations. One man was killed and 40 persons were injured in bombings at King's Cross and Victoria railroad stations in London yesterday. At Liverpool an explosion damaged the Mt. Pleasant post office and a wooden bridge was blown up at Maghull, in the Liverpool suburbs. Man Killed, 15 Injured One man was killed and 15 persons were injured in an explosion at King’s Cross railroad station here. The man killed was Prof. Donald Campbell, a lecturer at Edinburgh Universi

1939-06-01.text: LONDON (UP)—The new British submarine Thetis on test trials off Birkenhead was reported “a few hours overdue” tonight and the British admiralty immediately began a search. The submarine, built by Cammell Laird and Co. at Birkenhead, carried members of the firm as she proceeded on acceptance trials. She carried out surface tests but after diving was not seen again. The Thetis was commissioned last March 4 at Portland. Her normal complement is 55 men.

LONDON, May 31 (4)—Thomas Smith, the second flier within two weeks to attempt a solo Atlantic crossing, apparently has joined his predecessor, Charles Backman, Swedish airman, and others before him who couldn't beat the long odds. The principal hope for the young Californian who tried to span the ocean in a 65-horsepower monoplane was that he had landed at some remote spot in Scotland or Ireland and had not been able to communicate with authorities. Then, too, there was the possibility he had been picked up at sea by some vessel without radio equipment. Smith took off from Old Orchard Beach, Me., at 2:47 a.m., CST, Sunday with enough fuel for from 36 to 42 hours of flight. Backman started May 15 from Bangor, Maine, for a non-stop flight to Sweden and has been unreported.

A “new stalemate in prolonged negotiations to bring Soviet Russia into the British-French front left London and Paris shocked but still hopeful today and brought smiles in Rome and Berlin. The deadlock was caused by the statement of Soviet Premier-Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov last night. He told the supreme Soviet, Russia’s parliament, that Britain’s proposals for a mutual assistance agreement—backed by France—said nothing about assistance to the “three countries on the northwestern borders of the U.S.S.R.” Presumably, therefore, Russia wanted guarantees for Finland, Latvia, and Estonia besides those countries already holding pledges of aid—Poland, Greece, Turkey, and Rumania. Molotov, however, kept London’s hope alive by acknowledging that Britain and France were taking a “forward step” in their efforts to build a front and by saying that negotiations are “not yet over.” German N

LONDON, June 1.—(4)—British official sources expressed belief today that Soviet Russia eventually would be brought into the British-French front but said Russia's insistence on guarantees for the Baltic states on her borders presented “a difficult problem.” There was no official comment on the speech by Vyacheslaff Molotov, Soviet Premier and Foreign Commissar, rejecting the latest British-French proposals but one spokesman pointed out that Molotov himself said negotiations still were under way. The foreign office awaited a formal note from Moscow before determining the specific points at variance. Molotov’s speech indicated the main point was how the proposed British-French-Soviet mutual assistance pact would apply to other European states. Molotov said it must guarantee all the countries on Soviet Russia's western borders—Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Poland and Rumania. The British-French

PARIS, June 1 (UP)—France was believed to have urged Great Britain in diplomatic consultations today to satisfy Soviet Russia's demand and extend the Anglo-French "peace front" guarantees to include the smaller Baltic states along Russia’s western frontier. Soviet Premier Molotov in a frank speech before the Supreme Soviet last night assailed the failure of Britain and France to include the Baltic buffer states, Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania in the network of anti-aggressive guarantees. French Foreign Minister Bonnet conversed at conference with Britain’s ambassador Sir Eric Phipps on Molotov's speech and was believed to have stressed the necessity of finding some immediate compromise solution to overcome Moscow's objections to the Anglo-French draft treaty for a tri-power military alliance. A French spokesman said that the French government for its part has no objection to satisfying Ru

LONDON, June 1 (4) — All available warships in the vicinity were ordered to search for the new British submarine Thetis today when she failed to reappear after a test dive and the tug accompanying her reported “something is amiss.” The submarine, built by Cammell Laird and Company at Birkenhead, carried members of the firm as she proceeded on acceptance trials. She carried out surface tests but after diving this morning was not seen again. Commissioned March 4. The Thetis was commissioned last March 4 at Portland. Her normal complement is 53 men. Officially described as a “patrol type” submarine, she has a displacement of 1,095 tons on the surface and 1,579 tons submerged. She is 265 by 26 by 12 feet. The Thetis was begun in 1936 and launched last year. She left the yard this morning for trials in Liverpool Bay beyond the lightship at the mouth of the Mersey River. The admiralty tersely

London, May 31 (#).— Hopes that Soviet Russia can be brought into the British-French bloc suffered a severe jolt tonight as a result of Moscow’s surprise rejection of Britain’s latest proposals. Some saw a ray of hope in the face that Soviet premier and foreign commissar, Vyacheslaff Molotoff, who announced the rejection in Moscow, did not rule out further negotiations, but the stinging implications of his speech before the Soviet parliament left little room for optimism. Complete Surprise His declaration came as a complete surprise to British officials, who had been expressing confidence for the past week that they had evolved a formula—with the help of the French—which would meet Russia's approval. Paris dispatches showed Russia’s stand was just as much a surprise in the French capital, where the foreign ministry declined immediate comment. British officials took note of Molotoff’s sta

1939-07-03.text: London, June 29 (AP)—Fears that a major crisis would be precipitated soon in Danzig were expressed today in Britain where a movement was under way to strengthen still further the nation’s reserve of trained manpower, The British press, which voiced fears that Nazis were “preparing mischief” this weekend in Danzig, gave prominence to Winston Churchill's prediction yesterday of a summer of tension and to Anthony Eden's advice that Britain “be tough ... talk tough... act tough” to keep peace. Adolph Hitler’s Berlin newspaper, Voelkischer Beobachter, ridiculed reports of impending Nazi action as “wild rumors over an immediate Nazi coup in Danzig.” But overnight reports were received here from Warsaw that well-trained Germans were being organized into a Danzig “Free Corps” for any emergency in that free city, which Nazis say will “come home” to the Reich, Britain awaited an official Nazi repl

The diplomatic curtains covering the specific reasons for British and French official fears of a Nazi coup in Danzig were partially drawn aside today when Prime Minister Chamberlain told the House of Commons his government had received reliable reports of “intensive measures of a military character” in the free city. Furthermore he said “a large and increasing number of German nationals have recently arrived in the free city ostensibly as tourists and a local defense corps is being formed under the name of Heimwehr.” Chamberlain’s statement put the stamp of officialdom on reports which could not be confirmed in their entirety in the free city. Danzig officials Saturday said the Heimwehr was composed of Danzig black uniformed S.A. men who had volunteered for police duty. Although it was admitted special “precautionary measures” had been taken it was denied any Germans with or “without a u

Danzig—4—The Bank of Danzig announced today the blocking of interest payments and amortization services on all foreign loans to the free city. Bond holders in the United States, England and The Netherlands are principally affected. All Danzig payments to foreigners will go into blocked accounts just as is done in Germany and investors must receive in return certificates on Danzig banks for the amounts due them. Transfer of payments abroad is impossible.

TIENTSIN, China, July 3. (UP) — Japanese spokesman said today that a compromise between the Japanese and British at Tientsin was impossible and that the Japanese might resort to force unless the British accepted demands made by the Japanese provisional government at Peiping. The demands of the so-called provisional government which purports to rule Northern China included joint control of the British-French concession at Tientsin by concessional authorities and the provisional government; permission for the provisional government to inspect banks in the business concession and rigorous control of publications.

Great Britain hammered home to the world today the dangers of Europe's sorest spot—the Free City of Danzig—in an effort to block Nazi expansion in eastern Europe. While British and French negotiations at Moscow sought to complete an alliance bringing the Soviet Union into the security front, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain announced in the House of Commons that a free corps was being formed in Danzig, after a large influx of Germans. Developments included: Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain reported to King George on the international situation, reviving interest in reports that he might soon include Winston Churchill and Anthony Eden—both publicly denounced by Adolf Hitler—in the cabinet, but political sources still wondered if Chamberlain would so openly challenge Hitler at present. The British and French governments continued a strong campaign of public demonstrations and speeches

(By the Associated Press) London, July 2 — British official circles said today Great Britain, France and Poland had agreed that any attempt to bring Danzig into Germany, either from the inside or outside, would be resisted by force. France and Poland already have informed the Berlin government of their decision, these circles said, and Britain will make her position clear this week through diplomatic channels. This disclosure came as Prime Minister Chamberlain bluntly reaffirmed that the British were prepared “to throw our whole strength into the scale, if need be, to resist aggression” against Britain or states whose independence she has guaranteed. Making a brief speech on civil defenses which was broadcast throughout the empire, the Prime Minister said: “We are living in critical and dangerous times. We are ourselves a peaceful nation and we desire no quarrels with anyone. “But let no

Rumors of Coup The prime minister announced that the government has received information of the arrival in Danzig of Germans, ostensibly as tourists, and that a fighting "free corps" was being formed. There have been repeated rumors of a possible coup in Danzig by the defense corps. Chamberlain did not say specifically that Britain would defend Danzig in case of an internal putsch rather than outside aggression from Germany, but the government has indicated in the past that if Poland resists a putsch, Britain will come to the rescue.

In Tokyo yesterday, the stage was set for what many expect may be one of the most momentous conferences in the history of the Orient, the British-Japanese discussions growing out of the Tientsin controversy. The chief delegates of the two nations, Major G. A. Herbert, British consul in Tientsin, and Sotomatsu Kato, newly slated to be Japan’s minister-at-large in China, arrived in Tokyo and immediately were closeted with superiors. There were indications the conference would be opened Tuesday. Some observers believed the conference would provide the instrument by which Japan would make her first great assault on the entire question of foreign concessions, (Continued on Page 3.)

1939-04-20.text: London, April 19 (#).—Britain offered a “no encirclement” pledge to Adolf Hitler tonight as the cabinet urgently stepped up its drive for more arms and allies. Foreign Secretary Viscount Halifax, discussing the “cry of encirclement” raised by Germany and Italy against the French-British defensive front, declared: “I would be prepared at any time to give a most solemn understanding on the authority of the government that no such idea would ever find a place in British policy.” Negotiations Pursued Lord Halifax said negotiations with Soviet Russia for an air pact were being actively pursued and he hoped “recognition of different points of view” would permit the “progress that we all desire.” It was reported reliably that, as part of the armaments speed up, Prime Minister Chamberlain had agreed to set up a department of supply to equip the expanding British army. LONDON, April 20.—(#)—Prime Minister Chamberlain announced in the House of Commons today that a new ministry of supply would be established to expedite the manufacture of arms for Britain's expanding army. Leslie Burgin, at present minister of transport, was appointed head of the new ministry with rank as a cabinet member. It had generally been expected that Winston Churchill, war-time minister of munitions who has been recommending a ministry of supply for over a year, would get the post. Presumably to quiet rumors that the new ministry would not have full powers over the supply of munitions, the prime minister announced that it would be a ministry of supply “in the full sense.” Chamberlain will offer a bill to establish the ministry. While Britain pushed forward preparedness measures she waited for reaction to the offer yesterday by Foreign Secretary Viscount Halifax of a “no encirclem

LONDON, April 19. — (P) — Charges that a 30-year-old armaments worker sold vital secrets of a royal ordnance factory to Germany, aided by the German consul at Liverpool, were made at a court hearing today at Chorley, Lancashire. The defendant, Joseph Kelly, was accused of selling the factory site plan and other secrets stolen from the armaments plant for about $140. He was held for trial under the official secrets act. Prosecutor G. R. Paling said Kelly got in touch with the German secret service with the aid of the Liverpool consul and then went to Cologne, Germany, to deliver the secrets. The name of the German consul was not given in court and it was understood he no longer was in this country.

ISTANBUL, Turkey—U.P)—The newspaper Vakit asserted today that Turkish-British anti-aggression negotiations had been successfully concluded. It added that the news was not officially confirmed so far. Vakit said the British-Turkish understanding, unlike the British-French agreement, does not guarantee aid to Rumania and Greece but Turkey is joining in a combination with Rumania and Greece with a view to constituting a strong peace front in the Near East. Such a combination, the paper said, is not aimed against any particular state, but at assuring Turkey’s own safety and general peace.

PARIS, April 20 —(UP) Great Britain and France have informed Russia that they are prepared to conclude a three-power military assistance treaty with her, it was understood today. Ivan Maisky, Russian Ambassador to Great Britain, and Jacob Suritz, Russian Ambassador to France were notified that the offer would be submitted formally to Moscow soon and that it would provide for a three-power alliance regardless of whether Poland and Rumania accepted Russian protection. France and Great Britain already have guaranteed to protect Poland and Rumania but the latter two countries have not consented to give right-of-way to Russian troops who might want to attack Germany. It was said authoritatively that the British-French-Soviet agreement, which would be a revival of the old triple entente, had virtually been completed but that negotiations were still under way intended to smooth out the objectio

London, April 20—The British Government was placed on a virtual war basis today when Prime Minister Chamberlain announced the creation of a Ministry of Supplies to co-ordinate all the military resources of the nation. The Right Honorable Leslie Burgin, and present minister of transport, was named chief of the new government department. Chamberlain’s announcement to the House of Commons was greeted with enthusiastic cheers. For many months various party leaders have demanded a ministry of supplies as an essential step in preparing Britain for any armed eventuality. There was a minister of supplies in Britain during the World War, a post held for some time by Winston Churchill.

LONGVIEW, April 20.- (14)-— Lue English, owner of a trailer house that exploded yesterday, died today, bringing the death toll in the blast to three. Clotele Blackwell, 8, and Mrs. English died yesterday, Thomas Manier, 27, and Bodie Blackwell, 5, were not expected to live. Two other persons were injured less seriously. The explosion in the trailer parked off a highway seven miles from here apparently resulted from ignition of wet gas escaping from a stove.

1939-12-30.text: | LONDON, Dec. 29 UR Naval circles confirmed today that a German submarine has attacked a British battleship of the Queen Elizabeth class, killing three persons and causing “some damage.” The vessel, however, is “safe and proceeding on her course,” it was said. (In Berlin the German high command in a communique said that a German U-boat had torpedoed a British battleship of the Queen Elizabeth class off the west coast of Scotland.) BERLIN, Dec. 29 UP - A German high command communique said today that a German submarine west of Scotland had torpedoed a British battleship of the Queen Elizabeth class. The Queen Elizabeth class includes the Warspite, the Valiant and the Queen Elizabeth. All were built in 1913 or 1914 and have a displacement of 30,600 tons. Each carries from 1,100 to 1,200 men. London, Dec. 29—(4)—The British battleship torpedoed by a German U-boat limped into port under her own steam tonight, the Admiralty announced, with four missing and one of the crew seriously wounded. The missing men were believed killed when the warship, one of Britain’s 11 battleships, was damaged by a German submarine in the war at sea which thus far has cost the British 16 naval vessels. The Admiralty issued the following communique after the German high command had announced a British battleship of the Queen Elizabeth class had been torpedoed “west of Scotland” by a German submarine: “a torpedo attack has been made on a British battleship by a U-boat. Some damage was caused and three men were killed.” Name Not Disclosed Subsequently an unofficial statement distributed by British news agencies said “it has been ascertained from inquiry at the Admiralty” that the battleship concerned w

DUNDUIN, LC. 2d—lisi—peace proposals to the Finnish people were reported by London listeners have been broadcast today by a Russian station over the wavelength of the Finnish Lahti station, which temporarily went out of action during an air raid. The announcer said Russians wanted to end the hostilities as much as the Finns and that if a truce were reached the Karelian area would be returned to Finland, all Finnish workers would be given holidays with pay and large estates would be liquidated. (In the negotiations which preceded the war Moscow offered to cede Karelian territory in return for Finnish concessions.) Finnish circles in London said the proposals were ridiculous, that Finns already had paid holidays and that most of the land was owned by peasants.

By The Associated Press, Problems of the home front today occupied Britain, France and Germany as they faced a new year that finds Europe sundered by war on the western front and the Russian-Finnish battlefields. Dissension in Ireland and India were problems confronting Britain as well as how to keep the British workingman contented under wartime conditions. France set up a $5,480,000,000 war budget for 1940 to be borrowed from the French people and provided for new aviation and naval expenditures. Adolf Hitler in a New Year's message predicted 1940 would bring victory to Germany. Northern Ireland, a part of the United Kingdom, was disturbed by reports of extraordinary military precautions in neighboring Ireland and feared that civil strife was impending in the former Irish Free State. Leaves for all Irish officers were reported to have been canceled and 5,000 soldiers concentrated aroun

Paris. (/P)-France winds up the year 1939 with plans to spend almost five and a half billion dollars—all to be raised by loans—to wage war in 1940, and with hints from her premier of a European federation after the war. The French reported sinking a German submarine, with a British bombing plane helping a French warship, and reported successful forays into German territory on the western front east of the Moselle. Premier Daladier, in presenting the 1940 budget to the senate yesterday, asserted that the French-British economic union was “open to all.” A clause in the military expense bill published in today’s official Gazette authorizes eight million to contract expenditures for war purposes during 1940 totaling $5,480,442,000. The sinking of a German submarine by the combined efforts of a French warship and a British bombing plane was reported. French sources said the warship was escort

HELSINKI—Finns predict major battle imminent as Russia replaces inexperienced troops with veterans. PARIS—French report sinking of German submarine; parliament sets up $5,480,000,000 war budget for 1940. BERLIN—Germany reports scouting flights over England and France; Hitler in New Year's message says Germany fights to liberate Europe from English "oppression." BELFAST—Northern Ireland disturbed by reports of military precautions in Dublin, fears civil strife. LONDON—British working man seeks to avoid regimentation in wartime.

London, Dec. 30. (AP)—The Ford Motor Company announced today a “wartime family allowance” for employees with two or more dependents. To help meet increased living costs, workers on an hourly basis will receive two cents an hour additional, and those whose salaries are under $100 a month will receive approximately $3 more.

| Columbus, O., Dec. 29—Dr. Julian S. Huxley says warring nations of the world are today in about the ‘evolutionary stage of the almost brainless dinosaurs which vanished from the earth millions of years ago. The English scientist today reminded the American Association for the Advancement of Science that the dinosaurs had brains little larger than a baseball and just about enough sense to eat when they were hungry. Dr. Huxley appealed to “countries like the United States” which are technically equipped and are not involved in the present war to “begin building up planning organizations on a large enough scale to function as a social brain” in order that civilization proceed normally after the war and not end in chaos. 1939-04-27.text: BERLIN, April 27 (AP) — Nazis prepared today to give a lavish reception to Chancellor Hitler's Reichstag speech tomorrow and discounted Great Britain’s conscription measure as a political move intended to frighten Germany. The attitude of the controlled newspapers was that Britain may “arm up to the neck” if she wishes. Propaganda Minister Paul Joseph Goebbels, apparently angered by the tone adopted by British newspapers toward Germany, wrote a lengthy article in Hitler's Voelkischer Beobachter attacking Britain’s policy of a balance of power in Europe, and declaring: “Germany is no English protectorate, and the English would do well to conduct their dealings with us in the way in which dealings with a big power are generally conducted.” Speech Is Secret Members of the diplomatic corps, including the American charge d'affaires, Raymond H. Geist, are expected to crowd the diplomatic galle

LONDON (P)—Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain announced in the House of Commons today that the battleship Repulse, one of the strongest units of the British fleet, will not take the king and queen on their trip to Canada, as previously planned. Their Majesties will travel on the chartered liner Empress of Australia, Chamberlain said. The change was made because of the tense European situation. The government felt that the Repulse may be needed at any time for service in European waters. It has been pointed out that the Repulse is the only big gun ship in active service capable of overtaking and destroying the German “pocket” battleships. The king and queen will sail on May 6.

LONDON, April 27,--(4"—Prime Minister Chamberlain warned the Labor opposition in the House of Commons today against forcing a general election on conscription as he opened the debate on the emergency conscription bill he announced yesterday, “I foresee that matters might be pushed to such an extremity that this government would not have any other choice” than to order an election, he said amid Laborite cheers and counter-cheers from the government benches, “But surely,” he added, “a very heavy responsibility would rest upon those who force such a conclusion at this time. Would Mean Confusion “An election would leave the country in a state of confusion and uncertainty, postpone for what might be vital weeks measures which the government thought necessary, check the output of munitions vital to us at this time and distract the attention of those who are responsible for government departmen

DUBLIN, April 27—Eamon De Valera, prime minister of Eire, announced to the Dail Eireann today that he had cancelled his projected visit to the United States “in view of yesterday’s grave event.” This was a reference to the announcement by Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain in the House of Commons yesterday introducing compulsory military service. De Valera made arrangements as long ago as last December to visit the New York World's Fair soon after its opening, and also to confer with President Roosevelt.

Ivan Maisky, Soviet Russian ambassador to London, returning from important policy conversations in Moscow said today that Russia would “assist Europe in case of aggression.” Arriving at this Danish capital en route by air back to London, Maisky said: “I return very content. Russia’s position in a possible conflict is perfectly clear. We are going to assist Europe in case of aggression.” Maisky’s remarks were regarded as a strong indication of progress in the effort by Britain and France to enlist Russia fully in their coalition. This development was reported as Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet conferred with Sir Eric Phipps, British ambassador to Paris, before the Frenchman started conferences with Rumanian Foreign Minister Grigore Gafencu. Diplomatic circles said the British envoy had brought the report that Gafencu, in his earlier talks in London, had expressed Rumania’s opposition to immediate entry into mutual assistance pacts. Britain and France already have pledged their aid to Rumania in event her independence is attacked, but it is a one-way pledge which they would like to make reciprocal.
