| BON BAB4ABSABR BAY PARIS, April 10.—(UP)—France and Britain were understood tonight to have agreed fully to halt Premier Mussolini by force of arms if he tries to spread his hold in the Mediterranean.

1939-04-24.text: Chamberlain told the House of Commons Monday there was “no special significance” in the return of British Ambassador Sir Neville Henderson to Berlin. Chamberlain explained Sir Neville had been called home from Berlin originally to report on German annexation of Bohemia and Moravia and that after he had a short period of leave he had been instructed to return. The Prime Minister added this action did not mean Britain was recognizing Nazi annexation of Czecho-Slovakia territory or Italy's conquest of Albania. BERLIN—Return to Berlin of British Ambassador Sir Neville Henderson was followed Monday by official disclosure the German ambassador to London, Herbert Von Dirksen, would go back to his post “very soon.” Von Dirksen had been recalled to Berlin soon after Sir Neville was summoned to London to report on the German occupation of Bohemia and Moravia in the breakup of Czecho-Slovakia last

LONDON, April 24 (GP) - United States Ambassador John P. Kennedy was reported authoritatively today to be arranging a deal by which the United States would supply about 10,000,000 tons and more of bushels of wheat to Britain for a supply of rubber and tin.

BERLIN, April 24 (—The return to Berlin of British Ambassador Sir Nevile Henderson was followed today by official disclosure that the German ambassador to London, Herbert von Dirksen, would go back to his post "very soon." Von Dirksen had been recalled to Berlin soon after Sir Nevile was summoned to London to report on the German occupation of Bohemia and Moravia in the break-up of Czecho-Slovakia last month. Sir Nevile reached Berlin by the Nord express at 8:30 a.m. (1:30 a.m. cst) today. At that very moment Von Dirksen was understood to be packing his luggage for his return trip to London. In spite of the suddenness of Sir Nevile's return, the British embassy said no arrangements had been made for him to call at Wilhelmstrasse and that he was carrying no special message. Nevertheless, his reappearance in Berlin was deemed by the average German to constitute a triumph for German diploma

By The Associated Press Italy claimed a new "faithful" collaborator for the Rome-Berlin axis today in Yugoslavia, as Britain began vital talks with Rumania on the alignment of European power. Signs pointed to a climax Friday, when Adolf Hitler is expected to reject President Roosevelt’s appeal for at least ten years of assured peace. Interrupted diplomatic links between Germany and Britain were in process of restoration. Sir Nevile Henderson, British ambassador to Berlin, returned to his post sooner than expected. Prime Minister Chamberlain told the House of Commons that return of the envoy lacked "special significance." Nazis said that the German ambassador to London also would return to his embassy. A communique promising "faithful collaboration" of Yugoslavia with Italy and Germany was believed to have paved the way for further tightening of the axis line-up through a non-aggression p

A government spokesman confirmed that Sir Nevile Henderson, ambassador to Germany, had taken back to Berlin a message from the Chamberlain government, Points Include, It was indicated that the message, purposely delivered well in advance of Hitler’s speech to the Reichstag next Friday replying to President Roosevelt’s peace message, included: 1. Re-affirmation of belief that European problems can be settled by peaceful negotiations, 2. A suggestion that Mr. Roosevelt's appeal offers a dignified opportunity for pacification and that Britain therefore hopes Hitler will not flatly and finally r

LONDON, April 23.—(?)— Britain returned her ambassador to Berlin today sooner than had been expected in what was reported unofficially to be an effort to placate Reichsfuehrer Hitler before his vital speech next Friday in response to President Roosevelt’s peace appeal. At almost the same time, Romanian Foreign Minister Grigore Gafencu arrived from Berlin to open important talks. Britain and France have pledged their support to Romania in defense of her independence, ap oes Henderson Departs. Tall, elegant Sir Nevile Henderson left London by train six weeks after he had been called home from Berlin “to report” on Hitler's dissolution of Czechoslovakia. Hitler called home his ambassador to London, Dr. Herbert von Dirksen, the day after Britain's action. Only four days ago Foreign Secretary Viscount Halifax, in a speech to the House of Lords, declined to set a date for the ambassador's retu

| LONDON, April 24. - (U.P) Foreign diplomats heard today that Sir Nevile Henderson was returned as ambassador to Berlin to deliver a “final appeal” from the Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain to Adolf Hitler to adopt a constructive attitude towards President Roosevelt's peace proposals. Henderson, it was declared, will explain that if Hitler follows Chamberlain's advice Britain would be ready to assume the initiative for round table discussions of Germany's legitimate aspirations, but otherwise a move towards some form of conscription in Britain is most likely. Reply Due Friday Hitler is due to answer President Roosevelt before the Reichstag. In the House of Commons, Chamberlain dodged a barrage of questions about security negotiations in Europe, saying merely: “The government is maintaining close touch with other governments, including those of Turkey and the Soviet Union.” Statement U

(By The Associated Press) LONDON — Vital Rumanian-British talks start; cabinet puts finishing touches on Britain's largest peace-time budget. ROME—Italy draws Yugoslavia closer to Rome-Berlin axis in rivalry with British-French line-up for sway over smaller European nations. BERLIN—British Ambassador Sir Nevil Henderson returns; Germany reciprocates: Will send her ambassador, Herbert von Dirksen, back to London; Nazis see moderation in British policy. PARIS — French government strikes at propaganda in Alsace-Lorraine, outlaws three organizations; France reported to have urged Britain to adopt military conscription. ALETTA, MALTA—Authorities rush preparations for suddenly-announced cruise by more than 30 ships of British Mediterranean fleet in eastern Mediterranean.

1939-01-06.text: London, May 5 ()—The British government was reported authoritatively tonight to have agreed to formation of a British-French-Russian military alliance, but details still are under negotiation. The British also framed a counter-proposal to the Moscow suggestion for a reciprocal guarantee of Baltic and Black Sea states, feeling that so broad a guarantee to those states was not practical at the present time. The British further put forward a scheme under which the Soviet Union would support Rumania and Poland in the event of aggression against either nation. This course to bring Red Russia into the British-French front of nations was understood to have been decided upon at a 90-minute meeting tonight of the committee, attended by Foreign Secretary Viscount Halifax, Sir Samuel Hoare, Home Secretary, and Sir John Simon, Chancellor of the Exchequer. It was authoritatively stated that Britain’s

| LONDON, Jan. 6.—Premier Benito Mussolini has rejected a plea of President Roosevelt to open Ethiopia to Jewish refugees, an authoritative source disclosed today. However, Mussolini agreed to use his good offices with Fuehrer Adolf Hitler to get for Jews the right to take a reasonable amount of their wealth out of Germany.

LONDON, Jan. 5.—(@)— Totalitarian Germany and Italy stormed at President Roosevelt’s defense speech to Congress while European democracies hopefully viewed it today as a possible prelude to major changes in American foreign policy. Heads of every government in Europe studied the speech as one of the most important declarations coming from Washington since the world war. The Nazi and fascist press accused the president of playing domestic politics and of deserting the isolation policy laid down by George Washington. British and French said they were encouraged by the President's hints of changes in neutrality legislation and what they considered a veiled threat of boycotting aggressor nations. Officials in most capitals were reluctant to comment in view of the unstable European condition and Prime Minister Chamberlain's imminent visit to Premier Mussolini in Rome. Newspaper comment includ

Dublin, Jan. 5 - (AP) — Jack Kelly, inmate of a poorhouse, was fined £1,000 (about $5,000) today for acting as a bookmaker in the institution. The prosecution said the 3,000 men in the poorhouse spent $2,000 a year in penny bets on races. Kelly was given 14 days to pay his fine or start serving an indefinite sentence.

LONDON, Jan. 5—(AP)—Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain today acclaimed the sentiments expressed by President Roosevelt yesterday before Congress as fresh evidence of “the vital role of the American democracy in world affairs and its devotion to the ideal of ordered human progress.” David Lloyd George, wartime prime minister and Chamberlain's political enemy for 20 years, agreed with him in welcoming the American executive's address. Chamberlain interrupted a lengthy conference with Viscount Halifax, foreign secretary, over their visit January 11-14 in Rome to issue the following statement: “Nobody who is charged with the heavy responsibilities of government could fail to be impressed by the solemn words with which the President of the United States yesterday greeted the elected representatives of the American people. “In these islands, where there is so clear a realization that only thro
QUAKE IS FELT Lahore, India, Jan. 6.——An earthquake of considerable intensity today rocked parts of British Baluchistan, Northwestern India. No damage or loss of life was reported.

International News Service LONDON, Jan. 5.—In a move unprecedented in modern times, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain tonight formally thanked President Roosevelt on behalf of Great Britain for his message to Congress in which he lashed the dictators and marshalled the strength of democracy against intolerance and aggression.

(Sy 2480 ASSUCIALEG Press) London, Jan. 5.—What to do about drastic cuts in the price of wheat, caused by successive bumper crops for a number of years, will be discussed by representatives of the world's principal wheat nations at the international wheat conference opening here next Tuesday. The conference was called at the request of the United States, Great Britain, France and Australia. Twenty-one nations will be represented.

1939-08-05.text: (By the Associated Press) | A British-French military mission left for Moscow today as Japanese expressed “extreme irritation” over Prime Minister Chamberlain’s declaration that a British fleet might steam to the Orient “in certain circumstances.” “Britain is playing a dangerous game,” said a Tokyo war office spokesman who interpreted Chamberlain’s words in the House of Commons yesterday as a “shrewd remark designed to intimidate Japan.” Japanese newspapers printed Chamberlain's statement that Britain has not “in the Far East a fleet superior to that of the Japanese” but deleted the warning that naval reinforcements might be sent. For the third successive day there was no meeting of British-Japanese negotiators who have been trying to solve differences between the two nations in the Far East. The British-French military mission is to open staff talks with Soviet military leaders consider

United Press Staff Correspondent London, Aug. 4—(UP) — Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, asserting that “it makes my blood boil” to hear of the stripping of Britons by Japanese soldiers and of other indignities, told the House of Commons today that Britain may be compelled to send her fleet to the far east. Although he spoke of “certain circumstances” which might force the dispatch of the fleet to Asiatic waters, Chamberlain admitted that Britain is in a tight spot and must move cautiously in dealing with Japan because of the menace of war in Europe. He warned of “graver and nearer” problems close to home and said “we must conserve our forces to meet any emergency which might arise.” “There are limits to what it would be prudent for us to undertake,” he said. Admiral Roger Keyes, a conservative, said the British Navy knows “how to handle the Japanese and bring them to their senses.” Th

(By The Associated Press) London, Aug. 4 — Prime Minister Chamberlain wound up Parliament for the summer today with a blunt warning to Japan that Britain may find it necessary "in certain circumstances" to send a fleet to the Far East. He did not indicate what these circumstances were, but said he hoped no one would think it was "absolutely out of the question for such circumstances to arise." "I do not indicate what these circumstances were, but said he hoped no one would think it was 'absolutely out of the question for such circumstances to arise.'" "I do not say that as a threat," he declared, "but only as a warning." The speech was one of the most pointed he made during the stormy session of Parliament which began November 8, 1938, and which saw him discard his so-called "appeasement" policy for building up the British-French front. Southampton, England, Aug. 5. (*)—Imperial Airways’ 24-ton flying boat Caribou took off at 2:14 (7:14 a. m. C.S.T.) today, inaugurating British transatlantic air mail service with a load of 1,500 pounds of mail for Canada and the United States. The Caribou will take on more fuel in the air over Foynes, Ireland, and then head for Botwood, Newfoundland. Another stop is to be made at Montreal before flying to Port Washington, N. Y., where the Caribou is due at 8 p. m. C.S.T. Sunday. The Caribou and her sistership, the Cabot, will operate weekly mail service during August and September but will carry no passengers. Piloting the craft was Captain J. C. Kelly Rogers with a staff of four, including Co-Pilot Captain S. G. Long, a native of Colorado, who is returning to the United States for the first time since he left as a youth to join the British navy.

| The Japanese, apparently in retaliation for Washington's denunciation of the trade treaty with Tokyo, turned their attention to Americans as well as British in China for abuse today. In Yochow, according to Chinese sources, Japanese troops forced British and American missionaries to evacuate a church and then demolished the building. | In Peiping, plain clothes operatives of the Japanese-dominated provisional government seized two priests of the American Catholic University, to obtain from them the names of students who intended to go to Southern China. | One of the priests, the Rev.
