1939-02-09.text: CHATHAM, Mass., Feb. 9 (2)— Apparently convinced the British freighter Maria De Larrinaga had foundered, rescue vessels today searched the stormy north Atlantic for lifeboats in the hope of finding her crew of 37 alive. Late messages received by the radiomarine station here advised two of the rescue ships were steaming through wreckage-strewn waters, about 1200 miles east of New York, from which position the De Pepe yesterday reported she was sinking.

LONDON, Feb. 9 ()—Great Britain was reported reliably today to have taken new peace terms from the Spanish government to the insurgents after the latter had landed forces on the Balearic island of Minorca. The insurgent landing occurred after the departure of the British cruiser Devonshire from the island, where she had been sent to help negotiate a surrender. The new peace terms reported offered by Dr. Juan Negrin, Spanish government premier now in France, centered mainly on clemency for his followers. From Burgos, insurgent capital, word came at the same time that Generalissimo Francisco Franco, while still demanding an unconditional surrender by his foe, promised there would be no reprisals and that only those accused of crimes would be tried.

- PARIS, Feb. 8.—(4)—A British-French plan to get Germany and Italy out of Spain by countering Nazi-Fascist wartime help with peacetime gold was reported by informed quarters today. Diplomatic circles said Britain and France had offered to finance reconstruction of the war-torn country in return for a promise by Generalissimo Franco to eliminate German and Italian influence from a new insurgent state. There was immediate reaction in Italy to British-French overtures to Franco. The fascist press declared it was “too late” for eleventh hour moves by nations wanting to get on good terms with him and added that Italy insisted on a victory which would not benefit “those who, after having favored the exportation of (Continued on Page 2, Col. 6.)

Washington, Feb. 8. (AP)—It began to look as if a whole procession of European royalty would visit the United States this year. In addition to the announced visits of King George and Queen Elizabeth of England and members of the reigning families of Norway and Denmark, the state department is receiving hints that at least four more groups of royalty may cross the Atlantic. They are: King Zog of Albania and his bride of last year. King Boris of Bulgaria and Queen Giovanna, one of the daughters of the king of Italy. Princess Juliana, heir to the throne of the Netherlands, with her husband, Prince Bernard Leopold of Lippe-Biesterfeld. Grand Duke Jean of Luxembourg. The world’s fairs in New York and San Francisco are the attractions drawing most of the royalty to the United States.

| THOMASTON, MAINE — Mackay radio reported three rescue ships tonight were unable to establish wireless contact with a British freighter, which had reported she was “sinking in mid-Atlantic.” The three vessels sent nine or ten calls to the stricken freighter, all of which were unanswered, according to Mackay. Thomaston’s operator said the silence might indicate the vessel no longer had power to operate her transmitter. The operator here said he had heard nothing from the freighter since 7:10 p.m. when she repeated her S.O.S. several times.

ROME, Feb. 9 (The authoritative Fascist editor, Virginio Gayda, today suggested that British assistance in the effort for surrender of the Spanish island of Minorca might be designed to give Britain and France a foothold there at Italy's expense. He also declared Britain's "armed coalition" with France left open the possibility of bringing the United States into it.

LADY TE ASSOUCIALEU FC ES/ Shanghai, Feb. 8.—A British diplomatic request and inability to establish contact with 12 Americans and 53 other foreigners at Kuling caused Japanese army officers today to postpone a long-announced attack on the resort town. The officers agreed to extend the time limit for the evacuation of Kuling, where the foreigners have been stranded since last summer, beyond Friday, the original date set, but it was emphasized that "no commitments regarding possible military operations in that vicinity" could be made. An army spokesman said that "the army is willing to assist the isolated foreigners as far as conditions permit," but added that necessity would govern future plans. Increasing Concern Felt Foreign circles felt increasing concern for those at the mountain resort 15 miles south of the Yangtze river port of Kiukiang and 125 miles southeast of Hankow. The United

EAST HARTFORD, Conn., Feb. 9 (UP).—United Aircraft Corp. today announced receipt of an order from the British government for 200 airplane engines and constant speed propellers to equip a similar number of planes being obtained from the North American Aviation, Inc., of Inglewood, Calif. The cost of the engines and propellers, it was understood, would be about $1,500,000.

1939-02-22.text: LONDON, Feb. 21.—(#)—The House of Commons tonight approved Britain’s gigantic share in the international arms race a few hours after Prime Minister Chamberlain had admitted it might “lead to the bankruptcy of every country in Europe.” At the same time W. S. Morrison, cabinet member, speaking for Baron Chatfield, minister for co-ordination of defense, disclosed that the British and French general staffs were working on a joint inclusive plan to make effective use of all the two nations’ resources—men, munitions and war potentials—in event the two are involved in war. Double Borrowing Power, Chamberlain's government won approval of its plan to double its power to borrow for defense purposes, increasing the limit from £400,000,000 ($2,000,000,000) to £800,000,000 ($4,000,000,000) without division after the House had rejected by a vote of 310 to 127 a labor amendment to reduce the maximum. London, Feb. 22.—(GP)—"Unconditional recognition" of nationalist Generalissimo Francisco Franco's government in Spain within a "few days" was considered by the British cabinet today along with the Italian-French situation in northern Africa. The Earl of Perth, British ambassador to Rome, was instructed to report details of Italian troop movements in Libya, which adjoins French Tunisia. Italian Ambassador Dino Grandi was understood to have been told before going to Rome this week that Great Britain hoped Italian territorial claims on France would assume a "reasonable tone." Aid to France Seen. A hint that Britain was committed to sending another large army to the continent in the event of war emerged from two days of defense debate in the House of Commons. Chicago, Feb. 22 — (AP) — George Washington fought the British and farm problems with equal diligence. He was the father of his country and practically the parent of modern soil conservation. He tried crop rotation, terracing and sub-soil plowing at Mount Vernon and inaugurated tenant-farming. He was a surveyor, general and statesman, as well as first president of the United States, but fundamentally he was a farmer, an advanced, scientific farmer. Farmer Washington was thus depicted on his 207th birthday anniversary today by Dr. Avery O. Craven, professor of American history at the University of Chicago, who said the nation’s hero attacked the problem of how to make his plantation pay with the same shrewdness exhibited when he crossed the Delaware to take the Hessians at Trenton. Evidence that Washington was more than 150 years ahead of his time was found in Dr. Craven’s observation, ba

PARIS (UP) — French, Italian and British foreign offices investigated today a mysterious rumor which circulated in Paris that there had been a clash between French and Italian troops on the Tunis-Libya frontier last Friday. The French war ministry officially denied the rumor. The foreign office here and the British foreign office at London said they had no knowledge of any clash. At Rome, an official spokesman for the Italian press ministry said this afternoon that rumors of a clash between Italian and French troops in Tunisia were “absolutely unfounded.” “It is impossible to imagine upon what grounds such a fantastic rumor could have been based,” the spokesman said in a statement at 4:30 p.m., after an investigation of the rumors.

Newcastle, Feb. 21, (4).—Carrying the blessing of King George VI, the first battleship built under Britain’s big rearmament program slid gracefully into the Tyne today, clearing the stocks for immediate construction of a similar floating fortress. The King, wearing an admiral's greatcoat, christened the $40,000,000, 35,000-ton armored giant King George V in honor of his father. A crowd which lined the banks of the Tyne cheered as the monarch sent the ship down the ways with the cry: “May God bless her and those who serve in her!” As a precaution against the 'bemb terrorism' of recent weeks which was attributed by police to Irish Republican army sympathizers, the royal party was guarded by more than 1,000 policemen and arrived on a railway track especially re-laid against the possibility of bombing.

Paris, Feb. 22--(UP)—France and Great Britain may announce unqualified recognition of the Spanish Nationalist government after a special meeting of the French cabinet Friday, it was reported today. It was indicated strongly that France had been reconciled to recognizing the Nationalists without condition as the legal government of Spain. Senator Leon Bernard, Special French envoy to the Nationalists, returned to Burgos, Spain, last night from the frontier, where he had reported to Premier Edouard Daladier and Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet by telephone and diplomatic courier. Bernard was to begin a final series of conferences with Francisco Gomes Jordana, Nationalist foreign minister, late today on Jordana’s return from Barcelona where he took part in the triumphal entry of Generalissima Francisco Franco. It was understood that Bernard had definite instructions to reach agreement with J

The disclosure that the British and French general staffs were “continuing conversations” and a hint that Britain was committed to sending another large army to the continent in the event of war emerged today from the two days of defense debate in the House of Commons. Without a record vote the House granted the government authority to double its borrowing powers for defense this year, increasing the limit four billion dollars. There have been widespread reports that Britain planned to change radically her military policy from that followed in the last World War.

London, Feb. 22.—(I, N. S.)— Nations of the Balkan entente agreed today to recognize the insurgent regime of Gen. Francisco Franco, according to a Reuter dispatch from Bucharest. The Balkan countries will grant Franco de jure recognition, the report stated. It added each country will decide for itself the date on which such recognition will be extended.

1939-02-14.text: LONDON, Feb. 13. — Prime Minister Chamberlain indicated today that British and French recognition of the insurgent regime as the sole authority in Spain was imminent and defended British assistance to the insurgents in negotiations for surrender of Minorca. Under opposition questions in the House of Commons, Chamberlain refused to promise that the house would be consulted before recognition of insurgent Generalissimo Franco, asserting sharply, “The government must take the responsibility.” Britain, he said, was in close contact with France and, with the situation in Spain changing so rapidly, he could not give assurance against recognition. The French council of ministers was expected to consider and perhaps decide on recognition tomorrow. The British cabinet may decide Wednesday. HONGKONG, Feb. 14—(P)—Japanese naval and aviation units landed at dawn today at Yulinkan, at the southernmost tip of Hainan, the Chinese island near British and French empire lifelines, whose preliminary occupation Friday brought French and British diplomatic inquiries about Japanese intentions. (The United States destroyer John D. Edwards arrived from Hongkong today at Hoihow, North Hainan port, to investigate, and, if necessary, to protect American lives and interests on Hainan.) The landing placed the Japanese navy in a potential base 750 miles due east of Luzon, the principal island of the Philippines. An official statement said that by noon Japanese landing forces had penetrated 15 miles inland with a rapidity which indicated an apparent lack of Chinese resistance to the invaders’ occupation of the Sama Bay area—generally considered among the Far East’s potentially best although cur

New Britain, Conn., Feb. Ma (AP)--Stanley Andrukiewicz, 18, is serving ten days in jail because he hid his mother’s false teeth and eyeglasses. Mrs. Andrukiewicz told Police Judge William Hagearty that her son “revenged” himself upon her after she removed the tube of a radio which he persisted in playing too loudly.

LONDON, Feb. 13—-(AP)—A 23-year-old Irishman was charged formally today with murdering Mayfair’s “Black Butterfly” as Scotland Yard sought to establish whether the brunette playgirl was a spy for the outlawed Irish republican army and had been killed as a betrayer of its secrets. The accused man, Arthur James Mahoney, paled as he stood in the dock at Bow Street and heard police tell the court he had confessed stabbing “The Black Butterfly” — 26-year-old Georgina Hoffman—‘“‘because she had tricked me out of all my money.” While the tenor of Mahoney’s reputed confession failed to bear out a police theory the case might be linked with a terroristic campaign attributed to the outlawed Irish republican army, operatives were known to be checking such possible ramifications. Miss Hoffman, variously known as “The Black Butterfly” for her fluttering manner and raven hair and as “the girl in red”

TOKYO, Feb. 14 (#)—Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita today told Sir Robert Leslie Craigie, British ambassador, Japan probably would hold Hainan Island until the end of the Chinese war and possibly indefinitely on grounds of military necessity. This was virtually the same reply Arita gave the French ambassador, Charles Arsene Henry, yesterday when Henry asked for information on Japan's plans with regard to the island, which is near French Indo-China and the British colony at Hongkong. Sources close to the French embassy predicted France would be dissatisfied with Arita’s reply, but it was doubted that she would attempt any action to oust the Japanese.

LONDON. (AP). President Manuel Quezon of the Philippines offered lake-dotted Mindanao island as a haven for “several thousand” refugees as the intergovernmental committee received Adolf Hitler's latest plan for getting Jews out of Germany. The offer was made at a session of the refugee committee to which George Rublee, American director, presented his resignation. He was succeeded by Sir Herbert Emerson, League of Nations assistant high commissioner for refugees. Rublee, who said in resigning that he accepted the post only temporarily, presented Hitler’s plan which was understood to have stipulated: 1. That from 150,000 to 200,000 young “Jewish wage earners” be sent out of Germany as soon as possible. 2. That those remaining be permitted a certain amount of freedom to work and live, provided the younger Jews eventually arrange to take their parents and other relatives out of the country.

CROYDON, England Feb. 4 (UP). A British Airways liner for Paris carrying seven passengers made a safe landing at Croydon today after having circled the field for nearly an hour and a half because of a jammed landing gear. Ambulances and fire crews were standing by but were not needed. The ship is a commercial passenger plane of the type flown around the world by Howard Hughes.
LONDON, Feb. 14 (lo—Great Britain has informed Italy that she considers the sending of Italian reinforcements to Libya a violation of the British-Italian accord, informed sources said tonight.

1939-09-08.text: LISBON, Sept. 7.— — The 7,242 ton British freighter Manaar was sunk last night off Portugal by what survivors declared was a submarine torpedo, and early this afternoon 41 of her crew of 88 had not been accounted for. At least two were killed and three wounded. Survivors said that the Manaar, bound for Calcutta for Liverpool, was torpedoed without warning, and that while the crew was attempting to abandon her in eight lifeboats the submarine opened fire and destroyed one lifeboat, killing one man and wounding four. Lifeboats Missing. The Netherlands steamer Mars brought 29 survivors to Lisbon. The Portuguese liner Carvalho Araujo arrived with 15 British-Indian members of the Manaar’s crew. Early this afternoon three lifeboats were reported still missing.

GLASGOW, SCOTLAND, SEPT. 7, (AP).—Owners of the British liner Athenia, sunk Sunday night off the Scottish coast with 1,418 persons aboard reported today that 128 persons were dead or missing. The Donaldson Atlantic Line, however, still held slight hope that the death roll might be reduced. It pointed out that there was the possibility that outward bound vessels not equipped with wireless had picked up some survivors.

Paris, Sept. (.-—(4)--Prussian reinforcements were moving up today to join French forces reported officially already to have advanced on German soil. The French and British general staffs were in consultation to coordinate their forces. (In Basel, Switzerland, border advices said German advance guards on the western front were withdrawing slowly into the main forts of the Siegfried line. (The French had advanced as much as 15 kilometers—9% miles—in some places along the northern wing of the line, these reports said, but were moving cautiously.) Premier Daladier, who also is France’s war minister, conferred for an hour today with General Maurice Gustave Gamelin, commander of all French forces and probable generalissimo of combined British-French land forces. LONDON, Sept. 7—(P)—Prime Minister Chamberlain told Commons today Britain might “rest assured” its navy would increasingly bring under control the raiding activities of German submarines. In a general statement to the House of the state of Britain’s war activities and preparation, Chamberlain asserted also Royal Air Force planes had scored “at least two hits” on a German pocket battleship in their spectacular raid last Monday on the Kiel Canal. In discussing the submarine peril, he acknowledged “a certain percentage of our weekly losses (to shipping) must be expected.” Recalling the sinking of the Athenia, he denounced it as a German crime which has profoundly shocked and horrified the world.” And, he said, “no denials or interventions on the part of Germany will convince the public of German innocence.” Dominions Support Britain “We are greatly heartened,” the prime minister said at ano

LONDON — (UP) — Poland is fighting grimly for every yard of ground yielded to the Germans, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain told a cheering House of Commons today as Great Britain prepared for a war to the end against Hitlerism. Chamberlain reported to the House that arrangements with France for co-operating in the prosecution of the war are “working smoothly and well.” Britain's war effort is “rapidly gaining momentum,” he said. Any belief that Britain and France might temporize with Adolf Hitler and discuss a general settlement after the Fuehrer has accomplished a lightning conquest of Poland was dispelled by several factors. The Polish ambassador, Count Edward Raczinski, was understood to have reported to his government that the nine-man British war cabinet is unflinchingly determined to smash Hitlerism. NEW YORK, Sept. 7.—(4)—The United States lines today received a radio from the Washington which sailed from New York Saturday that she was “proceeding to the assistance of the Olive Grove” presumably in the vicinity of the English Channel. The United States lines said the Washington should be near the channel by this time. Lloyd’s register gives the Olive Grove as owned by the Grove Line of Glasgow with its home port as Glasgow. The register said it was a 4,060-tonnage craft built in 1929.

NEW YORK, Sept. 8—(AP)—Radiomarine Corp. today reported a radio saying the ‘steamer Jeanjadot advises saved crew 44 men of SS. Regent Tiger British torpedoed by submarine.’ Lloyd's register lists the ship as a British tanker of 10,176 tons.

LONDON, Sept. 7 (P)—Great Britain guardedly organized its offensive against Germany today on a long-term basis for a fight to the finish. The government has made plain by its brief and carefully worded communiques during the first five days of the war that it is mapping under cover a vast, co-ordinated campaign along three general lines. 1.—Military and aerial cooperation with France and Poland to harass Germany on two fronts. 2.—Sweeping naval operations to choke off German supplies, and intense propaganda to disorganize the economy of the enemy. 3.—Careful civil defense preparations to keep its own nation at a peak of efficiency and morale so as to be able to supply not only Britain's own forces but those of her allies with the materials for successful warfare. 1939-09-12.text: We ie Sept. 12—An historic senate struggle appears in prospect over President Roosevelt’s proposal to repeal the arms embargo provision of the neutrality act—a step which many legislators say would benefit England and France in their war with Germany. Sen. Borah (R) of Idaho and several of his Republican colleagues discussed the issue informally yesterday and one of them predicted afterward that the President will have to “fight for everything he gets” if he calls a special session to revise the neutrality act. Mr. Roosevelt has said he will call such a session between now and January. Indications are that the opposition to repealing the embargo will lose no time in getting its campaign under way, Borah already is arranging to make a radio address on the subject. London (4) —The British government announced today it was taking steps to remove between 7,000 and 8,000 members of the staffs of governmental departments from London but stressed the government itself was not moving from the capital. “The government itself will not evacuate London if it can possibly remain without loss of efficiency,” said a spokesman. It was explained that no government department was being moved entirely. Which departments were affected and where the employees were to be taken remained official secrets. British Forces In France Meanwhile official disclosure that a British expeditionary force had crossed to France was made today in a communique which said troops have landed but “are not yet in action.” The communique was at variance with the information ministry's announcement last night that troops already were taking part in advances on German soil. Paris, Sept. 12 (#)—Prime Minister Chamberlain met Premier Daladier “somewhere in France” today at a meeting of the supreme French-British war council. A communique said the war council “confirmed completely” a firm French-British resolution to “consecrate all their forces and all their resources” to aid Poland, which is resisting a “brutal invasion of its territory with so much bravery.” London, Sept. 12 (P)—The

WASHINGTON, Sept. 12 —(AP)— State department officials studied in silence today a report that a German submarine commander had served notice that all American ships to halt would be fired upon. They considered as well a statement that Great Britain had seized as contraband a cargo of resin consigned to Hamburg, Germany, on an American vessel. Officials declined any immediate comment on these reported incidents, which recalled to some persons the shipping troubles that kept this country's diplomats busy writing notes and protests during the early years of the World War. The officials indicated there would be no comment until reports were received from American embassies in the countries involved. Capt. N. New York, Sept. 12 (?)—An unidentified submarine was reported operating off Nantucket Lightship yesterday, officers of the British Arandora Star said today when the liner arrived from Cherbourg and Southampton with 441 passengers, 260 of them Americans. Captain Edgar Wallace Moulton, on orders of the British admiralty, declined to discuss the hazards of the 11-day voyage, but other officers said the ship received warnings nine times that submarines were in its vicinity. The last warning spoke of an undersea boat off Nantucket. The Arandora Star, a 15,500-ton vessel operated by the Blue Star line, is a cruise ship chartered by the Cunard-White Star to bring refugees back from Europe. She also carried $14,000,000 in gold. (2 £7 ASSOCIATED PRESS) Allied shipping losses approached the 100,000 mark in tonnage today as the British Ministry of Information, reporting on Germany's unabated submarine warfare, announced the sinking of the British tanker Inverliffey. The ship, a 9,456-ton vessel built in Hamburg last year and running between the Gulf of Mexico and England, was torpedoed near Havre, France, yesterday. The crew was rescued by the Standard Oil tanker R. G. Stewart, and later transferred to the City of Joliet, bound from New Orleans to Antwerp. One other casualty was reported today—the blowing up of the 2,795-ton Finnish bark Olivebank about 105 miles southwest of Esbjerg, southwestern Denmark. Fourteen were killed and seven saved. The survivors said their ship hit a mine. The British Ministry of Information said four British merchant ships had reported unsuccessful attacks by submarines. Since the war

LONDON, Sept. 1.—(4)—Japan has informed Britain she does not intend to be involved in Europe's war. The Ministry said, "A communication has been made to His Majesty's ambassador at Tokyo to the effect that the Japanese government does not intend to be involved in the war which has broken out in Europe. "They requested that His Majesty's government should refrain from taking any measures such as might prejudice Japan's position in regard to China." The communication from Japan was the first official notification of Japan’s neutrality in the European war and served to spike reports of a possible new military axis involving Germany, France, Russia, and Japan. Observers believed it indicated the German-Soviet non-aggression pact may have driven a lasting wedge between Hitler and the Japanese. LONDON, (UP).-—The Duke and Duchess of Windsor were reliably reported today to have arrived in England and to be staying at the country home of Maj. Edward Dudley Metcalfe at Coleman's Hatch, Sussex. According to present plans, it was said the Duchess will stay with the Metcalfes for the time being and the Duke will come to London to visit Queen Mother Mary at Marlborough House, to which she returned yesterday. Later, it was believed, the Windsors will establish residence at the home of the Duke and Duchess of Kent, No. 3 Belgrave Square, here.

1939-09-26.text: LONDON, Sept. 26 (AP) —The British war cabinet announced to parliament today the defensive arming of many merchant ships and the seizure of more German goods since the war started than Great Britain has lost in submarine attacks. Convoy System Used Winston Churchill, first lord of the admiralty, made this disclosure in the house of commons after Prime Minister Chamberlain, in his fourth war report, had announced complete agreement with France on “procedure for coordinating and perfecting” munitions and supplies. Churchill, after saying the British convoy system now was in full operation and merchant ships all over the world were being armed to fight off submarines and airplanes, declared: “and all its friends in every quarter of the globe will be able to develop their immeasurable latent forces, and their manpower can be concentrated in ever growing intensity on the task we have in hand,

LONDON, Sept. 2—(P)—Great Britain answered Premier Mussolini's suggestion to call the war quits on Germany's military conquest of Poland by intensifying today her preparations for a fight to the finish. An authoritative commentary on Mussolini's speech in Rome Saturday declared Prime Minister Chamberlain's statement of Britain's war aim—"to redeem Europe from the perpetual and recurring fear of German aggression"—still held good. Britain remained determined, it said, despite the complication of Soviet Russia’s occupation of eastern Poland. Informed sources, however, said Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax, who called Russian Ambassador Ivan Maisky to his office for an hour's interview Saturday night, had requested clarification of Soviet aims in eastern Europe.

P.)—The Warsaw radio announcer quoted German prisoners today that Colonel General Werner von Fritsch, former commander-in-chief of the German army, was assassinated by Nazi secret police and that many of his fellow officers on the Warsaw front had been arrested, because of their outspoken indignation. The prisoners were said to have reported that Von Fritsch could not possibly have “died a soldier's death on the battlefield” because they had seen him last Thursday enter a car at Grodzisk, 20 miles from Warsaw, and drive away in a southwesterly direction, away from the front. (The only official detail of Von Fritsch’s death was a statement by Colonel General Walther von Brauchitsch, army commander-in-chief, that he had died leading an artillery regiment on patrol.) | LONDON (UP)—The view of expert neutral observers in London, after nearly four weeks of war, is that Adolf Hitler cannot win a long war and Great Britain and France cannot win a short one. The French and British confidently expect to win the war, but they believe victory may be precipitated by the crackup of the German home front and not necessarily by an overwhelming victory in the field. Without claiming inside information on Allied plans, it seems to me that the tactics and strategy of the French and British at this time may be defined as pointed toward a war which will surely if slowly force Germany to capitulation. Naturally later developments might alter these fundamentals, and also this definition of Franco-British strategy does not mean that the Allies intend to pull their punches in military combat. ALBANY, N. Y., Sept. 26 CP, --The fall's first snow whirled across northern New York and parts of New England today, falling communication lines and impeding motor travel. Three inches of snow fell in Malone in northern New York, where telephone and power lines snapped and highways were made dangerous. Temperatures dropped overnight from the high 70's to near freezing. In northern Vermont, heavy rain gave way to snowflakes in the early morning and the storm increased in intensity during the forenoon. St. Johnsbury, Vt. also reported a heavy snowfall.

Berlin, Sept. 25 (P)—Germans in informed quarters explained tonight that the massing of troops near the three-cornered border of Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium, was a precaution against any French or British designs to find a “soft front” for a drive through neutral soil into the Reich. These sources said it would be against Germany's interests to carry on military operations there because of its proximity to the Ruhr coal fields and lower Rhine industrial regions. British Destroyer Lost A communique, meanwhile, announced the sinking of an unidentified British destroyer by a German submarine and the shooting down of eight French warplanes during an aerial battle in the West. The communique said maritime warfare was “yielding good results” and added that on the Western Front there had been “reconnoitering activity and artillery activity on both sides” at undisclosed points. The statement told of a mix-up today over the release of news of the return to London of Queen Elizabeth. The editorial said: “Nine out of ten men and women in the street are baffled, bored, fed up or furious * * *, “Against a debit (the sinking of the liner Athenia and the aircraft carrier Courageous and about 200,600 tons of shipping) we set the dashing raid on Kiel, some propaganda flights over Germany and the bare report of half a dozen U-boats sent to the bottom. . “Many ask what else have we done?” “This Ministry of Information has three separate functions: One, to censor news. ROME, Sept 25—(/P)—Italian newspapers today criticized proposals that the United States sell arms on a "cash and carry" basis as "false neutrality." At the same time, Virginio Gayda, authoritative Fascist editor, expressed doubt France and Britain ever would defeat Germany except in "a victory!" (Please Turn to Page Two)

1939-04-09.text: Tirana, April 10—(4)—The provisional Albanian government today pledged the loyalty of the Albanian people to Premier Mussolini and formally accepted Italian rule on their behalf. The president and secretary of the administrative committee broadcast loyalty addresses to Albanians and to Italy. Their speeches were relayed over all Italian radio stations. Contrary to expectations in Tirana, Mussolini had not arrived in time for the broadcast and it was rumored that he would come today. The "appeal" of Albanian leaders to Mussolini to permit them to form an Albanian Fascist party also was read over the radio. Thanked For Sacrifices "We express our thanks for your (Mussolini’s) sacrifices, which have saved the Albanian people from so many dangers," the appeal said. The addresses came as crowds gathered in the main square of this fallen Albanian capital in expectation of a broadcast by Mussoli

LONDON, APR. 8. (AP).—Prime Minister Chamberlain will return to London tonight from Castle Forbes, Scotland, to confer with his ministers on the Albanian situation, which was announced this afternoon. The Prime Minister left London for Scotland Thursday for a fishing Easter vacation. Announcement of Chamberlain's return followed quickly an emergency meeting of the cabinet in London. After weighing the implications of Italy's invasion of Albania, the ministers issued a formal statement declaring that the Albanian situation was “still obscure in regard to a number of important factors.” In informed quarters this statement was interpreted as indicating that the government had not decided to recall parliament immediately as had been demanded earlier by leaders of the opposition. Parliament began its Easter recess Thursday to extend until April 18. The statement issued from No. 10 Downing Str

Quillayute, Wash., Apr. 8 (AP) A coast guard crew brought 23 of the 29 men aboard the wrecked British freighter Temple Bar safely into this station today and reported the rest were “safe on the beach.” The ship was reported a “total loss.” The Temple Bar went aground about 4 a.m. today, about a mile and a half north of the Quillayute Needle, a rock a mile off shore and three miles south of the mouth of the Quillayute River. It sent out an SOS before the crew abandoned ship. The men walked up the beach to the station. Eric Reutercrona, coast guard boatswain's mate, said: “Some of the crew had gotten ashore in their lifeboats and some were drifting near the wreck in lifeboats when we reached them,” Reutercrona said. “Some of the men were badly frightened and most are still too excited to talk much. The Temple Bar is lying now with her bow slightly out of water and her poop deck awash. I th

London, April 8.—(4)—The British government, alarmed by the swift Italian invasion of Albania, is pressing to get Rumania quickly into a European defensive alliance and also hopes to conclude secret agreements with smaller Balkan states, diplomatic informants said tonight. Prime Minister Chamberlain abandoned a vacation in Scotland and will arrive in London tomorrow for consultation with his ministers. Ten members of the cabinet met in emergency session with Chamberlain participating by telephone from Aberdeen, after which a statement was issued that the Albanian situation was “still obscure in regard to a number of important factors.” No Decision This was taken to mean no decision was reached to accede to opposition demands for the recall of parliament, which is in Easter recess until April 18. Chamberlain may decide tomorrow. Informed sources said that the cabinet, at an emergency meet

- Budapest, April 8.—(#)—Little kingdoms of the Balkans, worried by Italy’s invasion of Albania, today were re-examining the possible effectiveness of any British-made system of security. Foreign offices in the countries of southeastern Europe had been considering the advisability of associating themselves with the British-French-Polish front against aggression. - But some observers believe that Italy’s move against Albania, driving a wedge between Yugoslavia and Greece, had reduced greatly the attractiveness of the British plan to the Balkans. Officially all countries of the region, particularly Yugoslavia, Rumania and Bulgaria, were expressing an optimistic view of developments. Foreign office spokesmen expressed hope the military action in Albania would be localized. But off the record comment was not so cheerful. Many political leaders in Yugoslavia admitted Italian occupation of Alb

SEATTLE, April 6—(AP)—The British steamship Temple Bar struck rocks off Carroll Island 20 miles south of the entrance to the Strait of Juan De Fuca today and apparently sank within a few minutes. U. S. Coast Guard headquarters here reported the last message from the ship was that lifeboats were launched and it was believed all aboard managed to reach shore safely. It was not known whether they landed on the island or on the Washington coast. The Coast Guard cutter Ingham steamed to the scene from Port Townsend. She expected to arrive about 3 P.M. (EST)

Fearing that further advance of the German-Italian axis partnership southward as a result of the Italian conquest of Albania would endanger Britain's empire communications, the four service members of the cabinet were said to have urged the public announcement and to have enlisted the support of the other seven meeting in an emergency session, Prime Minister Returns. The prime minister is returning tonight from his vacation in Scotland because of the European situation. 1939-05-03.text: LONDON, May 3.—The foreign secretaries of Britain, France and Soviet Russia were reliably reported tonight to have arranged to meet at Geneva May 15 in an effort to complete their projected alliance. The League of Nations council is meeting there then, and it was stated authoritatively that Maxim Litvinov of Russia, Georges Bonnet of France, and Viscount Halifax of Britain had agreed to take the opportunity for negotiations to end the present deadlock over the extent of the alliance.

London, May 3.—(A4)—Prime Minister Chamberlain told the House of Commons today that "the British government would be ready to consider proposals for the exchange of reciprocal assurances with the German government." Denying that there were any grounds for charges that the British government had adopted a policy of "encircling Germany," Chamberlain said: "What President Roosevelt proposed (in his April 14 peace appeal) and Herr Hitler offered (in his April 28 speech) was an exchange of assurances of non-aggression rather than a guarantee on a reciprocal basis such as was recently given by the British government to Poland. "The British government is certainly ready to consider proposals for the exchange of reciprocal assurances with the German government." (Continued on Page Five)

TOKYO, May 3.—(?)—Renzo Sawada, vice minister of foreign affairs, presented to the United States and British ambassadors today demands that the Shanghai municipal council, governing body of the Shanghai international settlement, be reorganized to give the Japanese a larger voice in its affairs and to permit more complete control of "terrorism" in the settlement. The minister invited Ambassadors Joseph C. Grew and Sir Robert Leslie Craigie to the foreign office and asked them to communicate his statement to their governments. Sawada declared that the structure of the Shanghai council was outmoded long ago and that "the Japanese community is not given due and fair expression in the administration of the settlement." He added that some measures must be taken immediately. (Japan now has two members of the council, Britain five and the United States two. Before the Japanese-Chinese war there

TOKYO, May 3. (U.P.)—Japan informed Great Britain and the United States tonight that she demands a “thoroughgoing reorganization” of the international settlement at Shanghai. The Japanese demands were conveyed to Joseph C. Grew, United States ambassador, and Sir Robert L. Craigie, British envoy, by Renzo Sawada, vice-minister for foreign affairs. Changes Demanded The vice minister demanded a “revamping” of the Shanghai land regulations—a step which might lead to abolition of the settlement in which the British have investments running into hundreds of millions of dollars. The ambassadors called at the foreign office separately, at Sawada’s request, and were given answers to representations they presented two months ago relative to incidents in and around the settlement in which Japan, Britain and the United States all are interested.

Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain told the House of Commons that Britain was ready to consider giving Germany reciprocal assurances of non-aggression, such as Hitler refused to give in blanket form to President Roosevelt but which he offered to negotiate with individual nations. Again Chamberlain denied any desire or intention of encircling Germany. The Prime Minister's statement assumed greater importance in view of the fact that Britain, pushed by France, was struggling with great difficulties in attempting—vainly so far—to bring Soviet Russia into the European anti-aggression front on terms agreeable to the western powers. Hitler strengthened his northern flank by proposing neutrality agreements with the Scandinavian nations. NAZIS RAP BECK The tempo of developments increased. The Nazis renewed with unusual vigor their newspaper barrage against Poland in advance of the speech which P

The German government undertook to strengthen its ties with Scandinavian and Baltic countries and the German press intensified against Poland a campaign similar to that which preceded the demolition of Czechoslovakia. With indications increasing that there soon will be a showdown on German demands against Poland, the Nazi diplomatic and newspaper undertakings perhaps were related. Berlin diplomatic quarters said that Chancellor Hitler had offered nonaggression pacts to Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Finland and had made similar approaches to Estonia, Latvia and other countries. If such accords are obtained, they would strengthen his position in or against the French-British front of nations—especially if, as some Scandinavian observers stated, the pacts obtain pledges to Germany to maintain neutrality in the event of war in the Baltic. Berlin, May 2 a quarters tonight saw in the controlled press signs they interpreted as new Nazi attempts to put pressure on Poland. German newspapers accused Great Britain and France of encouraging Poland to resist Germany’s suggestions for control of Danzig and a highway across the Polish corridor. The controlled press also accused Polish papers of telling the people “thick lies” about the former German free city, object of a long back-to-the-Reich agitation, and East Prussia, which Pomorze separates from Germany. The frequent return of the two allegations indicated “an inspired origin.” German officials said they would propose nothing more to the Poles. Chancellor Hitler in his Reichstag speech Friday said his “one-time only” offer to Poland was rejected. He said he promised Poland a 23-year non-aggression pledge and a guarantee, with Poland and Hungary, of Slovak independence in retur

Berlin, May 3.— (4) — Hugh Carleton Greene, chief Berlin correspondent for the London Daily Telegraph and five other British subjects in Germany have been ordered to leave the country by May 24. British sources said the expulsion orders were “reprisals” for the ousting of Germans from England. (Britain was reported Tuesday to be preparing to expel more than 50 German nazis from England. It was understood they were accused of trying to spread nazi propaganda.)

1939-05-02.text: LONDON, May 2.—(#) — Great Britain advanced efforts to check the spread of Nazi doctrine within her own borders by ordering the expulsion of an undetermined number of "undesirable" German residents. The foreign office sent to Berlin today a "simple acknowledgment" of the German note renouncing the 1935 naval agreement between the two countries. A spokesman said the government "will probably send its observations advising the German government that it has no intention in the near future of negotiating a new Anglo-German naval agreement"—which Hitler suggested in his speech. The home office disclosed that it had sent to the German embassy a new list of Nazis living in Britain who were not wanted here because of their "individual activities." Newspaper Man on List. Some of them, said the Star, are newspapermen, but “it is not their newspaper work but their activities in connection with Nazi organizations that is suspected.” The expulsion orders followed extensive investigation of activities of Nazi organizations throughout the United Kingdom. Berlin, May 1.—(#)—Adolf Hitler strove tonight to isolate Poland from British and Hungarian friendship while using May Day to strengthen the bonds uniting him and his regime with youth and labor. His offensive against the unyielding Poles appeared to include attempts to bring Hungary more completely into the German orbit by closer economic and political ties in return for more territory in Slovakia that Hungary desires. The German press also sought to induce Britain to back down from her pledge of assistance to Poland, a pledge which has not yet been signed formally. Called Risky “For the English the question arises whether, since denunciation of the German-Polish treaty, their guaranty to Poland has not become much more risky than it previously was and more risky than London had foreseen,” the Frankfurter Zeitung said. Other editorials said England had acted on ‘false Polish information

LONDON, May 1 (UP).—A British government spokesman declared today that “if Poland fights, Britain and France will fight too.” It was confirmed officially that the British ambassador to Warsaw, Sir Howard Kennard, in discussing Adolf Hitler's Reichstag speech on Saturday with Foreign Minister Josef Beck of Poland, stressed that Britain is ready to support Poland with all her armed forces if Poland resists a threat against her independence. Sound Another Warning One other significant move was made to warn Hitler against any attempt to win Danzig or the Polish corridor by force. The foreign office promptly disassociated the British government from a Sunday night radio broadcast from Paris, carried by the British Broadcasting Company, describing France as unwilling to fight for Danzig. It was understood the Polish embassy is reporting to Warsaw on the matter, which may have a further dramati

London, May 1. (P)—Bills calling for military conscription of men aged 20 years for six months of training and enabling the government to call up reserve forces when it deems necessary were introduced today in the House of Commons. The texts were not published immediately but it was reported that the conscription measure included Northern Ireland. Prime Minister Eamon de Valera of Ireland was understood last week to have warned the British government not to extend conscription to his northern neighbor. The bills were introduced by Prime Minister Chamberlain and War Secretary Leslie Hore-Belisha after a cabinet meeting in which Foreign Secretary Viscount Halifax reported on Poland’s reaction to Reichsführer Hitler’s Friday speech and was said to have announced that British negotiations with Soviet Russia were “making excellent progress.”

London, May 2.—(/P)—Britain wants “to conclude an agreement with Soviet Russia but we must discuss what is the best form,” Prime Minister Chamberlain told the House of Commons today. In a brief statement on long drawn out negotiations between London and Moscow on some form of mutual assistance pact, Chamberlain added: “Although I quite understand that there might be a certain sense of impatience (over delay in announcement of an agreement), there is no want of good will on the side of the British government.” Chamberlain spoke in answer to the Opposition Laborite leader, Clement R. Attlee, who said: “Is the Prime Minister aware that many people are disturbed at the slow progress which is being made in these conversations, and that they have not felt that the British government are pressing on as rapidly as they might?” The government, meanwhile, proceeded with the difficulties of conscri

BATH, England, May 2 (®).—A frail, little black man fasted and prayed today that the African empire he once ruled as “king of kings” be restored to him. It was the third anniversary of the flight from Addis Ababa of the conquering lion of the tribe of Judah, Haile Selassie I, emperor of Ethiopia.

LONDON, May 1—Prime Minister Chamberlain assured the House of Commons today that negotiations to bring Soviet Russia into the British-French alliance were moving "with all possible dispatch" and formally introduced Britain's first peacetime conscription. His cabinet earlier had considered new Soviet proposals brought back from Moscow Saturday by Ivan Maisky, Soviet ambassador to London. These were said in diplomatic quarters to offer a promise of early success for a British-French-Russian front to protect smaller states in both eastern and western Europe against any aggression. Some informed persons expected Chamberlain to announce such a pact before the end of the week. He said today, however, that "it is not a very simple matter and one in which other governments have to be considered besides our own." Of these other governments Poland was the chief one. 1939-11-02.text: By The Associated Press Prime Minister Chamberlain to- day called Russia’s Premier Molotov’s foreign policy speech “a disappointment” to Germany. Making a weekly war report in the House of Commons, Chamberlain said “nothing has occurred to shake our confidence” that the German submarine menace can be overcome and asserted Britain’s war aims had been made amply clear. The Greek government meanwhile announced letters “contributing to the preservation of peace” in Southern Europe had been exchanged with Italy, a statement that followed Rome reports the two nations would sign a non-aggression pact. Finns See Russians Finland and Soviet Russia opened another chapter in negotiations which form one of the many offshoots of Western Europe’s waiting war. WASHINGTON, Nov. 2.—(4)—The coast guard heard today that the British freighter Coulmore was safe, but it continued the search just to make sure. The Camperdown station in Nova Scotia advised the coast guard cutter Bibb at 2:30 a.m. eastern standard time, that she had heard directly from the Coulmore that she had eluded the submarine threat which had caused her to send a distress signal. The Bibb, which was leading a flotilla of coast guard and navy vessels in the search for the Coulmore, immediately started for land, messaging headquarters that the Canadian advice "justified closing the search." However, to be on the safe side, the coast guard ordered the cutter Duane, another of the neutrality patrol ships in the Atlantic, to proceed to the area about 680 miles east of New York to look for the Coulmore. When the decision to resume the search was made, the Bibb advised authorities that s

LONDON, Nov. 1.—The government today announced plans for rationing of food in Great Britain. Bacon and butter will be rationed beginning about the middle of December, William S. Morrison, minister for food, announced in the House of Commons. Bacon and butter will be rationed at four ounces — a quarter of a pound — a week per person. That amount, he said, will depend on “imports continuing at the present rate as we have good reason to think they will.” (In Germany, butter is rationed at 112.2 grams or about four ounces a week per person. The meat ration is 500 grams or about a pound a week per person).

Washington, Nov. 2 (#) — The coast guard received word today that the British freighter Coulmore was safe. The word was received by the coast guard cutter Bibb from a Canadian radio station at Camperdown at 2:30 a. m. The station said it had heard directly from the Coulmore that she was safe. The search for the vessel was suspended. The Bibb was the leader of a squadron of coast guard and navy vessels scouring the Atlantic for the freighter about 680 miles east of New York after the interception early yesterday morning of a distress signal which indicated the freighter might have been attacked by a submarine. The position given by the Coulmore at that time indicated it was just inside the neutrality safety belt around the Americas fixed at the recent Pan American neutrality meeting in Panama. The Bibb relayed the Camperdown information to Washington, saying that the radio information “ju

BERLIN, Nov. 1. — The supreme army command’s communique today raised to six the number of planes shot down by the Germans on the western front and in the North Sea Monday. Four of them were British, the announcement said. Identity of the other two was not revealed. Yesterday’s communique said four planes were shot down Monday. Today’s communique reported only desultory artillery fire and reconnoitering activity on the western front.

London, Nov. 1—(AP)—The sinking of the 5,317 ton British steamer Bronte was disclosed today with the arrival in England of her crew aboard a rescue vessel. The crew of 40 and one passenger were rescued by a ship which unsuccessfully attempted to tow the crippled Bronte to port after it had been attacked by a submarine. The Bronte sank.

LONDON. (UP). Government officials, military leaders and newspapers joined Monday in warning the British people to get ready for a lightning blow from Germany. In anticipation of a German peace bid this week, and a British and French rejection, the government sought to prepare not only the fighting forces but the people of the United Kingdom as a whole, for anything that the — might try — and to reply to it. Prime Minister Chamberlain was expected to address the House of Commons Tuesday on the diplomatic situation, and particularly the apparently increasingly close partnership between Nazi Germany and Communist Russia. Chamberlain was confidentially expected also to reject in advance any bid to induce the allies to accept peace on the Stalin-Hitler terms. All sorts of reports circulated as to the possibilities of this week. The most surprising was offered in Monday's Daily Mirror. This p

Wiin Int BNIilion EA-PEDITIONARY FORCE, In France, Nov. 2—(AP)—A hail of anti-aircraft shells from British and French batteries and machine gun bullets from British planes knocked down two German Heinkel bombers this morning when three of them attempted a scouting raid over the British lines. (A dispatch from Lille, France, said two British fighting planes brought down a German bomber in a skirmish over northern France. It was not disclosed immediately whether this was the same encounter.) Bursts of smoke from anti-aircraft shells encircled the three German planes. Out of the sky to the east streaked five British pursuit planes. Soon thereafter two of the German planes spun to earth. A general headquarters communique failed to mention the third machine, which streaked homeward trailing smoke.

1939-11-28.text: London, Nov. 28 UP)—King George, opening the first war session of Parliament, assured the empire today that the royal navy is keeping “free and open the highways of the sea.” The King, who yesterday signed an order in council extending the British blockade by authorizing seizure of German exports as well as imports, referred only briefly to pending wartime legislation. “You will be asked,” he told the House of Commons, "to make further financial inquiries. Britain's concern in the Russian-Finnish dispute was shown by disclosure by authoritative sources that Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax had invited the Russian ambassador, Ivan Maisky, to clarify Soviet policy relating to Finland. The two conferred yesterday. London, Nov. 27—The story of a blazing sea battle in which two German raiders, one the pocket battleship Deutschland, sank the armed merchantman Rawalpindi off the southeast coast of Iceland, was told tonight in a vivid admiralty communique. Fighting until riddled by shot and shell, the Rawalpindi went down with colors flying in a fight against overwhelming odds, on November 23, the admiralty said. Britain’s warships are searching night and day now for the swift, heavily-armed raiders which eluded a British cruiser in darkness and storm after sinking the 16,697-ton Rawalpindi with an estimated loss of 280 lives. Stringent Economic Reprisal Planned A stringent economic reprisal was decided on today by Great Britain to counter Germany's intensified sea warfare by armed raiders, mines and submarines, which added three more ships to the growing toll of merchant vessels. LONDON, Nov. 28—(U.P)—The Allied orders for seizure of German exports on the high seas will become effective Monday despite the complaints of neutrals, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain announced today in the House of Commons. The announcement was made soon after King George had opened a new session of Parliament with a speech from the throne. The King emphasized that all of the energy of the Empire was concentrated on winning the war and declared that the British navy was “keeping open the highways of the sea” for transportation of supplies despite the furious Nazi mine offensive. The Allied powers indicated that every effort would be made to make hardships of the “double blockade” as light as possible for neutrals. British warships in all seas are standing by for the Admiralty’s code signal starting the blockade. Neutral shippers will be given a ‘few days’ grace to dispose of German e

BERLIN, Nov. 28 (U.P)—Nazis reported officially today that a British heavy cruiser had been sunk by a U-boat east of the Shetland islands. The cruiser, of 10,000 tons, was torpedoed by a U-boat under command of Lieut. Commander Guenther Prien, the youthful, rosy-cheeked German who commanded the U-boat that slipped into Scapa Flow and sank the British battleship Royal Oak with loss of 810 lives, Nazis said. The heavy cruiser sunk was of the London class, according to the German report of the sinking, and had a complement of 650 men. The London type British cruisers are the Shropshire, the Sussex, the Devonshire and the London. The cruiser would be the 10th British warship sunk by Germany since the war began. The London type cruiser has eight eight-inch guns, eight four-inch guns and 20 smaller guns; eight torpedo tubes and carries one aircraft to be catapulted into the air. The British ha

(By Associated Press) The mounting Finnish-Russian crisis shared the European spotlight today with the increasingly bitter German-allied conflict of the sea. While British maritime losses from the war with Germany mounted and the western front remained quiet, Finland replied with an offer of compromise to Russia’s demands for withdrawal of Finnish troops from the frontier. Finland agreed to make such withdrawal if Russia did likewise. Deny “Hostile Intentions” The Finnish government, denying “hostile intentions,” suggested the dispute be referred to a joint commission established last year to take care of border problems. Thus Finland tactfully left the door open for Russia to renew negotiations which were broken off Nov. 13 when the Finns refused Soviet demands for military concessions and border revision. Archibald MacLeish, the Librarian, immediately announced the document would have the same 24-hour armed guard as that given the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence, near which it will be displayed. BERLIN, Nov. 28 (AP) — The British fleet, in the opinion of German military experts, now has been cleared not only from the North Sea but also from the north Atlantic. Authoritative commentators said that the British “auxiliary cruiser” Rawalpindi, destroyed in a naval engagement “off the coast of Iceland, was discovered absolutely alone between the Faroe islands and Greenland. Moreover they quoted 26 Rawalpindi crewmen whose rescue was announced today as saying they were “100 per cent surprised” to find a whole German navy group, including at least one heavy cruiser, so far out in the Atlantic. German experts who are authorized to inform the foreign press state that the British have been so frightened by the combined German navy and air prowess that they have ordered the navy to withdraw from both the North Sea and the north Atlantic. Capt. Prien, the victor of Scapa Flow.” Lieut. Capt. Guenther Prien is the 31-year-old U-boat commander who became a hero overnight by slipping into the Scapa Flow naval base in the Orkney islands, north of Scotland, to sink the battleship Royal Oak Oct. 14. The Shetland islands are about 100 miles north of Scapa Flow. Nothing Known (Official quarters in London said nothing was known of the German claim of destroying a heavy cruiser. Loss of a British submarine was disclosed in the House of Commons in an admiralty review of naval warfare which asserted Britain is gaining “a definite mastery” over German submarines. Whatever results from the mediation offer of King Leopold and Queen Wilhelmina, observers at Brussels expressed belief it would make doubly difficult any immediate violation of Belgian or Netherlands neutrality by the warring powers. Fear that war would start in earnest on the western front in a few days was voiced by some quarters commenting on reports of German troop concentrations near the Netherlands frontier. The American freighter City of Flint, recently released from a German prize crew by the Norwegian government, will remain at Bergen several days. The United States minister, Mrs. J. THE HAGUE, Nov. 8.()—Official circles hinted today that King Leopold of Belgium and Queen Wilhelmina of The Netherlands might follow up their offer to serve as peace mediators with diplomatic contacts in Berlin, London and Paris. While these circles would not speculate on the probable outcome of the dramatic peace appeal delivered last night by the two sovereigns to Europe’s warring powers, an atmosphere of moderate but cautious optimism was apparent here. It was conceded that this optimism was based on the belligerent powers’ apparent reluctance to initiate major offensives rather than on any reaction produced thus far by the mediation offer. If the offer is not rejected outright, government circles said, it might be possible to make careful contact with the belligerents and thus give them further time to express their views. Some sources intimated the proposal was prompted by belief th

OFFERED mediation by the monarchs of Belgium and The Netherlands raised only scant hopes today for European peace. The three nations who received the offer, Britain, France and Germany, said only that they would consider it. Britain said consultations with France will be held before replying. Unofficial French quarters and the Paris press predicted “no” will be the French answer. Hitler Weighs Reply Germany's reply is pondered by Adolf Hitler, who “welcomed” a similar offer Aug. 29, three days before the German invasion of Poland started. Speculation immediately arose whether Queen Wilhelmina and King Leopold made their sudden move because they feared imminent military developments which would embroil their nations or whether they considered circumstances propitious for ending the conflict. (The Germans evidently took the Halifax broadcast speech as a reply to and rejection of the offer of King Leopold and Queen Wilhelmina, although copies of the speech were furnished to the press hours before the offer was announced. British officials said Halifax’ broadcast was arranged days before delivery.) Hitler Is Silent. The German sources said it was not known whether Adolf Hitler would make a formal reply to the offer to negotiate a settlement of the European war through Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop. London, Nov. 8 (4).—British warships, aided by two Polish destroyers, were reported to have fought off an attack by German aircraft today, while the British planes engaged Nazis in a “number of air actions” over the North Sea. The Admiralty, describing the air-naval battle, also in the North Sea, said the warships all escaped damage, and the Air Ministry said all British planes returned safely from the encounter. It was not known whether there were any enemy casualties. Plane Driven Off An Air Ministry communique telling of the air battles said an enemy plane approaching the Shetland Islands, north of Scotland, was driven off by anti-aircraft fire and chased away by British aircraft. “Several other enemy aircraft were sighted and two were engaged by Royal Air Force patrols many miles out over the North Sea. The enemy aircraft escaped into clouds and it is not known whether they were able

His speech was the climax of the anniversary observance here. “The (present) war broke out only because England wanted it,” he said, “If they say they didn't want war and they must make war to end war—war liar this war? bog long as are not Sarat woven gins Bway age” volun-ta “Today a British minister, with tears in his eyes, says, ‘Oh, how he would like to have an understanding with the Germans if only we could have faith in their leaders’ words.’ The same thing I would like to say. “How I would love to make peace with the E

Bergen. — (4) The American freighter City of Flint, recently released from a German prize crew by the Norwegian government, will remain here several days, it was reported today. The United States minister, Mrs. J. Borden Harriman, called meanwhile on the British naval attaché, presumably to continue negotiations in regard to disposition of the vessel's cargo.
London, Nov. 8 (4)—The 7,603-ton German freighter Uhenfels has been captured and taken to Freetown, Sierra Leone, British colony on the west coast of Africa, it was disclosed today.

1939-07-12.text: (BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS) Powers and politics were the means with which Europe’s opposing blocs of nations sought today to forge new strength. Power served Britain and France in a display of aerial preparedness which gave them opportunity to test their air forces in unison and brought a flood of angry headlines in the Berlin press. Politics brought forth plans for a virtual alliance of Bulgaria and Yugoslavia in an apparent step toward realization of a German project for a “little axis” of Bulgaria, Yugoslavia and Hungary in southeastern Europe. Flight Elates Britons In London, the British press elatedly described as a “flawless performance” a round-trip flight of 200 Royal Air Force bombers over French territory yesterday. The flight, on which London and Paris will exchange results of their “fire” on each other’s aircraft, will be followed by a return visit of French warplanes. Flights

Fascist Italy stirred up new worries for Europe today by removing Dino Grandi as ambassador to London and hastening expulsion of foreigners from Tyrol on charges of espionage in behalf of Great Britain and France. Both moves by Premier Benito Mussolini, coinciding with boosting of Great Britain's defense estimates to the peacetime record of $3,326,000,000 created concern in western European capitals largely because of mysterious circumstances surrounding the Fascist decisions. Americans Banned The expulsion of foreigners, including Americans from the Italian Tyrol, was ordered without delay for reasons "of a political and military character" due to espionage activities of "certain elements belonging to the western unions," according to an official announcement in Rome. France, Great Britain, The Netherlands and Switzerland reported considering a joint protest to Rome, believed however th

PARIS, July 12.—(UP)—Great Britain and France are firmly determined to conclude the now deadlocked negotiations to get Soviet Russia into their European security front, Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet told the United Press today. It was understood that the Council of Ministers had decided to press for conclusion of the negotiations. There were unconfirmed reports that this was decided upon to prevent Germany and Russia negotiating an agreement under which the Soviets would remain neutral in event of a European war. Nazis Seek Pact These diplomatic reports were understood to have coincided with information to the French government that Berlin and Moscow had been in contact within the last 10 days. SHANGHAI, July 12 (P) — The Japanese navy notified United States and other foreign consuls today that it was blockading three additional Fukien province ports beginning Saturday and would not be responsible for the safety of third power vessels at those ports thereafter. American and British officials were expected to give the same notice they have given previously—that they would hold Japanese responsible for damage to property or injury to their nationals. The ports to be blockaded are Chuanchow, Tungshan, and Chaoan. A few American missionaries were believed to be at Chuanchow, but none at the other points. No American vessels are involved.

France and Great Britain have chosen “the French Fourth of July”—Bastille Day next Friday—to show off their joint military power. Plans for the demonstration were approved Tuesday by the French cabinet and even while the cabinet was in session, 200 maneuvering British bombers flew from England to Bordeaux and back on a practice flight which further demonstrated the close collaboration of the two powers. The Bastille Day plans are to give the French national holiday an unusual British flavor. British officials will stand with President Albert Lebrun and the French cabinet to watch 30,000 troops, the pick of France's home and colonial forces, and a crack battalion of English soldiers parade. About 50 British planes will join 100 of the French air force in a review. Meanwhile, troubles increased for the British in China. They sent a warship steaming into the northern port of Tsingtao after

- Paris, July 11 (4)—The cabinet approved plans today for a great Bastille Day celebration Friday showing the world in general and the Rome-Berlin axis powers in particular the might of combined British-French land and air power. While the cabinet met, 200 British light and heavy bombers roared south over French territory. The heavy warplanes flew to Bordeaux and back to England without landing. Bastille Day—France’s “July 4”—marks the 150th anniversary of the fall of the Bastille July 14, 1789, at the start of the French revolution. Leslie Hoare-Belisha, British war secretary, and high commanders of Britain’s land, sea and air forces have accepted Premier Daladier’s invitation to stand with President Albert Lebrun and the French cabinet to review the Bastille Day parade before the unknown soldier's tomb.

BUFFALO, N. Y., July 12.—()—A 15-ton patrol bombing plane, built for the British air ministry, took off from the Buffalo harbor today en route to Botwood, Newfoundland, on its 5,900-mile flight to England. Pilot Russell Rogers pointed the nose of the huge twin-motored flying boat northward after an uneventful run of approximately 800 feet in the water and a preliminary ten-minute cruise to warm up the engines. The ship landed here early Tuesday to refuel, which delayed its flight 24 hours and spoiled the plans of Rogers and his three-man crew for a one-stop flight from San Diego, Calif., to Felixstowe, England. When the group left San Diego Monday, they planned to stop at the Bay of Exploits, Botwood, only long enough to refuel, then continue across the Atlantic, but headwinds encountered near Chicago rapidly reduced the fuel supply and they decided on the unscheduled stop here. (United Press Staff Correspondent) London, July 12—(UP)—Supplementary war office estimates of $370,000,000 issued today brought Great Britain’s defense estimates for the current fiscal year to the peace time record total of $3,320,000,000. The estimates included $121,400,000 for the new militia, the unique peace time conscript army; $61,750,000 for a reinforced territorial army or national guard, and $165,000,000 to accelerate the army defense program. For the moment the war office asked only $470,000 as a token of the big new appropriations to come. British and Rumanian delegates signed today an agreement reached in May by which Britain grants Rumania a credit of $25,746,000 and agrees to purchase 200,000 tons of Rumanian wheat. As the new estimates were announced, it was understood that a mass flight of bombing planes to Poland was contemplated as the next step in Britain’s new “show t

1939-10-13.text: London, Oct. 12—Prime Minister Chamberlain told Adolf Hitler today he could have peace if he wanted it, but it “must be a real and settled peace” and not that outlined by the Führer last Friday. Replying to Hitler’s peace overtures, Chamberlain scorned “an uneasy truce, interrupted by constant alarms and repeated threats.” He said the proposals of Hitler's speech were “vague and uncertain and contain no suggestion for righting the wrongs done to Czechoslovakia and Poland.” “The German government and the German government alone,” Chamberlain declared, stands in the way of the “peace we are determined to secure.” The Prime Minister said that, lacking proof of Hitler's will for peace, Britain and France “must persevere in our duty to the end.” The Prime Minister said that by acceptance of Hitler’s peace Britain would “abandon her claim that international disputes should be settled by discus

London, Oct. 12—(4)—The British navy was reported today to have captured the 13,615-ton German steamer Cap Norte. The report, issued by the British Press Association, said the Cap Norte, a ship in trade between Germany and South America, had sailed from the Brazilian port of Pernambuco Sept. 17. The capture of the Cap Norte had been hinted in yesterday’s remarks by Winston Churchill, First Lord of the Admiralty, in the House of Commons. Churchill related that during the period from September 24 to October 9, Great Britain had a favorable balance of 7,806 tons of shipping in comparing her seizures with her losses from German submarine attacks. He explained that Britain had lost 29 tons to German sub-

LONDON, Oct. 7 — (AP) — The admiralty announced that two British minesweepers were attacked by German flying boats in the North Sea this afternoon. No casualties were suffered by either side, the announcement said.

NEW YORK, Oct. 13—(#)—The American liner President Harding radioed today that she had rescued the crew of 36 of the British freighter Heronspool while proceeding to aid the attacked French tanker W. Emile Miquet. The Heronspool was sunk off the Irish coast. The Harding said it found the tanker in flames. The crew apparently had drowned. Captain James E. Roberts sent the following message to the United States Lines in New York: "At 2:10 p. m. (New York time) Thursday responded to S O S from French tanker W. Emile Miquet in Latitude 50.08 north longitude 14 west. At 1:50 a. m. sighted and rescued crew of 36 in boat from British steamer Heronspool. None missing. Reached W. Emile Miquet afire. No sign of crew. Proceeded at 9:37 a. m." The Harding left Le Verdon Oct 11 for New York with 597 passengers aboard.

Lendon——Three British ships were lost and a fourth was abandoned in a sinking condition as the result of large-scale German air raids on North Sea shipping involving at least 13 ships last night and early today. The trawler Pearl was abandoned after three of her crew had been wounded by German raiders. Two other trawlers, the Newchoice and the Camparnus, and the 487-ton steamer Serenity were sunk. This new phase of warfare, pitting planes against small ships, also sent the trawler Eileen Wray into port with a damaged hull. Acknowledgment of the air raid losses followed a British admiralty announcement that a submarine had penetrated German defenses at the mouth of the River Hibe and sunk a 6,000-ton German cruiser. Germany reported four British merchantmen had been sunk and three warships damaged in the raids yesterday. Loss of a Nazi cruiser was denied by German officials. The last traw

(UP) —Great Britain and France today rejected the “impossible” peace terms offered by Adolf Hitler and warned Germany to choose between definite guarantees for permanent European security or “war to the utmost of our strength.” The allied powers cannot trust the “unsupported word” of the Nazi government, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain told the House of Commons, again implying that Germany must eliminate the Hitler regime to “achieve a real and settled peace. “What stands in the way of such peace?” he asked dramatically.
