Virginio Gayda, often the unofficial spokesman of the government, said Mussolini alone could not “accomplish the miracle expected of him.” “He has need,” Gayda wrote in the Giornale D'Italia, “of responsible men of goodwill who listen to his words and understand with honesty the spirit in which he speaks them.” Gayda, like other Italian commentators, remained pessimistic as to the outcome of the exchange of notes between London and Berlin. NO BRIGHT HOPES The margin of time in which to avert war, he said, was lessening.

LONDON, Aug. 28.—Great Britain sent her ambassador flying back to Berlin today with a message declining to accept Adolf Hitler’s terms for solution of Germany’s quarrel with Poland but leaving the way open for further efforts to save European peace. Sir Nevile Henderson, carrying a portentous message that may climax Europe's desperate war of nerves, left by airplane from Heston Airdrome at 5 p. m. for Berlin, where Hitler and his high government and military aides awaited Britain's word.

Europe played a colossal game of power politics toward its showdown Monday. With war or peace in the balance, Sir Nevile Henderson, British ambassador to Germany, flew from London to Berlin to hand Adolf Hitler Great Britain’s reply to his demands on Poland and his “suggestions” for a solution. There appeared to be no question that the reply was adverse, but couched in language that the British government hoped would keep alive the hope of peace by urging direct negotiations between Germany and Poland or—if that is impossible—offering the services of the London government as mediator if desired. Germany's military preparations were completed, with perhaps 244 million men under arms and war supplies assembled. Official sources in Warsaw reported Germany’s troops in East Prussia were ordered completely mobilized. Food was being rationed and wardrobes were limited by decree in Germany. Sand

Paris, Aug. 28. (AP)—Protracted negotiations over the issue of peace or war were seen by French official quarters today as likely unless Adolf Hitler replies with force to Britain’s latest note. The British note which Sir Nevile Henderson was carrying by plane to Berlin was communicated to the French government. A person who saw the text said it was “technical and juridical,” calling for a full reply by Germany. Unless Germany makes a sudden coup attempting to enforce her claims on Poland, this person said, the conversations will take a long time, perhaps two weeks.” A Point by Point Reply The British note was said to reply point by point to Hitler's proposals. At the same time Premier Daladier was drawing up a second letter to Adolf Hitler today in an effort to dissuade the German Fuehrer from going to war and keep the way open for peaceful negotiations. London, Aug. 28 (GPi)—A million and a half school children tramped the streets of London and 30 other key cities in the cold light of dawn today as Britain prepared for any emergency with a rehearsal of its evacuation plans for children. By 6 a.m. the streets of the poorer sections of London were filled with children. Instead of their lunches they carried gas masks; instead of books, a change of clothes and 48 hours’ rations. It was the dreaded “first day back” after the summer vacation for many, but there were not any stragglers. The children treated evacuation as a huge joke. They laughed and yelled, brandished sticks at an imaginary “old Hitler,” and sang on their way to school. Their mothers walked along. They talked in low tones. There wasn't any gaiety among them. LONDON, June 26. — Double guards were stationed at all balloon barrage, anti-aircraft and other territorial army stations in the London area today in the belief that "Irish Republican Army" terrorists intended to strike at key defense points. Magistrates issued 139 search warrants to Scotland Yard to aid them in raids during which thirty suspects were arrested as the result of a series of bombings in London during the week-end. Twenty of the suspects were held. It was reported that fifty "I. R. A." terrorists had been sent to principal British cities from Ireland and were spending about $5,000 a week on bombing activities. Scotland Yard and Roman Catholic authorities united in a campaign against the terrorists, and Irish government authorities increased their watchfulness after disorders in three Irish cities yesterday. The statement was made in a formal protest by Shigenori Tashiro, Japanese consul general, to British Consul General Edgar G. Jamieson. London, June 25.—(P)—Britain is planning to take retaliatory measures against Japan before the end of the week, informed quarters said today, unless the Japanese agree to negotiate the Tientsin dispute. Faced by a growing demand for “strong action,” the cabinet was said to have decided to authorize such measures at its regular meeting Wednesday if the Japanese government continues silent. So far Tokyo has refused to answer requests for a clear statement as to whether wide demands made by Japanese military authorities in North China were approved by the government or whether Japan would be willing to settle the Tientsin dispute on a local basis. (Japanese began their blockade of the British and French concessions a week ago last Wednesday. Shanghai, June 26,—(4’)—The British embassy announced today that Rev. and Mrs. A. T. Caswell, Canadian missionaries, were killed at Changteh, Hunan province, last Saturday when Japanese airplanes bombed the Canadian Holiness Mission at Changteh, of which the Caswells were members. Headquarters of the mission are in Ottawa. (A telegram from the Changteh mission to the British consulate at Chungking, temporary Chinese capital, said the Japanese made repeated power dives over the compound, razing the mission’s walls despite British Union Jacks clearly painted on them. 1939-06-11.text: LONDON, June 10. (U.P)—Foreign embassies heard today that a sudden new bid for British-German understanding by Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain was actuated by information that new Central European developments might be imminent. There was no hint here of any impending trouble though Poland showed interest in a concentration of German Nazi storm troopers in Danzig for a sports festival starting Monday, and a London newspaper had reported movements of troops to Czech cities near Poland.

PARIS, June 10—(#)—French diplomats tonight warily appraised reports reaching diplomatic circles from Germany that Reichsfuehrer Hitler was drafting a specific plan for world appeasement to offer to the U. S., France and Britain next month. In Berlin, sources close to the fuehrer expressed surprise at the reports and said that as far as they knew Hitler had no such plan in mind. Speculation here was restrained pending determination whether the reports, which originated in usually well-informed Berlin sources, might be designed to sound out real possibilities of concessions following British Foreign Secretary Viscount Halifax's expressed willingness to consider a world conference of Nazi demands if Germany would renounce a policy of force. Juan Les Pins, France, June 10; (INS)—Maxine Elliott, 68-year-old stage star of the late nineties and Broadway darling of pre-World War days, was reported dying today at her home here. A sister, Lady Ford Robertson, flew from London to be at her bedside.

LONDON, June 11.—(Sunday) — British Sunday Newspapers expressed amazement today at the New York City reception of King George and Queen Elizabeth and glee at its success. A Sunday Express banner headline said: “New York Goes Crazy Over King And Queen.” The tabloid Sunday Graphic's headline was: “King Gets Crazlest Welcome Ever,” and the Chronicle-Referee said: “New York Goes King Crazy.” The Staid Observer, in an editorial headed “Thanks America, A Wonderful Welcome,” (Con. on Page 2; Sec. LONDON, June 10—Leaves of London’s entire police force, numbering almost 20,000 men, were stopped today in a desperate drive to ferret out headquarters of the Irish Republican Army, blamed for a fresh series of incendiary bombings. Explosion of three more bombs in mail boxes today led to the special police orders. Fifteen persons, most of them postal workers, suffered minor injuries today in the most widespread wave of bombings since the campaign of terrorism attributed to the Irish Republican Army began in England. Thirty bombs, of the same incendiary type employed in past disturbances by the I.R.A., were placed in mail boxes in four English cities. Authorities thought the bombings had no demonstrative relationship to the visit of King George and Queen Elizabeth to Washington and New York, but felt the outbreaks resulted from the sentencing of four men to jail at Stirling, Scotland, for

LONDON. (4)--Into the pattern of its preparedness program, the British government is working an emergency plan to shift the bulk of its administrative machinery from London to safety zones in the country. The plan would send 200,000 officials to temporary department headquarters. Only key officials would remain in London, working and sleeping in bomb-proof offices. Since Germany took Czechoslovakia, every office has had its basement reinforced, walls lined with sandbags and every basement stocked with anti-gas materials. Details of the plan to move the government offices from London are a closely guarded secret.

TIENTSIN, China, June 10.—(UR)—Japanese intend to blockade the British concession here Wednesday unless British authorities hand over a man suspected of assassinating Cheng-Si-keng, Chinese controller of customs under Japanese administration... Tension was mounting in the city and British army mobile patrols in the concession were reinforced.

New York, June 10.—King George and Queen Elizabeth came in triumph to the melting pot today and found the city of New York transformed into a citadel of warmth and royal welcome. The warmth was from the sky as well as the heart. For the mercury hovered near the 90 mark as Britain’s monarch and his gracious queen stepped from the destroyer Warrington at the Battery to enjoy the triumph and endure the torture of a long drive through the steaming city to the New York World’s Fair. They had come across the bay from Fort Hancock, Sandy Hook, to the accompaniment of a deafening welcome from harbor guns and harbor craft to set foot on the soil of New York for the first time at the spit of land that thrust Manhattan Island into the sea. | London, Jan. 19.—(AP)—Frank Chamberlain, only son of the British prime minister, escaped harm today from a bomb blast apparently aimed at him in Ireland as authorities in Britain and northern Ireland drafted thousands of police reserves to combat terrorism attributed to the outlawed Irish republican army. On a vacation in Tralee, Ireland, 25-year-old Chamberlain was jolted from his sleep before dawn when a terrific explosion at the rear of his small hotel tossed several neighbors from their beds, splintered hotel walls and tore a hole in a nearby retaining wall. Hundreds of windows in the area were shattered and police immediately undertook an intensive hunt through the Dingle peninsula, long a hotbed of anti-British republicanism on the far western Irish coast. On the political side it seemed likely to strengthen the so-called Extremists, as diplomatic quarters saw it—men like Paul Joseph Goebbels, propaganda minister, and Heinrich Himmler, chief of the dreaded Gestapo, or secret police. LONDON, Jan. 20:—Great Britain received a note from Germany today, confirming the Nazi government’s determination to achieve equality with the British navy in submarines and to build five 10,000 ton cruisers armed with 8-inch guns.

Jerusalem, Jan. 20.—(P)—One British soldier was killed and five wounded today when a land mine exploded under a military railway car in which they were patrolling the Jerusalem-Ramleh railway near Ramleh.

LONDON, Jan. 20. —(INS)— An emphatic warning that Italy will more than match any French intervention in the Spanish war has been delivered to Britain by the Italian Government, it was revealed today. International News Service learned today that when Italian Foreign Minister Count Galeazzo Ciano received British Ambassador Lord Perth Wednesday evening, he made plain the Italian position on this matter.

Tenuous as were the reports, they caused natural interest in diplomatic quarters and efforts were made at once to check them in Berlin, Rome and Geneva. London—The number of ships sunk during the European war jumped to 215 today—the 100th day of the conflict—with reports of five new sinkings aggregating at least 18,987 gross tons. The tonnage of one vessel, unlisted in shipping registries, was not announced. All of the new victims flew the British flag raising Britain's wartime toll to 116 ships of 485,848 tons. Four lives were announced as lost, raising the sea war's known death list to 2,419, but fate of the crews of three of the vessels was unknown, as the ships merely were listed as long overdue and considered lost. The new losses included Britain's eleventh naval vessel, the minesweeper Ray of Hope, sunk by a mine with the loss of four lives. The steamer Willowpool also was a victim of a mine, but the crew of 38 was saved. Missing Vessels The ships for which hope was abandoned were the steamers Ashlea, Newton Beech and Trevanion. Br

PARIS, Dec. 11 (@P).—Heavy German patrol action on the western front, notably in the Saar region near a section of the Allied line just taken over by British troops, was reported again today by military sources. The British have received their baptism of artillery fire, it was announced, and are taking part with the French in patrol activity. In the German scouting sorties raiders at some points reached French advance posts, but French reports said they were repulsed with hand grenades.

London, Dec, 10 (#).—Reliable sources tonight said Britain has agreed to allow Finland to purchase British war supplies despite a previous rule against export of war goods. Relaxation of the ruling, which refused manufacturers permission to sell munitions which the Allies need in their own war, took on a special significance in view of the League of Nations meeting tomorrow to hear Finland’s demand that Russia be declared an aggressor. The most pressing need of Finland, observers said, is pursuit planes to fight off Russian bombing attacks. At the same time sea warfare claimed two more ships and reports were received of enemy flights over Suffolk, Eastern Coast country. Both ships destroyed today belonged to neutrals. Reuters, British news agency, said in a Stockholm dispatch that the 1,928-ton Swedish steamer, Vinga, sank following an explosion. The crew was rescued. The 398-ton Netherl

LONDON—(U.P)—The weekend toll of ships wrecked by mines and torpedoes was increased to six today. The admiralty announced that the navy drifter Ray of Hope, a small, auxiliary vessel of about 200 tons, had been sunk by a mine and that four of its crew were dead and five missing. The British steamer Willowpool, 4,815 tons, struck a mine and sank in the North Sea. The crew of 36 was rescued by a lightship. The 5,182 ton Belgian steamer Kabinda broke up on a reef off the southeast British coast yesterday. The small French coastal ship Dinark was torpedoed or mined off the southeast coast, the crew of 13 escaping. A small Dutch steamer Immerman struck a mine and was driven ashore at Kallandsoog, Holland. The crew of seven was saved. An unidentified British tanker was reported by Mackay Radio at New York to have been broken in two by a torpedo off the southwest British coast.

LONDON, Dec. 11.—(#)—Flying so low the swastika on its tail was clearly seen, a German plane was sighted this morning by fishermen a mile off the southeastern coast of England. They reported they saw it continue over a nearby coastal town and then speed across the channel without a shot being fired or raid warning sounded.

Pressing other nations for aid, Finland fought invading Russian forces with military and diplomatic weapons today while European warfare cost Britain new naval and merchant shipping losses. The embattled Finns, reporting they had checked Russia’s campaign on all fronts, took their case to the League of Nations, invoking league arbitration machinery and asking that Moscow be condemned as an aggressor. Heartening to Finland was a $10,000,000 credit from the United States for the purchase of food and other non-military supplies. Finland’s appeal was up for consideration after preliminaries in which the delegate from friendly Norway, Karl J. Hambro, was elected president of the league assembly. Hambro immediately warned the league it must do its utmost to halt the Finnish-Russian war. With the French Armies at the Front, Dec. 10.—(#)—King George of England, disregarding the danger of German patrol raids, visited an observation post at the front and inspected one of the giant Maginot line fortresses this weekend. The king arrived at a sector of the Maginot line that had just been taken over by British troops. The king, wearing the uniform of a field marshal, arrived in the French zone Saturday morning. After driving to headquarters of the British force in a camouflaged automobile, he inspected barracks housing various British and French units. He went through one of the giant Maginot forts in this sector and lunched in another, smaller one. Then, removing his overcoat, despite drizzling rain, he took his place on a makeshift wooden reviewing stand and watched British and French infantry parade. 1939-02-05.text: LONDON, Feb. 6.—(U.P)—In event of war, all Britain's armed forces will be at the disposal of France, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain said today in the House of Commons. Any threat to vital French interests, Chamberlain said, would evoke “immediate” British cooperation.

AA ENN NR Re ee, LONDON, Feb. 6(4)—Spanish insurgent authorities were reliably reported today to have informed the British government their peace terms were “unconditional surrender” of the Spanish government. This disclosure came on the heels of a report in authoritative quarters that Britain and France were making a fresh attempt to mediate the two and one-half-year old war in Spain. Informed sources said C. B. Jerram, assistant to the British agent at Burgos, insurgent capital, had called the attention of Generalissimo Franco's regime to a three-point peace offer by Dr. Juan Negrin, premier of the Spanish government. The insurgents were said to have told Jerram flatly that these terms were “utterly unacceptable.” One of Negrin’s points called for an insurgent guarantee against foreign influence in Spain.

PERPIGNAN, France, Feb. 4 —The Spanish government was reported in reliable quarters Saturday night to have requested Great Britain to open secret negotiations with Insurgents to end the savage two and one-half year old civil war. The reported overtures contained such broad qualifications, however, as to raise the question of their success. They were disclosed at a time when Premier Juan Negrin’s government took first steps toward abandoning all of Catalonia—Spain's northeastern corner—to Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco's conquering forces in an attempt to make a last stand in the central “island” quarter of Spain, embracing Valencia and Madrid. It was understood that in the request to the British government the Spanish government authorities stipulated that the peace talks be opened with three points enunciated by Negrin Wednesday as the background. HOLLYWOOD — (') — Twelve thousand film folks, with the world as a kibitzer, began choosing Monday the best picture and best actors of 1938. The list of nominees, compiled by the screen guilds, was released Sunday night. The list disclosed an upswing in rival British movie-making that was something of a shock. Of the ten pictures named as possibly the best last year, two—“The Citadel” and “Pygmalion”—were British products, and a third, “Grand Illusion,” was French. Two Britishers—Robert Donat and Leslie Howard—and Gallic Charles Boyer shared nominations as the five best male players of 1938 with home-grown Spencer Tracy and James Cagney. A British discovery, Wendy Hiller, broke into the ranks of the five women nominated for the best feminine performances. WASHINGTON, Feb. 4 (UP) — President Roosevelt's Senate leaders sought support for his foreign policies tonight as it was disclosed that American manufacturers may be called upon to provide 1,550 fighting planes for the armament programs of Great Britain and France. Extent to which the manufacturing resources of this country may figure in Franco-British rearmament plans was revealed as Senate Majority Leader Alben W. Barkley announced he plans to convene the Senate Steering and Policy Committee next week. The meeting will discuss the controversy which resulted from President Roosevelt's enunciation of cardinal points of his foreign policy and his sharp denial of reports he had placed this country’s defense frontier on the Rhine. A bomb explosion just before midnight tonight tore a hole in the outer wall of Walton prison at Liverpool where several men are being held in connection with bombing outrages attributed to Irish Republican extremists. LONDON, Feb. 4.—(#)— The houses of parliament were closed to the public today for the first time since the World War as a precaution while Britain sought to suppress the wave of terrorism attributed to the outlawed Irish Republican Army. The Sunday Dispatch reported raids on I.R.A. houses in Belfast resulted in the discovery of plans to blow up Buckingham Palace, Windsor Castle, the House of Commons and the Bank of England. The newspaper's report, which lacked official confirmation from any source, said the raids also uncovered details of a plot to assassinate British politicians and high police officials. (4)—Impressed by the prospect of faster deliveries, the British government has asked two United States concerns already working on orders for 400 military planes to increase the number to 650. The air ministry announced Saturday orders for the additional planes, about $13,000,000 worth in addition to the original $35,000,000, had been placed. Prime Minister Chamberlain is expected to announce broad guarantees to Greece and Turkey to parliament tomorrow, advancing another step the British-French program to halt aggression that was begun after Germany broke up Czecho-Slovakia last month. The declaration to be read in the House of Commons is expected to state that any act of aggression in the eastern Mediterranean would be considered an “unfriendly act.” Political informants said Chamberlain, meanwhile, was prepared to accept promises attributed to Premier Mussolini that, now that Italy has occupied Albania, he is willing henceforth to preserve present Mediterranean territorial alignments. LONDON, April 13 — (UP) — Great Britain and France today promised to fight any attack on Rumania or Greece and to resist with arms any attempt to change by force the status quo in the Mediterranean. In sweeping simultaneous declarations here and in Paris the two governments disclosed that swift action had blocked Fascist threats to occupy the Greek island of Corfu and warned the dictatorships that their armed forces were ready to oppose further aggression in Europe. The declarations were made while the British and French governments were meeting to discuss the situation in the Mediterranean. They materially strengthened the so-called democratic front which includes Poland and involves negotiations for support of Turkey, Soviet Russia and other nations. LONDON, April 12.--A declaration designed to forestall further German-Italian expansion toward the Dardanelles and still leave the way open for appeasement of Italy was under preparation tonight by Prime Minister Chamberlain for delivery tomorrow to an extraordinary parliamentary session. Edouard Daladier, the French premier, was ready to back up the British stand with blunt words of his own in a parallel declaration tomorrow: The air, land and sea forces of Britain matched those of her ever-ready French ally in rising to the new slogan “We've got to be prepared” which flames from every other London billboard. Warplanes sped over the east coast of Britain in all-night patrol—an extraordinary precaution against any “lightning thrust.” Anti-aircraft units were swollen well past full peace-time strength. LONDON, April 12.--()—An authoritative source said today that Great Britain had started an all-night air patrol of her east coast as an extraordinary precaution against attack. This action, which the air ministry refused to confirm but did not deny, was reported to have been taken merely as a precautionary measure. Anti-aircraft defenses of London have been almost doubled since the September German-Czecho-Slovak crisis.

WASHINGTON, April 13 (4)—The job of bartering American cotton and wheat for rubber, tin and other strategic war materials may be assigned to Joseph P. Kennedy, ambassador to Great Britain. Senators backing the scheme said today that Secretary Hull apparently had received favorably a suggestion that Kennedy be delegated to undertake preliminary negotiations.

The five major powers—Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Russia, have among them more than 33,000,000 men either under arms or in reserve—the greatest potential armies ever ready for action in history. Russia has 18,000,000 trained reserves and men in active service; France has 6,250,000, Italy 6,300,000, Germany 2,200,000 and Britain 550,000. Allied with the democracies and the dictators are 8,000,000 seasoned troops of secondary powers, which means that if war comes—statesmen insist it is still no certainty—41,000,000 men will be available for action. LONDON, April 12. (?—The Daily Mirror said today that German secret police uncovered a plot of a group of Czechs to shoot Adolph Hitler as he spoke at the launching of the battleship Tirpitz at Wilhelmshaven. In an undated article, the paper said the Gestapo on March 31, the day before the launching, searched nearby quays and arrested two Czechs who carried automatic pistols. In a raid on a nearby house, owned by a former Sudeten German, the article said they arrested four more Czechs, all armed. All of the Czechs calmly confessed to the plot, according to The Mirror.

WASHINGTON—Roosevelt represented as unlikely to offer mediation in European war unless Britain, France see desire. LONDON—Chamberlain may reply to Hitler’s plea on Monday; press cool toward Nazi terms. PARIS—France prepares for long war; Germans reported moving reinforcements to western front where quiet continues. ROME—Fascists say Mussolini ready to lend good offices if Britain, France signify interest in peace parley. MOSCOW—Russia maps week-end talks with Lithuania, Turkey as her influence expands in eastern Europe. COPENHAGEN—Finland may be next to send envoy to Moscow for conference.

The British reaction to the Fuehrer's speech yesterday was considered in responsible quarters as “not too bad,” but optimism was tempered by the fact that a wider opening for negotiations still had not come from London or Paris. Editorials in the controlled Fascist press indicated the government, however, was not stepping forward to push along the proposals. Newspapers merely advocated acceptance of Hitler's overtures as offering a “constructive basis for negotiations.” If Great Britain and France indicated their willingness to participate in a peace parley, informed sources said, the Italians gladly would lend their good offices for an exchange of ideas, or for communications between

London, Oct. 6.—(#)—Adolf Hitler’s peace proposals were promised a careful but wary examination tonight by a British government proud of its naval might and the quick dispatch of expeditionary forces to France. Britain’s cautiously worded comment on Hitler’s Reichstag speech coincided with accounts of achievements of its armed forces—that the Royal Navy "continues successfully to hold the seas" and that British expeditionary forces were arriving in France "in greater numbers and with a larger volume of material than was thought possible." An official British statement dismissed Hitler’s survey of past events with the assertion that it "abounds in perversions of the truth which will be readily recognized by the people of this country and indeed of the whole world."

PARIS, Oct. 6—(U.P)— France and England, if necessary, will wage total war against Germany's attempt to establish a European hegemony, Premier Edouard Daladier said today in a two hour speech before the Senate foreign relations committee. Daladier did not comment on Fuehrer Adolf Hitler’s speech before the Reichstag because the text had not arrived when the Senate committee met. However, he reiterated his Wednesday statement to the foreign relations committee of the Chamber of Deputies. He said that he would examine and submit to parliament reasonable propositions accompanied by iron-clad guarantees. But, Daladier said, France would not bow to a fait accompli by violence or to a dictate.

LONDON (UP)—The Ministry of Information said today that “no peace proposals are likely to be found acceptable which do not effectively free Europe from the menace of aggression.” In the first official British reaction to Adolf Hitler's Reichstag speech the ministry referred to the Fuehrer's proposals as “vague” and “obscure.” “ It is noted that the proposals contain no suggestion of reparations for wrongs done by Germany to other peoples,” the ministry said. “Nevertheless, they will be subjected to careful examination in consultation with the Dominion governments and the French republic.” No Basis for Peace Other high political sources indicated that Hitler’s speech failed to offer any basis for peace. “It is remembered that assurances given by the German government in the past have on so many occasions proved worthless that something more than words are required today to establish that

These were concessions in the Baltic and the right to send her armies into the Ukraine and White Russia, areas on the Soviet side of the German-Russian front. Demands Caused Failure A British-French plan to use Soviet Russia as a base of operations in defense of Poland, these sources said, failed because of a breakdown in military talks here last August as a result of the Russian demands. Great Britain and France, they said, had proposed sending large supplies, warplanes and troops to Russia in preparation for going quickly to Poland's aid in the event of the war which then had not started. 1939-01-29.text: LONDON, Jan. 28. (P) — Prime Minister Chamberlain shook up his cabinet today to put new drive into the defense and agriculture ministries—both vital to Britain's ability to wage war—at a time of growing European tension. - Admiral of the Fleet Lord Chatfield, one of the key figures in Britain's vast naval rearmament program, was brought into the cabinet as minister for coordination of defense. He replaced Sir Thomas Inskip, who had held the post since March 13, 1936. Sir Thomas took the dominions portfolio which Malcolm MacDonald had been holding along with the secretaryship of colonies. W. S. Morrison, who like Sir Thomas has been a constant target of criticism, moved from the ministry of agriculture to become chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster.

LONDON, Jan. 28. —(U.R)— The British cabinet was re-shuffled today to put Lord Chatfield, admiral of the fleet, in charge of the entire defense program, designed to build up Britain’s navy, army and air force to invincible strength. Lord Chatfield, a veteran strategist of the navy and one of the important factors in maintaining its efficiency during the post-war lag in building, will replace Sir Thomas Inskip in the vital cabinet post of minister for co-ordination of defense. Inskip primarily is a lawyer, not a military man, and the defense program under his direction has been the target of fiery criticism. He will be retained in the cabinet as secretary for the dominions, a post held temporarily by Malcolm MacDonald in addition to his job as colonial secretary, which he retains. He stresses Britain's growing strength for defense in a speech before a hometown audience of businessmen and told of international misgivings over the future. There have been fears in some quarters that Hitler would voice before the Reichstag colonial or other demands which, in connection with Italian clamor for French territory and Spanish Insurgent successes, would heighten Europe’s tension. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain told a war worried Europe Saturday night that Great Britain is perfecting her mighty land, sea and air armaments to resist any attempt to dominate the world by force. The British prime minister echoed the sentiments expressed in President Roosevelt’s recent message to congress cautioning the dictatorships, and declared that the world’s democracies “must inevitably resist” any act of aggression. He called upon the totalitarian powers to make a contribution to the peace which, he said, Britain so ardently desires. An emphatic reference to the role Premier Benito Mussolini had played in averting war last September, but only brief mention of Chancellor Adolf Hitler, caused observers to believe that the prime minister was steeling himself against any new German demands while holding out hope of appeasement with Italy. 1939-03-04.text: London, March 3.—(#)—The Madrid government, now deprived of the recognition of Britain and France, is embarrassing these two countries by apparently stiffening its resistance to the nationalists and thwarting the two democracies’ attempts to bring an early end to the Spanish civil war. The republicans were stubbornly holding onto their capital today, and also to the one-fourth of the country still in their hands, whereas British and French leaders expressed belief, as they extended formal recognition to the nationalists last Monday, that the war must end soon with Madrid's defeat, Want End Britain and France are anxious to have the war end and to penetrate into the new Spain’s economic life, in which Italy and Germany, as older friends of the nationalists, already are entrenched. LONDON, March 3.—(#)—Arrangements were reported tonight to have been completed for transporting 3,000 Sudeten Germans to western Canada for settlement in the Peace River district and northern Saskatchewan. The Czecho-Slovak government was said to have agreed to provide $2,000,000 which the settlers would take with them to establish themselves in farming communities. It was reported Canadian railway companies had completed preparations to take the first group of settlers early next month. The settlers will be those of German blood who refused to become citizens of Germany when the Sudetenland where they lived was turned over to that nation under the Munich accord of September 29, 1938. They have been living in refugee camps provided by the Czechoslovak government since they gave up their homes.

RAJKOT, India, Mar. 3—(AP)— Mohandas K. Gandhi began today his fifth hunger strike, determined to continue “unto death” unless the native ruler of Rajkot state meets his demands for administrative reforms. The frail, 69-year-old spiritual leader withdrew from the outside world at noon and spent the rest of the day lying on a rustic cot in his bare room. Only closest associates could see the bespectacled little holy man. Among them was his 15-year-old sister. She conversed earnestly with him for an hour. Gandhi demanded that the native ruler of Rajkot, Thakore Saheb Shri Dharmendrasinhji, give the people of the tiny Western India state “a voice in the government.” Physicians said Gandhi’s vitality is very low. British Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax told the House of Lords yesterday in announcing the British-Japanese agreement that he expected anti-British agitation would cease as a result, but instead new British-Japanese friction arose. Official sources said the “suspects” were being watched by Scotland Yard and Military Intelligence Service men. They also stated there would be an “immediate” roundup upon enactment of a government emergency bill designed to crush the outlawed I. R. A. Quick raids on homes of known I. R. A. members and sympathizers would be made under extraordinary powers granted by the measure, it was said, and “many” might be deported forthwith. The bill sped toward final passage before parliament’s scheduled adjournment Aug. 4 after a personal appeal by Home Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare who declared I. R. SHANGHAI, July 25.—(UP)— The British passenger steamer Haitan was reported today to have struck a floating mine between Formosa and Swatow, the Chinese port which is occupied by the Japanese. The steamer was at anchor, apparently disabled and taking water in two of its holds. The Haitan is a ship of 3,554 tons, owned by the British Douglas Steamship Co. Blockade Spreads The incident emphasized the extent of Japan’s blockade of ports on the China coast, which is supplemented by the sowing of mines in river mouths and the approaches to harbors. It was reported that the blockade may be extended to Shameen, the rich foreign area of Canton, as the Japanese announced that the Pearl River would be closed to navigation. The Japanese order, issued at Hong Kong this morning, gave notice that the river would be closed “for approximately two weeks.”

London (*)—Britain flapped her wings over Europe today in her most impressive show of aerial strength as 240 Royal Air Force heavy and medium bombing planes staged the greatest mass flight in the history of British aviation. As the last wave of 42 Hampden bombers was crossing the channel for exercises over France, a first wave of 60 Beaufighters was landing back in England after completing a round trip of about 756 miles in about three hours. The air ministry estimated that between 1,100 and 1,200 officers and men took part in the flights. The routes taken covered such widely separated areas as Paris, Lyon, the southeastern corner of the Bay of Biscay and the Gulf of Lions. Throughout the journey over France the British planes were intercepted by French fighters and reconnaissance craft. In the hundred and first Royal Air Force fatal accident since Jan. 1, three crew members were killed

Protest The British consul-general at Shanghai protested to the Japanese consul-general against the detention of H. Rose, chief of the international settlement municipal council’s public health department, by police of the Japanese-dominated Shanghai municipality. Rose, 100 Chinese and a Russian, all employees of the department, were detained on orders of the Chinese mayor. It was reported the Japanese-dominated puppet regime had threatened to hold them until the international settlement paid arrears for garbage dumping privileges. London, July 24.—(AP)—A modern counterpart of the abortive 17th century “gun powder plot” to blow up the historic houses of parliament was attributed today by Home Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare to terrorists of the outlawed Irish republican army. Sir Samuel told the house of commons of the bizarre plot today when he reported the government had discovered a document which he called “plans” and which he said outlined virtually all terrorist acts of the past six months. He declared it was “a very carefully worked out plan—the kind that might be worked out by a general staff.” Plot Wide Sir Samuel added that terrorism in England was being “stimulated by foreign organizations” and was timed to coincide with the international crisis. WASHINGTON — Administration officials indicated today that the parallel course of British and American foreign policy in the Far East may run in opposite direction soon as a result of Britain’s official recognition of Japan’s special position in China. This government, officials indicated, has no intention of recognizing that Japan occupies any such special position as a result of her military invasion of China. This government still considers that action a violation of the nine-power treaty and the Kellogg pact. The attitude of this government is summed up in the word “illegal”, which most officials customarily use in describing Japan's military operations.

Prime Minister Chamberlain made the two statements in the House of Commons amid openly voiced fears of opposition members that he was swinging again to the appeasement policy he pursued until the German army marched into Prague March 15. 1939-08-10.text: Tokyo, Aug. 10. (P)i—The United States and France were reported today to have declared to Japan their interest in economic problems arising from the war in China, adding a complication to the already stalemated British-Japanese conference. It was believed by observers that the question of including other powers in consideration of issues between Great Britain and Japan had become a new barrier to resumption of the talks. Sir Robert Leslie Craigie, the British ambassador, has insisted that Britain could not withdraw support from the central Chinese government’s currency because other powers were concerned. Authoritative sources, however, said that Sotomatsu Kato, Japanese minister-at-large in China, had pressed Japan’s desire for a speedy resumption of the negotiations with Britain at his third meeting with Sir Robert in three days. LONDON, Aug. 9—(#)—King George VI reviewed an impressive array of Britain's reserve fleet off Weymouth today beneath overcast skies which marred the nation’s gigantic display of sea, land and air power and forced a 24-hour postponement of London's first blackout since the world war. The British admiralty, gearing its mighty war machine to meet a possible autumn “emergency” in Europe, lined up 133 ships of the reserve fleet to demonstrate to the sailor king the nation’s maritime preparedness. Standing alone in an open cockpit of a streamlined royal barge, King George swept through miles-long lines of trim warships, ranging from the 29,150-ton battleship Revenge to small, swift torpedo boats. Near the monarch in the mahogany barge was fleet Admiral Jean Darlan, supreme commander of French naval forces, and Lord Stanhope, first lord of the British admiralty. LONDON, Aug. 10—Crews of 1,300 royal air force planes engaged in battle maneuvers have been ordered to keep close watch for foreign planes flying outside the three-mile limit of territorial waters during a gigantic postponed blackout test in twenty-eight English counties tonight, it was understood today. Air force authorities believed that the blackout of half of England, in dramatic simulation of wartime conditions, would be intensely interesting to certain foreign powers. They instructed pilots, observers and crews to identify and report any strange aircraft sighted along the coast. It was disclosed recently that royal air force men had reported sighting German planes cruising outside the three-mile limit. Two auxiliary air force planes flying off the Scots coast August 3 reported that they saw the German dirigible Graf Zeppelin flying along the coast. Holiday crowds watched the craft.
LEICESTER, England, (#)— Joseph Gamble, 78, built a steel shelter against a wall to protect him from bombs in time of war. As he passed by to get a stick of wood, it collapsed, killing him.

GIBRALTAR, Aug. 10 UP— More than 75,000 Spanish troops staged sham attacks against Gibraltar today, coincident with the three-day British air raid exercises on the “rock.” The troops were equipped with tanks and field guns and converted the neutral ground separating Gibraltar from Spain into a mimic battleground. Spanish sappers constructed a third line of trenches in the neutral ground, a few yards from the border. Gun emplacements and pillboxes have been constructed on the road between La Linea and San Roque, the nearest Spanish towns to Gibraltar, the approaches to which are heavily guarded. It was reported that at least four heavy artillery batteries are stationed on the coast around Algeciras, in Spanish North Africa opposite Gibraltar, dominating the Strait. Several other long-range batteries are at Ceuta, Morocco, within easy range of Gibraltar.

SHANGHAI, Aug. 10 (INS).— Japanese airplanes today dropped bombs on the British and French consulates at Chungking, provisional Chinese capital, according to British reports here. Four Chinese were killed in the British consulate, which was badly damaged, the reports said.

Belgrade, Yugoslavia, Aug. 9 (P)—Yugoslavia has refused German and Italian demands for use of her railroads and axis supervision of her economic and military centers in event of European war, it was learned tonight on the highest authority. With the full support of Britain and France, Premier Dragisha Cvetkovich will fly to Italy tomorrow in a Yugoslav army bomber, it was said, to tell Italy’s leaders bluntly that Yugoslavia is determined to maintain strict neutrality even if it is necessary to use her arms to do so. Germany and Italy were said to have described their proposals as a form of “benevolent” neutrality. Besides use of Yugoslavia's railroads and supervision of her economic and military centers in wartime, it was said the German-Italian demands would give them complete access to all of Yugoslavia’s war materials and foodstuffs in case of war.
