LONDON Aug 10--)-P --A number of "enemy" planes--craft sweeping in from the east—succeeded today in penetrating mock defenses as far as London in the third day of rival air force maneuvers. The sky was overcast and umpires commented this condition assisted the "invaders" in getting past the "defenders" in some sectors. In others, however, the necessity for low flying made the invaders better targets for anti-aircraft batteries. As the morning maneuvers progressed, the vast network of the civilian air raid precautions system was tuned up for a midnight blackout test over more than half of England. The test was to have taken place last midnight but was postponed because of bad weather.

1939-08-09.text: London, Aug. 9. (UP)—Britain’s big show of the air, sea and land power was marred today by aerial casualties —a five-man bomber vanished in the North Sea, four fliers died in a flaming crash and four were forced to “bail out” of a third bombing plane. A checkup established that a Wellington bomber disappeared at 2:50 a. m. today and was believed to have plunged into the sea east of Yarmouth. It was near Tollerton, in rural Yorkshire, that the four fliers died in a crash. The four airmen who took to their parachutes over Thetford were slightly bruised. They had been ordered to jump by a flight sergeant who himself stuck to the controls and landed the bomber with damage only to the undercarriage. The aerial exercises, a mythical struggle between “Eastland” and “Westland” — were resumed at dawn today with about 1,300 of Britain’s best warplanes in action. Waves of “raiders,” about 500 plane

London, Aug. 9.—Great Britain put the 133 warships of its formidable fleet reserve on active service today and prepared for the biggest ‘blackout’ test ever held in peace time as the country swung into the second day of a gigantic preparedness test. Five hundred balloons of the balloon barrage had been sent up to ring London. As would be the case in wartime, France had flashed word that planes were flying toward England and the air ministry had issued a preliminary bulletin, first, that eastland bombers were rumored to be preparing for an attack, then, that they had crossed the French coast at speeds approaching 300 miles an hour. In the defending fleet were secret fighting planes reported to exceed 400 miles an hour. Tonight's test, so far as the British public was concerned, was to be even more realistic. It was the first big scale workout of the air raid precautions and other services

- LONDON, Aug. 9 UP)—Private sources here reported today that Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy had suffered a heart attack, complicated by stomach ulcers, and that he had flown from Bologna to Rome for medical attention. Informants said that according to their advices today, Mussolini was now somewhat better but that he would need a long period of comparative rest. These sources regarded it as significant that Mussolini did not witness all of the war maneuvers in northwestern Italy and that he, as War Minister as well as Premier, absented himself today from the big review at Turin which marked the ceremonial end of the war games. ROME, Aug. 9 WP) — Best sources, checked today, said that Premier Benito Mussolini was perfectly well. It was explained that he returned to Rome when army maneuvers were already over and that King Victor Emmanuel had been scheduled in advance to review a parade

London Aug. 4 - Britain used 1,300 warplanes and 60,000 air defense soldiers in a gigantic test of air raid precautions tonight and at its conclusion the air ministry announced that all aircraft “attacking” from the direction of France and Germany had been detected. Listening posts succeeded in reporting every attacking bomber, it was announced, although the speed of the attack theoretically caught the defenders not fully prepared. Lifeboats put out from Walton on the Naze and Aldeburgh following reports that two bombers came down in the North Sea. Another bomber crashed in a field in Yorkshire shortly after midnight and first reports said five occupants were believed dead. After “photographic” raids on such strategic ports as Southampton and Portsmouth, raiding and defending planes returned safely to their bases. Renewal of the mimic aerial warfare will begin at dawn tomorrow while the

SHANGHAI, August 9—An angry Japanese protest disclosed today that the British destroyer Tenedo had landed bluejackets at Swatow to protect British subjects from a mob. The Japanese protest, which complained of the wounding of one Chinese, indicated that the British bluejackets had taken an active part in defense. A dispatch from Hong Kong conveyed the official announcement that at the request of the British Consul, the Tenedo had landed a bluejacket party at Swatow to protect the British Consulate Monday.

Great Britain warned Europe of its preparedness against attack today by the greatest air maneuvers in peace-time history, accompanied by a formidable fleet display off the south coast. The British tests were followed with the keenest interest by all of Europe, tense over what may develop out of the Danzig-Polish dispute. Five hundred war birds roared over the channel from France in a mock raid and were met by 680 defending planes and all of the country’s anti-aircraft defenses. Squadrons of fighting planes held mock fights over London, and bombers dropped mimic bombs. King Reviews Warships At Weymouth, King George reviewed the reserve fleet of 133 warships, which will join the regular fleet in maneuvers off the Scottish coast. Tonight, 20,000,000 people in an area comprising half of England will rehearse for war protection in a gigantic blackout test. Paris reported that the German-Polis

London, Aug. 9—Despite the countless millions spent on its defense, London remains easy prey for enemy air raiders, the British air ministry admitted today in the first official appraisal of widespread aerial maneuvers during the past 48 hours. Poor weather which cut down the visibility of "defending" forces enabled huge squadrons of bombing planes, representing enemy raiders, to break through at strategic points and wreak heavy damage upon London and its environs, the air ministry disclosed. The sham warfare in the air caused the death of five members of the crew of an "attacking" bomber which crashed and burned near York. Another royal air force plane was reported to have been forced down at sea off the coast of Suffolk.

JERUSALEM, Aug. 9.—(UP)—Three Jewish supernumerary policemen were killed and two wounded today by a land mine which exploded under a police truck near Ekron, the Jewish colony south of Tel-Aviv. A British police sergeant was killed and two British constables wounded later when a bomb exploded inside a patrol motor launch which left the Nathanya Jewish colony north of Tel-Aviv to trace a shipload of illegal Jewish immigrants reported approaching territorial waters.

1939-02-28.text: Prime Minister Chamberlain read to the House of Commons today a telegram from Generalissimo Franco asserting that the newly-recognized Spanish Nationalist government would maintain its independence. The Prime Minister read the message during a bitter debate on Britain's recognition of the nationalist regime in which the Laborite opposition charged that Italy and Germany would dominate Spain. The telegram said: "Spain is not disposed to accept any foreign intervention which might impair their (the nationalist government's) dignity or sovereignty." ASSURANCES Chamberlain also said Franco had given the British government "assurances against general reprisals for strictly political offenses." Amid opposition cheers, Labor Leader Clement R. Attlee moved a vote of censure against the British government for its recognition of the Franco regime as the legitimate government of Spain. Attlee said

PARIS, Feb. 28.—(UP)— President Manuel Azana of Loyalist Spain announced his resignation today while the British and French governments awaited news that Loyalist resistance in central Spain had collapsed. French and British warships were believed waiting off the Spanish Mediterranean coast to evacuate Loyalist leaders in event that Premier Juan Negrin and his associates decided that to continue the war was useless. Members of the Republican cabinet who were in Madrid left this afternoon for Valencia in response to a summons from Negrin, who awaited them there for an emergency and perhaps final meeting. Azana sent his resignation from Collonges-Sous-Saleve, in the French Alps, to Diego Martinez Barrio, vice president of the republic and president of the cortes of parliament. To Call Parliament Barrio said that as soon as he received it he would call a meeting of members of the parliament

JERUSALEM, Feb. 28 ().— British troops, acting to put down a new wave of Arab-Jewish terrorism in which 34 persons had been slain this week, killed 16 men today in a battle with a large armed band on the northern frontier of Palestine. Royal Air Force warplanes aided the soldiers. Another disastrous bomb explosion in Jerusalem probably was averted when police seized a time bomb in the David Street market where three persons were killed and six wounded in explosions yesterday. Two Jews were killed and three others injured by an Arab band today. British authorities conducted widespread searches for those responsible for destructive explosions yesterday here and in Haifa. An Arab strike was declared in Haifa in protest against yesterday's bombings.

PARIS. Feb. 27—(4)—Great Britain and France accorded full recognition to Generalissimo Francisco Franco’s nationalist government of Spain today after a weekend in which Madrid government leaders stated an armistice was being arranged to end the civil war. First Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain announced to the British House of Commons that his government had accorded recognition to the Burgos regime. Shortly afterward the French cabinet met with Premier Edouard Daladier and President Albert Lebrun and took similar action. The joint decision meant that only the United States and Soviet Russia among the great powers now recognize the old government of Spain as the real government. The Madrid government's ambassador to Paris and his staff made i (Please Turn to Page Two)

French government leaders got little comfort today from the speech in which Gen. Francisco Franco acknowledged recognition by the democracies of his nationalist Spanish government. The recognition cleared away the red tape of formality so that Britain and France could carry on an intensive drive to weaken German and Italian influence in Spain and, in consequence, maintain an equitable balance of power in the Mediterranean. Addresses Cheering Franco, speaking Monday to cheering crowds at Burgos which is his capital, declared precisely that “it would be unfair in these moments of triumph, when even those who fought against us recognize us, that we should not remember those who believed in us from the first day.... “To the sister nations, to our sister Portugal, to our beloved Italy, to friendly Germany, to the nations in America who also encouraged us then, we give our friendship and remem

The president of the Spanish Republic, Manuel Azana, resigned in exile today while France and Britain, anxious over German-Italian influence in Spain, watched the results of their recognition of Generalissimo Franco as the ruler of Spain. Azana, who fled to France after the fall of Barcelona January 26, sent his resignation to his constitutional successor, Diego Martinez Barrio, president of the Spanish cortes—parliament. But it was understood Martinez Barrio had declined the succession, leaving the Republican regime without a chief of state. Interest immediately focused on what effect Azana’s resignation would have on the plans of Premier Juan Negrin, General Jose Miaja, and other government leaders in the one-fourth of Spain remaining under their control. Though it was not known whether resistance would be continued against the Nationalists, the battle fronts of central Spain were quie

HONG KONG, Feb. 21. (A. P.)—Nine persons, including a British Indian policeman, were killed today when Japanese warplanes bombed a railroad station inside the borders of this British crown colony. Sir Geoffry Northcote, governor of Hong Kong, after a personal investigation, sent a report to London and requested the British consul-general in Canton to vigorously protest to the Japanese government. The raid led to the influx of several thousand refugees from the heavily bombed area adjacent to the Hong Kong border. In Shumchun Pye, just outside British territory, it was estimated that the planes had caused more than 100 casualties among civilian Chinese. The bombers also demolished a railway car in which a score of British policemen were sheltered near the station. British military authorities said the low-flying Japanese planes first dropped bombs in Chinese territory not far from the wes

(United Press Staff Correspondents Burgos, Spain, Feb. 28—(UP)— Generalissimo Francisco Franco pledged Spanish friendship to Italy and Germany and denounced "the eternal Jew" in a victory speech to a cheering crowd before his official residence last night, after announcement of British and French recognition. There was no note of hope in the speech for those nations which may seek to alienate Spain from the totalitarian countries which aided the Nationalist cause while France, particularly, was charged with aiding the Loyalists. "It would be unjust in these moments of triumph, when we are recognized by even those who fought us, if we did not remember those who since the first days believed in us, those who shed their blood with ours, those who placed their honor side by side with ours," he said. "Those strong and noble nations have conscience, virtue, spirituality and power. "Our affecti

1939-02-11.text: By The Associated Press London, Feb. 10.—The death of Pope Pius XI, an apostle of peace in a world tormented with strife, caused grief today among both Catholics and non-Catholics throughout the world. The pontiff was the spiritual father of 331,500,000 Roman Catholics all over the earth, but sorrow over his death was not confined to them. Flags throughout Europe flew at half staff and from many nations came expressions of sympathy, tribute and grief. In France, news of the Holy Father's death in his Vatican palace caused profound sorrow among the nation’s predominantly Catholic population. Special masses were ordered immediately in all parishes. Worshippers thronged to the great cathedral of the Westminster archdiocese in London and preparations were made for a requiem mass there. England’s only member of the college of cardinals, Arthur Cardinal Hinsley, who called Pope Pius “one of th

Tokyo, Feb. 10 (?).—A Japanese expeditionary force today seized the chief cities of China’s Hainan island, off the South China coast, 300 miles southwest of Hongkong and close to the empire lifelines of France and Britain. (Hainan, commanding eastern approaches to French Indo-China, has been considered within France's sphere of influence and observers believed Japanese occupation might mean trouble with France. (In Paris, however, it was authoritatively indicated that France would not act, assuming that the Japanese occupation would be temporary.) Imperial headquarters announced that Hainan’s capital, Kiungchow, and nearby Hoihow, chief port and provincial city, at the northern tip of the island, had been taken without resistance or Japanese casualties. Japanese units were said to be encircling the island. An admiralty spokesman said the expedition’s aim was to strengthen the Japanese bl

| LONDON, Feb. 11. (UP). — An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from | Rangoon, Burma, said today that ‘seven persons had been killed and 16 wounded when military police fired on a mob of 10,000 who, ‘marching and wrecking shops as jthey shouted demands for release \of men in jail, defied orders to dis- | perse. It was assumed that the Rangoon disorders were a continuance of |those which invoked stern meas- ‘ures for several weeks. Students and oil field workers, particularly, had demonstrated in protest against allegedly repressive meas- ures of the government, and many had been arrested as agitators, |

Washington, Feb. 10.—(#)—The state department announced today the issuance of licenses in January for the sale of $4,471,471.50 worth of airplanes to Great Britain. Four million dollars of this was specifically for fighting planes. The number of planes was not mentioned, but, on the basis of price, probably was not more than 100. January, the state department announcement showed, was a good sales month of war supplies, the licenses issued totaling $6,271,030.86.

Perpignan, France, Feb. 10 (P).—Premier Juan Negrin of government Spain flew back to Spanish soil today apparently still determined to fight to the end against the Insurgents. But Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco's forces had planted their banners at Puigcerda, the last frontier post abandoned by fleeing government troops in northeast Spain, and neutral observers predicted peace in Spain within a few days. Despite firm government declarations of continued resistance and denials of any peace negotiations with Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco, the date of February 18 was suggested for the surrender of central Spain. The civil war then will be just 31 months old. Conference Held In London, British Prime Minister Chamberlain conferred with a cabinet committee on the question of early recognition of the Franco government by both Britain and France. Chamberlain was said to beli

Bucharest, Feb. 11. (AP)—Soldiers, firing rifles and pistols in a brisk clash with terrorists, last night repulsed what appeared to be an effort to seize the Bucharest state radio station. An announcement of the clash was withheld until this noon, and there was nothing in a brief communique to indicate whether the attackers were outlawed Iron Guard conspirators who have played major roles in Rumania’s recent domestic troubles. The communique stated that one of the attacking groups was killed and 15 captured.

PARIS — The German government today invited Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet to go to Berlin to talk over general European peace problems with Joachim Von Ribbentrop, German foreign minister, the foreign office made known. Central Europe, Spain and Italy’s aspirations were mentioned as chief problems suggested for discussion. It was said that Robert Coulondre, new French ambassador to Berlin, came here specially several days ago with a report of talks he had had with Ribbentrop, who then emphasized that a conference with Bonnet would logically follow the recent signature of a France-Germany good neighbor treaty, which Ribbentrop came here to sign. France was understood to be consulting the British government on the proposed talks because of the desire to keep all French-British continental policies coordinated.

PARIS, Feb. 11—(UP)—France has asked Japan to explain the object, duration and nature of its occupation of Hainan island, off the south coast of China and opposite French Indo-China, the foreign office announced today. The representations were made through the French ambassador at Tokyo to the Japanese foreign office, it was said. Joint Protest France has consulted the British government regarding the occupation, considered of great importance to powers with interests in the Far East, and have decided to adopt a common policy of protest if inquiry shows that the occupation is likely to be permanent, it was understood. The French government was reported to believe that the occupation was effected to aid Japan in controlling ship movements and preventing China from receiving arms. Japan has persistently accused the French government of tolerating a clandestine traffic in arms to China desp

1939-10-25.text: By Associated Press. BERLIN, Oct. 25—Germany’s next war move probably will be to loose a shower of bombs on England, the benign newspaper Nationalzeitung of Essen said today. This daily is known to be especially close to Field Marshal Hermann Wilhelm Goering, air minister and No. 2 Nazi. Hence its editorials command special attention. “The moment has come when the war desired by England must rain down upon the British Isle itself,” Nationalzeitung said. “The patience of a people has limits. In their doubtless indignation the German people to a man now turn against the British war inciters in order, by a fight which hereafter will be relentless, to create the necessary guarantees for their security from such irresponsible machination.” Meanwhile the High Command’s Suereammecounes reported another company of French troops had been driven from German soil on the western front. How many rema

(By the Associated Press) Great Britain confronted the prospect today of weakening her North Sea blockade to combat fast and powerful German surface raiders ranging the Atlantic in the fashion of 1914. Already the United States City of Flint has been seized and at least four British merchantmen sent to the bottom—three of them apparently sunk under the very nose of a British convoy near Gibraltar. This brought the total of belligerent and neutral vessels sunk to 90, of which 45 have been British, and the tonnage total to 399,319—exclusive of cargoes. The known loss of life mounted to 1,774. Information from Norway where the City of Flint was taken by her German prize crew before going to Murmansk, Russia, indicated at least two German warships had penetrated the North Sea blockade and were roaming the Atlantic. They are the 10,000-ton pocket battleship Deutschland and the 65,400-ton crui

London.-(/?)-The air ministry announced today that Royal Air Force reconnaissance during the past 24 hours “included night flights over Berlin.” The announcement said night scouting flights also were made over Hamburg and Magdeburg. The air ministry's announcement came as the house of commons awaited Prime Minister Chamberlain's comment on the “fight to the end” speech delivered last night in Danzig by German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop. Chamberlain was expected to deal with the speech in his weekly war report, which is scheduled for tomorrow. It was understood he probably would reiterate British determination to fight to “crush Hitlerism,” but there was no indication that statement would elaborate Britain’s war aims, Von Ribbentrop’s speech apparently left British officials unmoved and brought a salvo of hatred retorts from the press.

NEW YORK, Oct. 30.-A doubled police guard today protected the British Queen Mary and French Normandie, largest passenger liners in the world, against possible sabotage. Squads of 25 police and two sergeants were assigned to day and night pier guard duty after Lieut. Commander Coddington of the U.S. Naval Intelligence reported his office had learned one of the two ships would be sabotaged “within the next few weeks.” The 81,235-ton, 975-foot Queen Mary, camouflaged a battleship gray, and the 83,423-ton, 981-foot Normandie, still flaunting her bright red funnels, are tied side by side in their Hudson river berths. Both ships have been retired from passenger service by the war.

DANZIG, Oct. 24.—(AP)—Germany is determined to fight Britain to the bitter end and is supremely confident of victory, Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop told the world tonight. In a 90-minute address von Ribbentrop warned Britain that by continuing the war she was ‘playing dangerously with the fate of her empire.’ “The present British government may go down in history as the grave-digger of the empire,” he told a group of veteran Nazi fighters which formed his immediate audience in this one-time free city, now incorporated in the Reich. The Nazi foreign minister let fall not a single hint of a possible compromise to end the war before the conflict at arms goes into its bitter conclusion. “Chamberlain refused the hands of the Fuehrer stretched out in a gesture of peace,” he shouted at the climax of his address. “Now the German people takes up the challenge. The German people is ready

Four more British merchantmen and a Greek vessel heavily laden with scrap metal were sunk and another British sinking more than a week ago was reported yesterday as intense diplomatic exchanges arose over the seizure of the American freighter City of Flint. Loss of the five British ships sent England’s toll to 45 and the losses of all nations to 90 ships. Tonnage losses of all nations rose to 339,319, exclusive of millions of dollars worth of cargoes. The total known loss of life was 1,774. As far as it could be learned from the usually reticent British sources it was the worst day they had suffered since the war began. Germany indicated a new phase in her U-boat campaign by sinking in succession three British ships near the strongly fortified Straits of Gibraltar. These ships, the Menin Ridge, 2,474 tons, Tafna, 4,413 tons and Ledbury, 3,528 tons apparently were part of a British Convoy

| LONDON, Oct. 24.—(@)—The British government promised the House of Commons a “constant endeavor to secure the largest possible measure of publicity” in the U.S. today while newspaper placards reported the “U.S.A. angry” over German seizure of the steamship City of Flint. Sir Edward Grigg, parliamentary secretary to the Ministry of Information, set forth the government’s publicity aims in reply to a question in Commons on the volume of “German propaganda” in America compared with the “shortage of information from British sources.” “I am aware that the demand in the U.S.A. for information regarding our war effort and purpose is still to a considerable extent un- (Please Turn to Page 7, Col. 2)

By FREDERICK KUH: (United Press Staff Correspondent) LONDON — Germany has agreed to aid in the expansion of the Russian navy, information reaching London indicated today. The reports came as the American embassies at Berlin and Moscow investigated the status of the American freighter City of Flint, which a Nazi prize crew sailed to Russia’s Kola Bay. According to the reports, Germany would aid Russia in building up its mysterious fleet in compensation for raw materials and other supplies which Russia has promised to send to Germany. Russia announced Sunday that P. P. Tevossyan, Russian shipbuilding commissar, would leave for Berlin soon at the head of an economic mission. Early this year, according to information here, Russia negotiated with companies in the United States for a supply of special machinery needed in building up its navy. These negotiations failed. Russia had been buying m

1939-11-10.text: London—(U.P)— Loss of H.M.S. Northern Rover, a small British Naval auxiliary vessel, was announced by the admiralty Friday. The announcement said: “The secretary of the admiralty regrets to announce that H.M.S. Northern Rover, a small auxiliary vessel, is considerably overdue and must be presumed lost. The next of kin have been informed.” The admiralty did not say how many men were aboard the vessel.

London, Nov. 9.—()— Prime Minister Chamberlain envisaged little chance today for quick peace in Europe’s “strangest of wars” and warned that at any moment it might change to a violent conflict. In an address to the lord mayor's luncheon, read by Chancellor of the Exchequer Sir John Simon because Chamberlain is ill with gout, the prime minister said he believed Germany would turn down the Belgian-Netherlands peace appeal. He blamed “stiff-necked” German leaders who “speak no language but that of force.” “We do not want to continue the war a day longer than is necessary if a satisfactory settlement can be obtained in another way,” he said. “Since we have been compelled to take up arms we shall not lay them down until we are assured that Europe has been freed from the threats which have so long paralyzed the life of her peoples,” The prime minister declared that “We know that we cannot fail

LONDON, Nov. 10. (UP)—The air ministry announced today that Royal Air Force planes engaged two enemy aircraft off the east coast of England this morning and forced down one, which later sank. Members of the crew were captured. The second German plane managed to escape, the ministry said. The engagement took place over the North Sea.

Bergen, Norway, Nov. 9 (UP) Captain Joseph A. Gainard of the American freighter City of Flint said today that the ship will unload its cargo here and sail for the United States as soon as possible. The cargo originally was destined for England. The ship was seized by Germans but was restored to its American crew by Norwegian authorities after the Germans had brought it into a Norwegian port.

LONDON, Nov. 10.—W.P—Four officers and 23 men are missing from H.M.S. Northern Rover, auxiliary naval vessel, the Admiralty announced today. The ship, long overdue at its base, was presumed to have been lost. The Northern Rover, 655 tons, was a steam trawler until the outbreak of war when it was taken over by the Royal Navy. The announcement said: "The secretary of the Admiralty regrets to announce that H.M. Northern Rover, a small auxiliary vessel, is considerably overdue and must be presumed lost. The next of kin have been informed."

(By FAC ABROCIATING AICS) The possibility that Europe’s war of waiting might turn swiftly into a conflict of carnage and destruction appeared to be increasing yesterday following Wednesday’s unsuccessful attempt to assassinate Adolf Hitler. Prime Minister Chamberlain of Great Britain warned that at any moment the war might become a “violent conflict,” and nervousness in the neutral Netherlands and Belgium increased perceptibly with rumors of intensified German activity on the Western front. The Netherlands, after ordering civilians to leave their homes in villages in the new “water line” regions, began flooding strategic areas for defense, and Belgium increased her mobilization to about 600,000 men. The bomb which exploded in Munich’s historic Buergerbrau Hall just 11 minutes after Hitler left the building, killing seven persons and wounding 63, burst only a short while after the Fuehrer

Hong Kong.-(?)-Passengers of the British air liner Dardanus, brought here from Canton today by an American naval vessel, said five Japanese planes staged a 20-minute attack at close range on their ship and continued to fire machine gun bullets into it even as the pilots landed it. Japanese officials said the plane was forced down Tuesday at Waichow island because it flew too low over a prohibited area en route from Hong Kong to Janoi, French Indo-China. The three passengers, one of them O. Cuevas, Puerto Rican employee of the Intercontinent Corp. of New York, said the report the plane was forced down was a “masterpiece of understatement.” Kenneth C. Krentz, United States consul at Canton, protested to the Japanese consul there against endangering the life of an American passenger. The other passengers were a Norwegian and an Iranian. Japanese held the plane and its mail sacks at Waichow

London—{INS}— German planes attempted a raid or reconnaissance on the east coast of England Friday, the British air ministry announced. One of the raiders was forced down and sank in the North Sea. Another, engaged in combat by British fighting planes, escaped in the clouds. The crew of the plane that was forced down boarded a dinghy and presumably escaped with their lives before the aircraft sank. Two planes of the Royal Air Force coastal command participated in the combat. Previously, a German plane, believed to be a powerful Heinkel bomber, flew over the Shetland Islands north of Scotland on a reconnaissance flight but was driven off to the southeast by British anti-aircraft fire.

1939-05-14.text: | LONDON, May 13 (UP).-All of Europe looked toward the Soviet Union tonight as the final big link in an anti-aggression chain through which Great Britain and France have lined up—on paper—a formidable coalition of powers in Europe, North Africa and the Near East. The speed with which the united front can be completed and the effectiveness with which it meets the first major test—now threatening to come in the Free City of Danzig—will be of utmost importance in the future. Poland broke the comparative calm of this weekend by issuing an official warning to Germany that any move to achieve return of Danzig to the Reich by force would find the Polish army of probably 1,300,000 men ready for war. The announcement was believed to be intended to forestall a possible Nazi surprise move over the weekend. With Great Britain having reiterated her pledge to fight with Poland if necessary and with Fo

CALLANDER, Ont., May 13— (Canadian Press)— Marie, tiniest of the Dionne quintuplets, averted a tearful situation today when she and her sisters learned England’s Princesses Elizabeth and Margaret Rose were not accompanying the king and queen to Canada. Details of the royal visit, in somewhat fairy-tale form, were told the little girls by one of their nurses. Almost in a chorus the sisters asked if they would be able to see the princesses when they go to Toronto May 22 to meet the king and queen. Told the princesses were remaining at home with their grandmother, Queen Mary, the quintuplets became silent and tears welled in their eyes. Then suddenly Marie smiled, “Maybe,” she suggested to Nurse Molly O’Shaughnessey, “The grandma queen would be lonely if the princesses did not stay at home.” A moment later the sisters were chattering about how happy the grandmother queen would be playing wi

WASHINGTON, May 13.—(AP)—Germany will be shut out of commercial transatlantic airlines to the United States until some time after the lines of Great Britain and France are established and making money. Informed officials, who gave this as their conclusion, said today it was based primarily on economic reasons. Germany asked over two years ago for permission to establish regular service to this country but no favorable answer thus far has been given—nor will it be given for some time. Officials here say this is the situation: Air accords already have been entered into with Britain and France for the operation of air lines across the Atlantic. The accord with Great Britain dates back to December, 1935. The accords provide for reciprocity—each country can operate a two-way service to the United States and the United States can operate a two-way service to each of them. And here is the crux

PARIS (France held her military forces ready on land and sea Saturday night in preparation for what diplomatic circles considered likely to be a weekend of heightened international tension. Her army was on the alert in the Maginot zone along the eastern frontier, near German fortifications which Hitler and high Nazi officers were reported to have decided suddenly to inspect. A strong detachment of the Mediterranean fleet moved late Saturday into Tunisian waters on the eve of the speech Premier Mussolini of Italy is to deliver today. The fleet movement coincided with the arrival of reports here that Mussolini would speak violently on strained Italian-French relations. The German fleet, returning from maneuvers near Gibraltar, was believed to be steaming up the Atlantic coast. The French squadron shifted to Tunisia, one of the French territories in which Mussolini has asked increased Itali

Warsaw, Mar 13, (UF)—Poland officially warned Germany tonight that her army of 1,900,000 men stood ready for war if any attempt were made to seize the free city of Danzig by force. It was understood that the government was awaiting a scheduled Nazi demonstration in the free city on Monday as an indication of the German attitude. With the heavily-armed powers of Europe aligned more firmly than ever in opposing blocs, the declaration of the Polish government emphasized the grave danger—it not the certainty—that any explosion at Danzig would touch off a general conflict. "Any attempt to alter the present state of affairs in Danzig will have an immediate effect, immediate action by the Polish military forces which at present are in a state of readiness for war," the statement said. The government's declaration was understood to have been made by common official sources. This was necessary in

ROME (*--France again became the target of Fascist press attacks Saturday as Premier Mussolini departed for Turin to make an address today which some sources expected might decide future relations between France and Italy. In some diplomatic quarters it was thought that Mussolini in his speech might give France a “last chance” to settle Italy's claim against her peaceably. In recent days the Italian press had been calling on France and Great Britain to take steps toward settling Europe’s “open problem” in which it includes Italian colonial aspirations—before it is “too late.” Newspapers have mentioned Fascist demands on Djibouti, on the French-owned railroad at that port to Addis Ababa, and on Tunisia and for part control of the Suez Canal.

Aboard Empresa of Australia May 13—(Canadian Press)—Dense fog still held the liner Empresa of Australia in the iceberg region of the North Atlantic late today, making certain that King George VI and Queen Elizabeth would be a day late arriving at Quebec for their tour of Canada and the United States. During the day the ship had only one good run, about 8 a.m. (EST) when the fog cleared somewhat and her idling engines again began driving westward. The fog closed down again in 20 minutes, however, and the liner had to stop. Between daybreak and 12:30 p.m. (EST) she made only 35 miles. Once, when the specially assigned lookout men sighted an iceberg directly in the path of the liner, the ship's engines were quickly reversed. Warning of that particular iceberg was given by the wave of cold air noticed by all on deck. The King and Queen were on the promenade deck at the time and were able to

- LIMA, Peru, May 15—()—An Indian girl said by physicians to be five years old has given birth to a six-pound baby at the Lima Maternity Hospital—to the amazement of 60 physician witnesses. The baby, a boy, was delivered in a 35-minute Caesarean operation yesterday morning. The infant was said to be well-formed and today both the child and mother were reported by the hospital to be in excellent condition. The Caesarean was performed by Dr. Gerardo Lozada and Dr. Alejandro Musalleu and among the 60 spectators was a commission of physicians preparing a report on the amazing case of precocious motherhood. The child mother, Lina Medina, was born Sept. 23, 1934, according to her parents, and that is the date on her birth certificate. But Dr. Hipolito Larrabure, chief surgeon and director of the Lima Maternity Hospital, said her birth certificate apparently was in error because Lina still has

1939-04-07.text: LONDON, APR, 6. (AP)—The British government announced today a mutual defense agreement with Poland, a drive to rid Britain of German agents and assurances from Albania that her integrity was unimpaired despite reports of impending Italian military occupation. The Poland-British agreement, still to be signed and sealed, represented the keystone of British efforts to raise defensive barricades against aggression in Europe. Britain's part in the Poland-British alliance was a week old but Poland's promise to aid Britain against any aggression was new—the product of three days of conversations here between British statesmen and Poland's foreign minister, Josef Beck. Prime Minister Chamberlain told the House of Commons that “pending completion of a permanent agreement, Colonel Beck gave an assurance that the Polish government would consider themselves under an obligation to render assistance t

London, April 6.—Prime Minister Chamberlain welded Poland into the French-British anti-aggression front today and took steps to purge Britain of German spies. Then he left for Scotland on an eastern fishing trip. Before adjourning the House of Commons for its Easter recess until April 18, the Prime Minister announced that Britain and Poland had agreed to go to each other's aid "in the event of any threat, direct or indirect, to the independence of either." He added that conversations were proceeding with a view to adding other nations to the "halt Hitler" bloc. Sir Samuel Hoare, the Home Secretary, disclosed that a German spy hunt had been going on in England, informing the House that three alleged Nazi spies had been expelled from the country within the past few weeks. The length of the Prime Minister’s vacation will depend on the international situation, momentarily tensest in the Adri

LONDON, April 7.—Intense diplomatic activity to widen the European anti-aggression bloc by including Hungary and Rumania today followed the first word of Italy’s invasion of Albania. Great Britain, at the insistence of Polish Foreign Minister Col. Joseph Beck, was understood to have agreed to allow Poland to sound out Hungary on prospects of joining the mutual defense front. (In Warsaw, the Budapest government was reported to have assured Poland already that Hungary would join Poland in resisting Nazi influence and expansion if her military forces could be strengthened). The Italian embassy in London issued a statement today saying that Italian troops would be withdrawn from Albania “as soon as the recent disturbances are terminated.” The Italian spokesman said occupation of Albania—which British officials consider a breach of the Anglo-Italian agreement guaranteeing the status quo in th

(Copyright 1939 by United Press) LONDON, April 7 — Great Britain, seeking to bring Rumania and Hungary into the “Stop Hitler” bloc, consulted with France today on the Fascist invasion of Albania in apparent violation of the British friendship treaty with Italy. Although Sir Alexander Cadogan, permanent foreign undersecretary, was understood to have described the Italian attack on Albania as a “clear” violation of the treaty, it was said that neither Paris nor London envisaged any practical measures that could be taken to restrain the Fascists. The friendship treaty concluded a year ago guaranteed maintenance of the Mediterranean status quo. Meanwhile, the British drive for a united peace front appeared to be progressing with Rumanian efforts to arrange with Turkey to keep the Dardanelles open to British and French warships in event of war.

The embassy in London issued a statement Friday saying Italian troops would be withdrawn from Albania “as soon as the recent disturbances are terminated.” The Italian spokesman said occupation of Albania—which British officials consider a breach of the Anglo-Italian agreement guaranteeing the status quo in the Mediterranean — was only temporary. He denied that Italians had met resistance from the regular Albanian army. “According to information reaching London,” the spokesman declared in a statement, “Italian troops landed at four points on the Albanian coast today and met with slight resistance from Albanian irregular troops. This resistance was not offered by the regular Albanian army.” ___ Intense diplomatic activity sought.

Berlin, April 6.—(P)—A double-barreled German attack was launched tonight against what Germans described as a Polish “change of front into the English war policy” against Germany. The foreign office mouthpiece, Deutsche Diplomatisch Politische Korrespondenz, joined the officially inspired Deutscher Dienst in expressing German irritation over the results of Polish Foreign Minister Joseph Beck’s talks in London. (Prime Minister Chamberlain announced Poland and Britain had agreed to go to one another’s aid in event of any aggression ‘threatening the other’s independence.) Want Nothing Adolf Hitler's Voelkischer Beobachter said Germany ‘wants nothing except the return of a small enclosed space inhabited exclusively by Germans (meaning Danzig) and a free route to the German northeast (apparently the right to build an automobile highway to East Prussia across the Polish corridor).’ The newspap

(Copyright 1939 by United Press) — LONDON, April 7 — Great Britain sought to include Hungary in a “Stop Hitler” bloc today as Benito Mussolini’s Fascist legions fought their way through Albania. The occupation of Albania was regarded here as the answer of the Berlin-Rome “axis” to Poland's entrance into a British-French anti-aggression combination. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain replied by: 1—Starting active negotiations to include Rumania in the “Stop Hitler” bloc. 2—To sound out Hungary on the possibility of a British guarantee of her independence, provided she agreed to resist any crossing of her territory by German soldiers. Negotiations, so far exploratory, were proceeding in London, Paris, Warsaw, Bucharest and Budapest on the Hungarian plan. Rumanian Minister Viorel V. Tilea, fresh from Bucharest with instructions from King Carol, began negotiations regarding Rumania's partici

Chicago (P)—Sam Simonson, who has been an umbrella repairman for 42 years, applied for his annual peddler's license and was reminded by Detective Edward Fitzgerald that last year he said he was going to retire. “'I can't retire now?' the 74-year-old umbrella man said. “It's that fellow in England — Chamberlain. He's made everybody umbrella conscious. Business is booming.”

1939-01-25.text: NEW YORK, Jan. 24.—(#)—The British air ministry tonight began an investigation into the mysterious power-failure crash of the 19-ton Imperial Airways flying boat Cavalier, with the loss of three lives at sea, as the captain of the lost plane said “definitely” the tragedy was not caused by icing. “The Cavalier was equipped to combat ice,” said 31-year-old Capt.

ABOARD U. S. S. OMAHA, Jan. 25.—Anti-aircraft of part of the foreign warship fleet off Llanveras opened up on insurgent warplanes today when they bombed the landing stage in front of the British embassy. The foreign warships, including United States, British and French vessels, are anchored off Llanveras to rescue nationals from the Barcelona area. All foreign warships, including the Omaha and the U. S. S. destroyer Badger, cleared their decks for action and manned anti-aircraft guns when the planes from Rebel General Francisco Franco's aerial fleet bombed Llanveras. A dozen shots were fired by one or more ships in the foreign fleet. Officers believed it was a French destroyer that opened fire, but could not confirm the identity of the guns.

London—(U.P.)—Europe’s big powers braced themselves Wednesday for the diplomatic shock that many statesmen fear will follow the showdown in the Spanish war. The drive of the Insurgents into Barcelona may not mean the end of the two and a half year old war, but dispatches from almost every European capital reflected the view that the marching armies of Rebel Gen. Francisco Franco are bringing closer, and closer a test between the democratic and totalitarian powers in the Mediterranean. The pay off may come at almost any hour. How grave that test will be and whether there will be another great international crisis remains to be determined, but factual developments on the continent appeared to leave little doubt that preparations are being made to meet any eventuality. In essence, the situation centers on the fact that Italian—and some German—forces are fighting with the triumphant Spanish

New York, —(#)— An inquiry into the crash at sea of the Bermuda-bound flying boat Cavalier was under way today with the British air ministry as the guiding force. Capt. G. C. Pirie, air attache of the British embassy, flew from Washington Tuesday to take charge of the investigation of the tragedy which cost three lives. Pirie questioned Capt. M. R. Alderson, pilot, and First Officer Neil Richardson, two of the ten survivors of the crash. The United States will take no official part in the inquiry, but at his own request James Payton, air safety inspector of the civil aeronautics authority, will be an unofficial observer. Pan-American Airways said its “Bermuda Clipper,” the only remaining flying boat in the New York to Bermuda service, would maintain its regular schedule. Bookings were reported normal.

London, Jan. 24. (?)—As the Italian and German-backed forces of Francisco Franco thrust at Barcelona tonight anxiety grew in British government and opposition quarters over what an insurgent victory in Spain would mean to British and French interests. Prime Minister Chamberlain, while having refused to summon Parliament to consider the Spanish situation ahead of its scheduled meeting next Tuesday, agreed to meet a deputation of labor leaders tonight to hear a new plea for action to help the Barcelona government. Eden Warns of “Foreign Victory.” Despite arguments of the opposition and some conservatives that a Franco victory would be a serious threat to Britain and France, Chamberlain has refused to relax the British nonintervention policy. Former British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden warned last night that “if Franco wins his victory is a foreign victory.” In Rome the Fascist press, rep

LONDON, Jan. 25. (A—C. G. Gray, one of Great Britain's best authorities on fighting planes, asserted today that Germany's air strength was only "something over 3,000 machines" and sought to reassure those who fear Britain is far behind. Describing as "bunk" a statement attributed to Col. Charles A. Lindbergh that Germany had 9,700 fighting planes to Britain's 1,500, Gray said he had "too much respect for Charles Lindbergh's intelligence and honesty to believe he told a story anything like that." Gray, co-editor of the authoritative directory, Jane's All the World's Aircraft, made his statements in the magazine, The Aeroplane. Gray said it was a "joke to put Britain's fighting air strength at 1,690 planes" and added, "I do know on quite reasonably good authority of one particular type of British high-speed bomber of which more than 1,000 have been delivered and (SAN NAZI PLANES, page 19)

PARIS, Jan. 25. — France and Great Britain today agreed to appeal to rebel Gen. Francisco Franco to refrain from mass reprisals against loyalists in Catalonia and an urgent message was dispatched from London to the insurgent capital at Burgos. The action was agreed upon as reports from the French frontier indicated that, because of a lack of transportation, hundreds of thousands of men marked for execution or imprisonment if captured, might not be able to escape into France. These advices said that insurgent troops were attempting to close a pocket between Barcelona and the French frontier in order to cut off the escape of loyalists listed in Franco’s card index—said to contain 2,000,000 names—of enemy individuals. The French frontier guards were reinforced by fresh mobile guard platoons in preparation for an exodus of an estimated 150,000 refugees from loyalist Spain. Britain and France

NEW YORK, Jan. 25 -— Vague and at times contradictory statements today confronted investigators for the British government attempting to fix the cause for the crash of the Bermuda-bound Sirliner Cavalier Saturday in the Atlantic with a loss of three lives. Although the last S. O. S. calls from the falling ship indicated its four giant motors suddenly stalled because of ice conditions, the skipper, Capt. M. R. Alderson, insisted that was not the cause. "The ice hazard was negligible," said Capt. Alderson, one of the 10 survivors rescued by the Esso Baytown, an oil tanker. "I have flown through much worse weather without mishap. Why all four motors failed, forcing the ship into mountainous seas, is a mystery to me." Depositions taken from the 10 hardy survivors, now scattered to their homes and hotels, will be introduced at a formal inquiry to be held later in Canada or Bermuda. The presen

1939-03-26.text: LONDON, Mar. 25. — (AP) The governments of Europe looked today to Rome, whence may come from Premier Mussolini an indication of what the Nazi-Fascist powers hope to do next. Premier Mussolini makes an important address tomorrow, and there was some belief here today that he might enunciate demands upon France for colonies in Africa. If he does, there likely will result another period of high tension like that of the past ten days—during which Adolf Hitler of Germany, the Italian anti-Communist partner, obliterated Czecho-Slovakia, regained Memel-land from Lithuania, and thrust the Nazi economic machine to the Black Sea by an accord with Rumania. SLOW EFFORTS In the meantime, the British government slowed efforts to form a four-power league against Germany with France, Soviet Russia, and Poland. Poland has been cool to the idea because, Polish political informants said, she does not wish t

Washington, March 25.—()— Charging Great Britain with encouraging Germany to swallow up Austria and condoning the dismemberment of Czechoslovakia, Senator Borah, Republican, Idaho, asserted tonight Chancellor Hitler has “no better friend” than England. In an address prepared for delivery over the radio, the dean of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee made clear he thought there was no reason for this country to take any step to aid the European democracies. “What they (the democracies) are contending for is the realization of their imperialistic scheme and not the destruction of Nazism,” he said. Prelude to Neutrality Debate. Borah made no direct reference to the impending controversy over neutrality legislation in the Senate, but his address was accepted as a prelude to the general debate expected to come next week when the Foreign Relations Committee considers changes in the law. An

LONDON, March 25.--(P)— Gold shipments to the United States during Europe's latest war scare have topped those which went across the Atlantic during the September Czecho-Slovak crisis. The flow which started in the last few days totaled £28,000,000 ($144,000,000) today compared to £28,000,000 ($143,000,000) in September.

Victoria, B. C., March 25—-(Canadian Press) -- Eight persons drowned and a number of families were made homeless today by flood waters in the Peace River district, a report to British Columbia police headquarters said. The report came from the provincial police detachment at Pouce Coupe. Police there said a woman telephoned the word to them just before communication lines went out. The East Pine River had broken over its banks and flooded the countryside, she reported. The eight drowned were members of a family named Warren.

LONDON: March 25 (AP)—Britain’s attempt to build a new ring of steel around expanding Germany waited today on Poland and It waited on Poland to decide where to seek to bolster her threatened security and on Premier Mussolini to show how much he still counts on the Rome-Berlin axis to give him belated rewards. Growing impatience meanwhile was manifest in political quarters at the government's delay in bringing out a vigorous new collective security policy to replace Prime Minister Chamberlain's discarded appeasement program. Critics of the government blamed the delay in constituting the proposed anti-aggression front on its apparent unwillingness to take these steps: 1. Give definite military commitments to Eastern European countries to gain adherents for a “stop Hitler” bloc. 2. Impose some form of conscription immediately to show Britain’s resolve. Continued on Page 2, Column 7

LONDON, March 5—(CINS)— A serious tug-of-war developed tonight between a pro-Italian and a pro-Russian faction within the British cabinet on the eve of an important speech by Premier Benito Mussolini in which he is expected to demand the cession of French Somaliland to Fascist Italy. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, it was learned, has been told secretly through former French Premier Pierre Laval and other intermediaries that a British-French-Italian Mediterranean pact, modeled on the Locarno treaty, is possible provided that Britain and France do not line up with Soviet Russia. The information supplied by Laval, one of the most ardent advocates of an understanding with Mussolini, has caused a split in the British cabinet, it was understood. The group eager to follow Laval’s advice and to make a deal whereby Mussolini would join in some sort of Mediterranean agreement was said to be h

VICTORIA, B. C., March 25. (U.P) — A brief radio message to provincial police headquarters from isolated northeastern British Columbia today said eight or more persons drowned when ice broke in the Murray River near the Alberta boundary. One body was recovered. It was feared the death toll might be higher than the first report, but it was believed no further word would be received until communications could be restored Monday.

Madrid.-(4?) Indications of an imminent peace in the 32-month-old Spanish civil war were seen today in preparations for early resumption of railway traffic into and out of Madrid. (Reports reaching Hendaye, France, said negotiations for surrender of republican Spain were so far advanced that nationalist troops might march into Madrid today or tomorrow.) Repairs were being made on wrecked rail lines. Observers believed this indicated that nationalist negotiators had arranged with Madrid’s national defense council to have the railroads ready to bring foodstuffs into the city quickly after peace was signed.

1939-12-05.text: LONDON—AP—King George VI has arrived in France on a visit to British troops, it was announced today. The King landed in France this afternoon from a British destroyer.

London, England, Dec. 5—(P)— Torpedoing of the London steamer Horsted, 1,670 tons, was reported today after 13 survivors and the bodies of three crewmen were landed. Five of the crew were reported missing after the sinking in the North Sea. The Horsted, a coal ship, was en route to a northeastern port to pick up a cargo when a submarine attacked her off the eastern coast yesterday, it was said. A British warship picked up the survivors and the three bodies.

London, Dec. 4 (4).—The 10,086-ton steamship Doric Star was reported sunk in the South Atlantic today by the German pocket battleship Admiral Scheer. The Admiralty announced the Blue Star Line vessel, believed used in carrying meat from South America, had been attacked by a German raider. "As no further information has been received it is presumed she has been sunk." Unofficial information was to the effect she had been sunk in the South Atlantic, and that the raiding warship was the 10,000-ton Admiral Scheer. The British fleet has been hunting the Admiral Scheer and her sister pocket battleship the Deutschland, which are known to have been roving the seas in search of British and French shipping since the early days of the war. The Admiral Scheer was first reported in South Atlantic waters when she sank the British freighter Clement off Bahia, Brazil, Oct. 2. Survivors later identified

United Press Star Correspondence LONDON, Dec. 5 (U.P)—Great Britain and France started a new trade war against Germany today as their war fleets imposed effective at midnight last night a blockade of German goods destined to neutral nations throughout the world. — British and French financial powers started the new drive—to knock Germany out of markets still accessible to her. They planned to break the Nazi economic structure by buying goods of countries neighboring Germany at prices Germany could not pay, and supplying goods to those countries at prices lower than Germany could offer. France started the drive by sending a fleet of tankers to seek cargoes of Rumanian oil which Germany desperately needs. It was reported that the ships already had left for the Black Sea. The cost of the drive to Britain alone will be, it was estimated unofficially, upwards of $300,000,000 a year. Both Brit

LONDON Dec. 5—(AP)—Sources close to the government indicated today that Prime Minister Chamberlain would accede to demands of labor and liberal leaders by designating one day next week for secret parliamentary discussion of one subject—war supplies. Although parliament met secretly to discuss various subjects during the World War, the government has hesitated this time for fear of engendering false reports. Meanwhile, Britain lost valuable food supplies when the German "pocket battleship" Admiral Scheer sank the 10,086-ton refrigerator ship Dorie Star in the south Atlantic with a cargo of meats from New Zealand and Australia.

London, Dec. 4—(F)—An authoritative source said today that Britain had devised a “very satisfactory” new secret weapon to combat German magnetic mines. Announcement that fishermen volunteers on trawlers minesweepers were using a new method closely guarded by the navy came as the allied blockade of German shipping was extended to include the seizure of German exports even though carried in neutral ships. Neutral experts commented that it was feasible to drag metal nets between two wooden trawlers to detonate the mines harmlessly. (Berlin sources said they believed Germany would lay a belt of magnetic mines around the British Isles and the region would be declared a danger zone in retaliation for the exports blockade.)

Lisbon, Dec. 5. ()—Joseph P. Kennedy, United States ambassador to London, departed for New York this morning on a trans-Atlantic Clipper. [The London embassy announced November 23 Kennedy had been called home by the state department for consultation, the nature of which it did not disclose.]

London, Dec. 5 (Pi) - Another British vessel, the 10,086-ton steamer Dorie Star, was chalked up as a victim of the wide-ranging German sea raider, the Admiral Scheer. A British Admiralty announcement yesterday said the Dorie Star presumably went to the bottom after being "attacked by a German raider" in the South Atlantic. Unofficial information was that her attacker was the 10,000-ton packet battleship Admiral Scheer. This was the first report of the German sea raider since November 16 when some survivors of the British tanker Africa Shell, sunk in the Indian Ocean off the East Coast of Africa, identified the enemy ship as the Admiral Scheer. The Blue Star liner Dorie Star had a crew of seventy and accommodations for six passengers. No reports on the state of the Dorie Star's crew were available here, and it was not known whether she carried passengers. In addition, the Admiralty report

1939-11-04.text: LONDON. (UP). Bodies of four German seamen were washed ashore on the Kent county coast and caused belief that a German submarine had been sunk. A submarine, wrecked, was found recently on the Goodwin sands in the vicinity but the bodies found Saturday had not been in the sea long and it was believed they were from another one. Each of the bodies bore an identity disc with a foreign name. Naval authorities said the men probably died while attempting to escape from a sunken u-boat. Each body wore an escape apparatus, showing that they had been aboard a submarine.

Paris, Nov. 4,—(4)—Great Britain and France, grasping at the chance offered by the United States’ lifting of the embargo, conferred today on a joint plan for purchases of war materials overseas. Following the arrival Thursday of Winston Churchill, first lord of the British admiralty, authorized sources disclosed that the French and British governments were studying such questions as payments, shipment and distribution between them of American arms. Warplanes such as the Curtiss Hawk, which the French regard as one of the most flexible fighting ships on the western front, were understood to be the American product in which the Allies were most interested. Berlin, Nov. 3 (4)—Nazi Germany appeared resigned tonight to the prospect that lifting of the United States army embargo would open a vast arsenal to Great Britain and France. “We do not underestimate the importance of this development,” an authoritative spokesman said, “but of course it is a matter with which Germany had calculated, and as far as possible discounted. There was little evidence of irritation in official quarters over lifting the embargo. One spokesman, reflecting opinion in high quarters, said he found satisfaction in the evidence that there was considerable opposition within the United States to removing the arms ban. “The close preliminary vote in the House of Representatives indicates about 30 men in that body could have retained the embargo,” this spokesman added. “This is a close decision—surprising in view of the tremendous push to sway American opinion and that the

LONDON, (UP) — New warnings were issued to British shipping in the Atlantic and the Caribbean Sea to beware of German sea raiders. The warnings were the result of a growing admiralty conviction that it was the powerful German pocket battleship Admiral Scheer which sank the British merchantman off the Brazilian coast, and that the ship was now at large in the south Atlantic. It was forecast that the Admiral Scheer might now proceed to Caribbean ports and that possibly other raiders had been prepared to commence operations there. Reports that the German liner Columbus had left its port of refuge at Vera Cruz caused speculation whether the German admiralty had ordered it, and perhaps other ships, to proceed to designated ports, get guns, and take the seas as raiders.

PARIS (UP) — France figured out the implications of the United States arms embargo repeal act and estimated that, aside from the war materials involved, it had released 500,000 French and British men for the armies. It takes 7,000 man-hours to build the fuselage of a fighting airplane and 30,000 hours to build a big bombing plane, it was said. French enthusiasm was increased by the fact that the American planes already in France have proved their worth. French experts say that, though the German Messerschmidts are faster, the American planes are more easily maneuvered and have not lost a single air combat, at times French have been outnumbered by one. The embargo vote in congress was called the biggest international development since Russia, while negotiating with the Allies, concluded an agreement with Germany. It was understood that the French and British governments would study togeth

PARIS, Nov. 3.—(AP)—Winston Churchill, British first lord of the admiralty, held a series of surprise conferences with high French naval officials today regarding the war at sea while reports from the western front told of increased activity by German land troops. The British naval chieftain talked for two hours with Premier Daladier, conferred twice with Cesar Campinchi, French naval minister, and lunched with Rear Admiral Jean Darlan, supreme commander of French naval forces. After talking with the British official, Daladier called a conference of his economic advisers. Churchill arrived yesterday but his presence was not disclosed until today. Military dispatches meanwhile told of a sudden burst of German troop activity south of Zweibruecken, accompanied by a series of protective barrages. The Nazi big guns opened up with heavy fire on French front lines in this shift of operations to

LONDON, Nov. 4 (UP) - The 1342-ton Norwegian steamer Sig and the 11,108-ton Danish steamer Canada were reported today to have been sunk by explosions. Fifteen survivors of the Sig were landed at a port on England's northeast coast. Three of the crew were missing.

NEW YORK, Nov. 4 (P)— United States shipping to Great Britain and France halted abruptly today in accordance with the revised neutrality act. The United States Lines, biggest American shipper to the allied countries, cancelled the sailings of three loaded ships—the President Roosevelt, Washington and American Farmer, which were to have sailed yesterday, and prepared to withdraw its other eight ships now abroad or at sea. - The plans of other lines operating to neutral European ports was in doubt until President Roosevelt defines the war zones from which American ships are barred.

1939-06-22.text: SOUTHAMPTON, England, June 22 (#)—King George and Queen Elizabeth returned to British shores today from their glittering North American tour amid the cheers of thousands of proud subjects. Their trans-Atlantic liner, the Empress of Britain, tied up at her pier at 2:30 p.m. (7:39 a.m. C.S.T.). Beneath a drab and misty sky the king and queen gazed from the bridge of the Empress on a brilliant panorama of color beneath—waving flags and the pennants of smaller craft in the harbor and flower-bedecked welcoming arches. Their two children, 13-year-old Princess Elizabeth and eight-year-old Margaret Rose, who had joined their parents at sea a few hours earlier, were on the bridge tugging with excitement at their father's arm. Cheers and sirens made a terrific din as the king and queen waved again and again. Queen Mother Mary, walking apparently without any stiffness from her automobile accident o

SHANGHAI, June 22 (#)—United States and British naval authorities were said today to have rejected flatly a Japanese demand for removal of British and American destroyers and citizens from the South China port of Swatow. Reliable sources reported Admiral Harry E. Yarnell, commander-in-chief of the United States Asiatic fleet, refused to order the destroyer Pillsbury and 40 Americans to leave Swatow, which Japanese occupied yesterday. British authorities said they had refused a Japanese demand to remove the British destroyer Thanet and the 80 British subjects living in the city. The new Japanese friction with foreign powers came as other sore spots showed fresh irritation. The American, British and other foreign consulates at Amoy joined in a protest to Japanese against diversion of foodstuffs from the Amoy international settlement on Kulangsu island which Japanese blockaded June 15. The United States destroyer Pillsbury and the British destroyer Thanet refused to leave Swatow harbor. Soon they were joined by the U.S. destroyer John D. Pope and the British destroyer H-51 (believed to be the scout.) The situation in ports all along the China coast was considered extremely grave, with the Japanese demanding domination and the foreign nations defending their rights vigorously. Southampton, England, June 22 (UP)—King George and Queen Elizabeth returned today from their visit to Canada and the United States to receive a welcome home which rivaled the wild acclaim which greeted them in the New World. The Empress of Britain, steaming slowly up the Solent, was greeted by shrill blasts from a hundred ships. Pleasure and excursion boats swarmed around the Great White liner. Nine royal air force planes dipped in salute dives over the ship before it docked. Crowds Cheer Rulers Bands blared patriotic songs and crowds along the shore cheered. Rain and fog had slowed up the liner’s progress and prevented a planned naval demonstration but the weather cleared as the liner docked. Princesses Elizabeth and Margaret Rose arrived with their parents, having been taken out to sea on a destroyer for an affectionate reunion. The king, queen and the princesses were on the bridge as

Tientsin. (AP) The sudden appearance of British bluejackets today halted Japanese examination of cargo being discharged by British lighters while blockaded. British further were heartened by a message of sympathy and hope from the London government and the ending of the milk shortage. These developments occurred on the ninth day of the Japanese blockade of the British and French concessions. A Japanese military patrol withdrew at the sight of the bluejackets after the soldiers had begun inspecting the cargo being discharged at the British bund. The message from London, from Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax to Consul General E. G. Jamieson, expressed the government's sympathy to the blockaded British for the difficulties and indignities they are being made to suffer. The British consulate general disclosed a new series of incidents in which it charged Japanese gendarmes forced Britons to un

MOSCOW, June 22—(4)—The Soviet Russian government again has received coldly security pact proposals painstakingly formulated by London and Paris. A Soviet communique issued after British Ambassador William Seeds, French Ambassador Paul Emile Naggiar and William Strang, special British envoy, visited foreign Commission Vyacheslav Molotov ironically observed that the newest British-French proposals not only fell short of the mark but were not even new. The impression grew Strang’s mission to Moscow had failed. This, however, was not necessarily taken to mean the long-standing negotiations to bring Russia into the French-British front had collapsed entirely. The latest British-French proposals sought to meet by compromise Soviet insistence the Baltic states of Finland, Estonia and Latvia be given direct, triple guarantees of assistance against attack whether they want them or not.

TIENTSIN, June 22—(Thursday)—(AP)—Britain’s Tientsin garrison was reinforced and the inflow of food increased today as the Japanese army took stronger measures to enforce its blockade of the British and French concessions. British authorities took measures to prevent any incident that might aggravate the situation. With both sides refusing to yield, the blockade seemed to have developed into a test of patience. (Secretary of State Cordell Hull said in Washington that John K. Caldwell, United States consul-general at Tientsin, had handed the Japanese a protest from the American Chamber of Commerce there against blockade restrictions and inconvenience to American business activities.) Britons still were willing to negotiate lifting of the blockade. (Continued on Page 2)

SWATOW, June 22—(Thursday)—The Japanese naval commander, following occupation of this Chinese port, today ordered all foreign warships, including the United States destroyer Pillsbury, and the British destroyer Thanet, to leave the harbor by 1 p. m. (midnight, E.S.T., Wednesday) The United States and British ships were on duty protecting 40 American and 80 British residents during yesterday's occupation by Japanese military and naval forces of this city, one of the last seaports on the South China coast that had been left in Chinese hands. What the Pillsbury and Thanet commanders would do in response to the Japanese order was not disclosed immediately. The Japanese naval force here consisted of two aircraft carriers, five destroyers, two troop transports and five armed trawlers. One thousand persons were killed and many more wounded in yesterday’s attack by 800 Japanese who marched sudde

1939-04-16.text: By The Associated Press London, April 15.—(#)—Both Britain and France tonight grasped President Roosevelt's plea for at least 10 years of peace as an opening for a non-aggression pact, while the leaders of Germany and Italy were silent. But Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini, to whom the president addressed his appeal, were believed to be in frequent telephonic communication on a reply they may make jointly. The president’s intervention was a “Saturday surprise” far different from those that Europe has grown accustomed to receive from Hitler since his rise to power six years ago. Prime Minister Chamberlain hailed it as ‘statesmanlike initiative.’ A British government statement which he authorized called it ‘a real opportunity of averting the catastrophe which overhangs Europe.’ France quickly and unreservedly accepted the American telegram as a proposal for a 10-year no-aggression pact.
