SIDNEY, Neb., July 8.—(14)—The gins of a special officer who had received his badge an hour earlier, and a Plainsland police chief cut down one bank bandit suspect and sent his partner racing from town with a hostage in a gun battle at Sidney's main business intersection. Tonight ranchers, hastily organized into informal posses, state police, federal agents and other officers searched the plains for a trace of the second man, suspected of having joined earlier with the dead man in the $5000 to $10,000 robbery of the Fort Morgan, Colo., Farmers State bank. The suspect killed was struck in the head by a bullet fired by Special Officer Vizina, garage employee, who had been sworn in by Police Chief S. H. (*) — Lord Halifax, British Foreign Secretary, declared Thursday that the time had passed when the independence of European nations could be destroyed by the actions of one state. He said it was clear now that any further attempt at aggression would “meet with wide and resolute resistance.” The Foreign Secretary spoke in a foreign affairs debate in the House of Lords. German Attitude Hit At the same time, Prime Minister Chamberlain told the House of Commons the recent attitude of Germany on the colonial question was placing further obstacles in the way of a possible step toward adjustment of that problem. Washington, June 8.— (4) — The labor department today ordered the release of Sean Russell, self-styled “head man” of the outlawed Irish republican army, who was taken into custody at Detroit while the British king and queen were across the border in nearby Canadian territory. Officials said the department’s immigration service had telegraphed the release order to Detroit, They said the service had approved bond posted for the Irishman’s release pending a hearing on deportation proceedings Saturday at Detroit. Some members of the house of representatives had threatened to boycott congress’ reception of their majesties unless Russell were released. They appealed to President Roosevelt yesterday to intervene, and early today Representative Sweeney, democrat, Ohio, told reporters they were awaiting word from the chief executive.

NIAGARA FALLS, N. Y., June 7.—For the first time in history, a reigning British monarch set foot upon United States soil tonight when King George and Queen Elizabeth arrived here and were greeted with democratic informality by Secretary of State Hull. Just 19 minutes after the royal train crossed the unfortified border from Canada at 9:39 p.m. E.S.T., it sped southward again toward Washington, where President Roosevelt and his official family will receive the king and queen tomorrow at the beginning of a four-day state visit. Station Guarded. Armed guards were mounted around the railroad station tonight as the Tennessee-born secretary of state, host for the government on this historic occasion, stepped forward to greet the nation’s royal guests. Secretary Hull extended a welcome shorn of the ceremony which had attended the progress of the couple through more than 600 miles of a Canadian

WASHINGTON, June 7.—(4)—A king and queen are coming to town tomorrow and Washington is ready to make them welcome with the dazzling grandeur of official pageantry and the loud, friendly acclaim of countless plain folks who can’t forget their story-book days. For George VI of Great Britain and his queen, Elizabeth, President Roosevelt, and many another, dropped everything—to see to it that their 36-hour stay is one of unbroken enjoyment. Meanwhile hundreds of thousands of Washingtonians and visitors from all points of the compass were ready to strive for a glimpse of the royal visitors. Six months of worried planning at an end, officials looked at the alternate union jacks and American flags for police protection, and announced, with a suggestion still of hopefulness, that everything was ready. And “everything” includes a lot. The royal couple is scheduled to arrive at eleven o'clock, acc

Washington, June 8.—(A’)--Today’s programme for the first visit ever made to Washington by a British ruler: 11 a. m. (EST)—President and Mrs. Roosevelt meet king and queen at Union station. Procession to the White House with full military honors follows. 12 noon—Procession arrives at White House and the royal visitors meet the diplomatic corps in the East room. 1 p. m.—Private luncheon at the White House. 2.30 p.m.—King and queen go sightseeing to Lincoln Memorial, National Cathedral, Rock Creek Park and other points. 4 p. m.—British embassy garden party starts. 4.45 p. m.—The royal couple leave the White House for the embassy, arriving there 15 minutes later. 8 p. m.—State dinner at the White House.

The vote against holding a late afternoon and night session on the administration-approved bill repealing the arms embargo and making other neutrality law changes was 12 to 11, members said: Rep. Tinkham (R-Mass.) who delights to twist the British lion’s tail, was overjoyed. Washington, June 8. (4?)—William R. Russell, tentmaker, was the most distressed man in the capital today. Because the British ambassador liked the tents Russell made to protect guests at the royal garden party in event of rain, Russell received one of the coveted cards of admittance to the party. But he lost it. Frantically, he urged police to watch out for card No. 68. At least one congressman did not hunt for a gray topper to wear to the royal garden party. Representative Cartwright (D-Okla.) said he intended to wear a cowboy hat. As the mercury started climbing steadily, the favorite quip of Washingtonians was about the hot water bottles of the queen’s ladies in waiting. Some undisclosed person abroad advised Mrs. Roosevelt to provide hot water at the White House so that the bottles could be filled. WASHINGTON, (UP).—Rep. Martin L. Sweeney, (Dem. Ohio), announced on the house floor today that he sent this telegram to King George VI: “Because London dispatches have characterized your visit to the United States as an official one, I believe that I am acting within the boundaries of propriety in demanding as a representative of the people in the congress of the United States that you publicly state what your government intends to do about payment of war debt due this nation in the sum of approximately five and one half billion dollars.”

1939-05-18.text: LONDON, May 18. (4)—The war office announced that five British army gunners were killed and six injured today in an explosion at Woolwich arsenal, the second there in two days. The explosion occurred during the loading of an anti-aircraft gun. Two persons were killed and two injured yesterday in an explosion in the Woolwich cartridge shop.

Quebec, May 17 (4).—Canada acclaimed King George and Queen Elizabeth today upon their arrival for an unprecedented royal tour and then pledged a new loyalty and homage to the British throne and its occupants. Hour after hour, from early morning until nearly midnight, the King and Queen went through the ritual of state functions, presentations, audiences, addresses and drives through the city. They slept tonight behind the thick walls of the old citadel on “the rock” which is now the summer home of Canada’s governor-general, Lord Tweedsmuir. Queen Wins Favor Through it all was the informality of the western world, evident despite the military and official character of the events. This appeared to be enhanced by the charm and the manner of Queen Elizabeth, who won feminine favor, by the modest demeanor of the King and by what Canadian Prime Minister W. L. LONDON, May 15—(AP)—The British government in a historic pronouncement of policy tonight outlined plans for turning strife-torn Palestine over to its Arab majority, stinging Jewish leaders into bitter declarations of opposition. A white paper setting forth Britain’s “final plan” indicated Britain was disclaiming five years hence any “obligation to facilitate the further development of the Jewish national home (in Palestine) by immigration.” Unable to obtain agreement between Arabs and Jews, Britain announced its own solution for the political future of the Holy Land, racked by virtual civil war for three years. Jews will be limited to one-third of the population of the country which Britain wrested from Turkey during the World War and now controls under League of Nations mandate. (Continued on page 2)

Two thorny problems confronted British diplomacy today—the Arab-Jewish strife in Palestine and the issue with Japan over foreign rights in China—as German attention to Bulgaria's territorial aspirations sharpened the rivalry of great powers in the Balkans. Following a night of disorder in which 25 persons were injured in the all-Jewish city of Tel Aviv, angry Jews estimated by their leaders at 175,000 demonstrated throughout the Holy Land against the British government’s decision to establish an independent Palestine under Arab control. Police said order was restored in Tel Aviv after fighting which police broke up with a baton charge. British reports said Jewish youths set fire to government district offices and then prevented fire apparatus from going to the scene. |. SHANGHAI, May 18. (A. P.)—All but a few marines of those landed last week by the Japanese at Kulangsu, International Settlement at Amoy, were reported today to have been withdrawn to nearby warships after a combined show of military and diplomatic force by the United States, Britain and France. One hundred twenty-six American, British and French bluejackets and marines patrolled Kulangsu—a force equal to the original strength of the Japanese landing party. The United States cruiser Marblehead and the destroyer Bulmer, the French cruiser Emile Bertin and four British warships were standing by Kulangsu, which is an island in the Amoy harbor. JERUSALEM, May 17—(AP)— British police fired into a crowd of Jewish youths demonstrating at Tel Aviv tonight against the newly announced British policy governing Palestine, and wounded several of them. The crowd of more than 5,000 Jewish youths, after taking an oath to fight for Jewish independence, had marched to the British government district offices. Raising a Zionist flag, they forced their way into the building, broke up the furniture and set fire to desks and tables, police said. Police fired first into the air, then as the disorders continued, shot into the crowds. The demonstrations at Tel Aviv, which is an all-Jewish city, were continuing as midnight approached. The government immigration department headquarters was badly damaged by an explosion later. No casualties resulted. LONDON, May 18.—The president of the extremist New Zion organization claiming to represent 750,000 Jews issued a formal statement today threatening armed resistance against Great Britain to assure that Palestine will “remain open to millions forced out of the European hell.” While Jewish organizations in many lands protested the British program on the grounds it would kill their hopes of a homeland in Palestine, the extremist organization leaders declared that Jewish groups throughout the world would combat the government’s policy.

1939-11-05.text: London, Nov. 3.—Italy will desert the Rome-Berlin axis completely and even possibly join Great Britain and France in the war against Germany if Reichsführer Adolf Hitler makes any aggressive moves against the Balkan countries. This was the belief expressed in high neutral diplomatic circles in London today, which at the same time acknowledged Premier Mussolini’s genuine and sincere desire to stay out of the conflict. Mussolini was represented in these circles as “pushed to the limit of his patience” by the Russo-German rapprochement—Communism still being poison to the Italians—and is actively building fences around Yugoslavia, Hungary, Greece and Turkey in an encirclement movement of his own to preserve the Mediterranean as Italy’s sphere of influence. WASHINGTON. (UP). President Roosevelt, invoking terms of the new neutrality act, late Saturday decreed as combat zones the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, the English Channel, all waters surrounding the British Isles and Ireland and the Bay of Biscay. All American shipping is barred from these specific areas, and Mr. Roosevelt said in a statement simultaneously with the proclamation that in addition the neutrality statute itself barred U. S. ships from ports in France, Great Britain and Germany. Mr. Roosevelt signed the combat zone proclamation, his third decree relative to the neutrality act of the day, at 3 p.m., two hours and 56 minutes after he signed the law itself. The new act opens United States markets to cash-and-carry trade by the European belligerents and there are no restrictions on export of arms and munitions. Recognizes State of War. BERGEN, Norway, NOV. 4 (INS).—The liberated American crew of the famous freighter City of Flint tonight made the ship ready for a dash into the open sea, to begin probably early next week. Calmly facing the possibility of becoming the center of naval fighting between Germany and Britain, the 41 American seamen under Capt. Joseph A. Fainard repainted the vessel's name and U.S. flags on her side, preparatory to the departure either for some British port or directly for home over the far northern route. Report Discounted An Oslo radio report that the 4963-ton ship already had sailed for “the west coast of Scotland” was officially discounted late tonight. It was stated the U.S. minister to Norway, Mrs. J. Borden Harriman, is expected at Bergen from Oslo on Monday to interview Fainard and members of the American crew. WASHINGTON, — President Roosevelt signs new neutrality bill, proclaims neutrality of United States anew; orders American shipping barred from combat area designated north of Spain, around British Isles, and Baltic ports. OSLO. — Question of how to get home or whether to try for British port confronts freighter City of Flint, anchored in Bergen harbor; Germany protests freeing of ship and internment. LONDON—Reports say Norwegian steamer Sig and Danish freighter Canada sunk by explosives; treasury and naval experts plan to swell British war chest to buy American supplies. BERLIN—Germans protest Norway's intervention in City of Flint case; authorities insist Reich has sufficient food to make British blockade ineffective; officials concentrate on internal affairs. MOSCOW — Finnish delegation confers with Soviet leaders for second time in two days; negotiations to continue.

LONDON, Nov. 4—(INS)— The Rome radio station tonight broadcast a report that 80,000 Red Army troops have suddenly been moved up to the Finnish frontier, a Reuter’s dispatch stated. The radio was quoted as announcing the Soviet concentrations were along that part of the border that is located on the Isthmus of Karelia, an area figuring prominently in the present Moscow negotiations between Russia and Finland.

LONDON, Nov. 4,—U.F)—Leslie Howard, motion picture actor, became a blackout casualty tonight when his automobile collided with another near Kingston. Howard, who was driving to his home at Dorking, was severely injured about the head and chest. Several of his teeth were knocked out. The actor was treated at a hospital and went home.

MOSCOW—A “hopeful” turn in negotiations with Finland was reported last night after the Soviet Union had been described as prepared to resort to extreme measures if necessary to enforce its demands for territory on Hangoe peninsula and at Petsamo port. A conference at the Kremlin in which Josef Stalin participated was understood to have kept negotiations going and to have left Finnish quarters more optimistic, although they still declined to comment. Moscow, Nov. 4.—(AP)—For the second time in two days the Finnish delegation was closeted with Soviet leaders at the Kremlin tonight but official silence cloaked the result of the vital negotiations. A breakdown in the conference which had been feared in some foreign quarters apparently had been averted since it was learned reliably that the negotiations would be continued. Indicative of the importance of the talks was the presence of Joseph Stalin at today’s one hour session. Foreign observers searched vainly for any information which might indicate whether the Russian army might march into Finland as it did into Poland or whether Finland would relent and accede to Russian demands for concessions in Finland and Finnish waters.
